passages: Works with Apple Home and Matter certification have allowed a wide array of third-party accessories to connect with Apple’s smart home ecosystem for years, and Apple Home Collection takes it even further.
Apple worked closely with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric to create an integrated Apple Home experience across the new product lineup.
1 These new accessories are simple to set up starting with one tap with iPhone, and everything is managed through the Apple Home app — no separate app or account required.
Each accessory is encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home, so only users and the people they choose can access their home data.
Products also automatically update their network credentials if a customer changes their home Wi-Fi, eliminating a common smart home frustration.

“Schneider Home’s new Smart Thermostat is a true collaboration with Apple to give customers a seamless way to help manage their home’s energy use, effortlessly blending efficiency with everyday comfort and simplicity.”
LG’s lineup of four cameras gives users a private and intelligent way to monitor their homes when using a home hub like Apple HomeView, HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K.
Camera footage is securely processed locally on the customer’s own Apple Home hub or in Private Cloud Compute and, for users with iCloud+, stored encrypted in iCloud for 10 days.
“LG Electronics has spent decades developing technologies and products designed around the way people live,” said Kihyun Jung, LG Electronics’ executive vice president.
Controls in the Home app allow the doorbell and lock to work together as a front-door system — letting users see who’s there and unlock the door in a single view or by asking Siri.
The new smart lock is Matter compatible and supports Aliro, working entirely locally so core access functions continue even without an internet connection.
LG’s Smart Deadbolt Lock brings a new level of convenience to home access.

Apple worked closely with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric to create an integrated Apple Home experience across the new product lineup. These new Apple Home Collection products feature a clean, minimal aesthetic and premium materials, with every detail considered, from how they mount and adjust to how they look and feel alongside Apple products throughout the home. Every camera captures up to 2.5K resolution video and recognizes people, familiar faces, pets, vehicles, and packages, with video history securely stored in users’ supported iCloud+ plan, so there’s no separate camera subscription. 2 Each camera works with iCloud+, giving users access to 10 days’ worth of event video history. On eligible iCloud+ plans, Apple Intelligence adds automatic video descriptions that summarize what’s happening in a clip, along with the ability to search footage using natural, descriptive language. 3 Built-in storage keeps cameras recording even when Wi-Fi goes down, and improvements to the way footage is captured and stored ensure detected moments aren’t missed during a network outage. Users can view live footage and camera activity at any time right from the Home app on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple TV 4K, or HomeView — with quick live snapshots that give an at-a-glance view without needing to open a full livestream. LG’s Smart Deadbolt Lock brings a new level of convenience to home access. Using Ultra Wideband technology, the lock can tell how close a user is and when they’re approaching the door. As a user with a home key on a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch walks up, the door unlocks automatically, with no tapping required. For flexibility, users can also tap to unlock with an iPhone or Apple Watch, use an integrated PIN pad, or rely on a hidden backup key slot. The lock can sense if the door has been opened, closed, or tampered with, alerting users if it’s open even while locked. Guest access can also be shared directly through the Home app, making it simple to grant a dog walker, house sitter, or visiting family member their own way in. Controls in the Home app allow the doorbell and lock to work together as a front-door system — letting users see who’s there and unlock the door in a single view or by asking Siri. When a visitor rings the bell, a chime sounds through HomeView, HomePod, or HomePod mini, and a notification appears on the user’s Apple devices, like iPhone or iPad. From wherever they are, users can see who’s at the door, speak to the visitor, and unlock the door for them. The new smart lock is Matter compatible and supports Aliro, working entirely locally so core access functions continue even without an internet connection. Two new Smart Thermostats are available — one from LG Electronics and one from Schneider Electric — so users can choose the product that best fits their home’s broader energy ecosystem. Using on-device intelligence from iPhone, Adaptive Temperature in the Home app automatically adjusts the thermostats based on whether someone is at home, winding down at night, or away, ensuring the home is always at the right temperature without any manual scheduling. In the contiguous U.S., Clean Energy Guidance can shift heating and cooling to cleaner, lower-cost periods for users with a compatible utility plan, and the Home app displays usage insights over time, including peak and off-peak rate information. Products also automatically update their network credentials if a customer changes their home Wi-Fi, eliminating a common smart home frustration. The accessories are designed to work together, and users can control every product with Siri. A single “Good Morning” scene can simultaneously adjust the thermostat, tilt an indoor camera down while a user is getting ready, and start music on HomePod. Using on-device intelligence from iPhone or Apple Watch, users can set up Apple Home to recognize key moments throughout the day: As the last user leaves for work, the thermostat adjusts for an empty home, the door locks, and cameras begin monitoring again. Before they arrive home, the thermostat begins adjusting the temperature, and the front door unlocks automatically as they approach. Privacy is foundational to Apple Home. Camera footage and personal data in the Home app are stored end-to-end encrypted and never accessible to LG Electronics, Schneider Electric, or Apple. Camera footage is securely processed locally on the customer’s own Apple Home hub or in Private Cloud Compute and, for users with iCloud+, stored encrypted in iCloud for 10 days. Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView.

She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home.

A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad.

extraction.body: I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView. I think it’s the shared, always-available household interface that my family might finally use. Is Apple’s first smart display my dream smart home dashboard? But is it the right product for Apple Home at this moment? A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad. HomeView gives you another interface for those things, but crucially one that is always powered, always unlocked, and always in the same spot in your home, making it easy to walk up to and interact with. I’ve tried using an iPad to control my smart home, run my family’s calendar, and be a shared device for controlling music. An iPad can’t be a hub for your Apple Home; HomeView can. An iPad famously isn’t a good multiuser device, and controlling home devices on one requires it staying logged in to your personal iCloud account; HomeView offers Apple’s first crack at easy multiuser switching. Apple designed HomeView as a communal device that sits in a fixed place in the home. Not having a battery or detachable screen is a feature for me, because devices that do inevitably wander off and die under a couch cushion. One feature I’m most interested in is HomeView’s role as a home video phone. Do you know how many times I’ve tried to call my daughter when I’m not home, and her phone is dead or on silent? Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView. Smart displays and speakers from Amazon and Google already help with this to some extent, but Apple’s version comes without ads (see the Echo Show) and may have a longer lifespan (RIP Pixel Tablet). She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said. "As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in a natural way.”" - Lilian Rincon, Apple Siri AI made this possible because it’s “much more capable,” said Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI at Apple. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.” Siri AI in the home has another big advantage over the competition: It doesn’t say too much. “A lot of these assistants out there are always asking questions because they want more information,” she said. I had hoped that, along with new hardware, Apple would bring more functionality and deeper Apple Intelligence integration to Apple Home to make the smart home smarter. Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing. As always, the smart home’s most important goal is to come up with an easier way to turn on the lights. HomeView’s simplicity may put off hardcore home automation enthusiasts, but I’d argue it’s perfect for their long-suffering spouses. I’ve tried every version of physical smart home control interface in my home, and you know who hasn’t used any of them? Because my family all have iPhones, and because the HomeView will always be there and will feel familiar, I can see them actually using it. That means I could set up a full Home Assistant instance and run a detailed dashboard on a tablet in my office, then feed the scenes and devices into Apple Home so my husband and daughter can just tap to control them on a HomeView in the kitchen. HomeView may not be the smart home computer I want Apple to make, but it is the smart home device Apple needed to make. It doesn’t have to run all the iPad apps or try to be a bigger version of my iPhone; it just needs to make the smart home accessible to everyone in the house. If Apple has pulled that off, it could be more valuable than any new smart home feature I’ve been wishing for.

sources.title: The best feature of Apple’s HomeView might be its simplicity
passages: An iPad famously isn’t a good multiuser device, and controlling home devices on one requires it staying logged in to your personal iCloud account; HomeView offers Apple’s first crack at easy multiuser switching.
Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView.
I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView.
Apple designed HomeView as a communal device that sits in a fixed place in the home.
HomeView may not be the smart home computer I want Apple to make, but it is the smart home device Apple needed to make.
She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home.

A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad.
An iPad can’t be a hub for your Apple Home; HomeView can.
One feature I’m most interested in is HomeView’s role as a home video phone.
Smart displays and speakers from Amazon and Google already help with this to some extent, but Apple’s version comes without ads (see the Echo Show) and may have a longer lifespan (RIP Pixel Tablet).
HomeView’s simplicity may put off hardcore home automation enthusiasts, but I’d argue it’s perfect for their long-suffering spouses.

That means I could set up a full Home Assistant instance and run a detailed dashboard on a tablet in my office, then feed the scenes and devices into Apple Home so my husband and daughter can just tap to control them on a HomeView in the kitchen.

HomeView gives you another interface for those things, but crucially one that is always powered, always unlocked, and always in the same spot in your home, making it easy to walk up to and interact with.
Because my family all have iPhones, and because the HomeView will always be there and will feel familiar, I can see them actually using it.
If Apple has pulled that off, it could be more valuable than any new smart home feature I’ve been wishing for.

extraction.body: I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView. I think it’s the shared, always-available household interface that my family might finally use. Is Apple’s first smart display my dream smart home dashboard? But is it the right product for Apple Home at this moment? A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad. HomeView gives you another interface for those things, but crucially one that is always powered, always unlocked, and always in the same spot in your home, making it easy to walk up to and interact with. I’ve tried using an iPad to control my smart home, run my family’s calendar, and be a shared device for controlling music. An iPad can’t be a hub for your Apple Home; HomeView can. An iPad famously isn’t a good multiuser device, and controlling home devices on one requires it staying logged in to your personal iCloud account; HomeView offers Apple’s first crack at easy multiuser switching. Apple designed HomeView as a communal device that sits in a fixed place in the home. Not having a battery or detachable screen is a feature for me, because devices that do inevitably wander off and die under a couch cushion. One feature I’m most interested in is HomeView’s role as a home video phone. Do you know how many times I’ve tried to call my daughter when I’m not home, and her phone is dead or on silent? Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView. Smart displays and speakers from Amazon and Google already help with this to some extent, but Apple’s version comes without ads (see the Echo Show) and may have a longer lifespan (RIP Pixel Tablet). She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said. "As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in a natural way.”" - Lilian Rincon, Apple Siri AI made this possible because it’s “much more capable,” said Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI at Apple. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.” Siri AI in the home has another big advantage over the competition: It doesn’t say too much. “A lot of these assistants out there are always asking questions because they want more information,” she said. I had hoped that, along with new hardware, Apple would bring more functionality and deeper Apple Intelligence integration to Apple Home to make the smart home smarter. Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing. As always, the smart home’s most important goal is to come up with an easier way to turn on the lights. HomeView’s simplicity may put off hardcore home automation enthusiasts, but I’d argue it’s perfect for their long-suffering spouses. I’ve tried every version of physical smart home control interface in my home, and you know who hasn’t used any of them? Because my family all have iPhones, and because the HomeView will always be there and will feel familiar, I can see them actually using it. That means I could set up a full Home Assistant instance and run a detailed dashboard on a tablet in my office, then feed the scenes and devices into Apple Home so my husband and daughter can just tap to control them on a HomeView in the kitchen. HomeView may not be the smart home computer I want Apple to make, but it is the smart home device Apple needed to make. It doesn’t have to run all the iPad apps or try to be a bigger version of my iPhone; it just needs to make the smart home accessible to everyone in the house. If Apple has pulled that off, it could be more valuable than any new smart home feature I’ve been wishing for.

After years of phone-centric habits, Apple’s new smart home device points toward a more ambient future, according to hands-on first impressions from The Wall Street Journal ’s Nicole Nguyen .
HomeView is a $299, seven-inch square tablet and speaker designed for smart home control, hands-free FaceTime calls, and interaction with the recently revamped Siri AI assistant.
As Nguyen notes in her reporting from New York City, the device’s clearest advantage over long-standing rivals from Amazon and Google is its deep access to data already on a user’s iPhone.⁠
In Nasdaq trading today, shares of Apple Inc. rose to hit a new all-time closing high.

IF Apple had a brain they would have offered a AppleTV with a built in FaceTime Camera and the software that is in the Continuity Camera feature that is very cool, but totally kludgy and nobody uses it because he have to futz with the phone and make a few false move every time you try to make a call.
The best feature of this software is how the iPhone camera can capture the whole room or find the speaker and zoom in on them gracefully.
It would be brilliant and it would immediately make FaceTime calls HomeFaceTime calls that display on your big screen instead of the tiny phone screen.
But they are too stupid to do this killer feature.
Homeview serves no real purpose and Apple TV is vastly overpriced by double for nothing more than a streaming box.
An OpenAI employee who left the ChatGPT maker for Apple sent more than 100 files about an unreleased product to a personal account…
Apple positions the product as both central to the home and private for each user, with pre-orders open now and availability starting November 13th in select countries.
Early looks from the event emphasize the design’s adaptability for counters, nightstands, or walls, along with room-filling audio and glanceable interfaces that shift based on distance.
The square screen sits on a compact speaker base (with a wall-mount option also available), letting it function as a shared household hub that can personalize the experience.

It uses facial recognition to identify up to six people and surface individual content — such as messages, calendars, or widgets — while keeping personal information protected behind that recognition (or an iPhone unlock as a fallback).

Siri AI, powered by Apple Intelligence, can draw on personal context from linked Apple devices for more helpful responses about schedules, messages, music, or home controls, while supporting features like recipe guidance, timers, and multi-camera live views for compatible HomeKit or Matter devices.

HomeView is a $299, seven-inch square tablet and speaker designed for smart home control, hands-free FaceTime calls, and interaction with the recently revamped Siri AI assistant. As Nguyen notes in her reporting from New York City, the device’s clearest advantage over long-standing rivals from Amazon and Google is its deep access to data already on a user’s iPhone.⁠

The square screen sits on a compact speaker base (with a wall-mount option also available), letting it function as a shared household hub that can personalize the experience. It uses facial recognition to identify up to six people and surface individual content — such as messages, calendars, or widgets — while keeping personal information protected behind that recognition (or an iPhone unlock as a fallback). Siri AI, powered by Apple Intelligence, can draw on personal context from linked Apple devices for more helpful responses about schedules, messages, music, or home controls, while supporting features like recipe guidance, timers, and multi-camera live views for compatible HomeKit or Matter devices.

Apple positions the product as both central to the home and private for each user, with pre-orders open now and availability starting November 13th in select countries. Early looks from the event emphasize the design’s adaptability for counters, nightstands, or walls, along with room-filling audio and glanceable interfaces that shift based on distance.

Nguyen’s hands-on account highlights the integration edge while the broader product introduction underscores privacy and ecosystem strengths. At the same time, the closed nature of the setup — requiring Apple devices for full personalization and limited third-party flexibility — means households outside the ecosystem may see fewer benefits than those already invested in iPhones and related gear. Whether the combination of Siri AI, facial recognition, and iPhone data access is enough to draw users away from established smart displays remains to be seen once the devices reach real homes. ‎ MacDailyNews Take: At just $299, it’s relatively inexpensive to just take a flier on one and see how much use it gets in our household.

sources.title: Michael Saylor Warns MSTR Investors to Prepare for ‘Difficult Years’ — Hold for at Least 4 Years - Yahoo Finance
passages: The post Michael Saylor Warns MSTR Investors to Prepare for 'Difficult Years' — Hold for at Least 4 Years appeared first on ccn.com .
Speaking during a live investor Q&A on Monday, Saylor said investors should approach both Bitcoin and Strategy shares with a time horizon of at least four years.
Holding for seven to 10 years would be preferable, he added.
For MSTR investors, Saylor's message was straightforward: short-term volatility , and potentially several painful years, should be expected rather than treated as an exception.
His preferred four-year horizon broadly corresponds with Bitcoin's halving cycle and allows investors to look beyond temporary bull and bear markets.
Despite weakness in MSTR , Saylor said repurchasing common shares is not currently a priority.
Strategy currently holds approximately $4.8 billion in cash, according to Saylor, providing several possible uses for its reserve.
Strategy is not prioritizing MSTR share buybacks and would likely consider them only if the stock traded at a substantial discount to net asset value.
Strategy's business model gives MSTR shareholders leveraged exposure to Bitcoin through a capital structure that includes common stock, convertible debt and several classes of preferred shares.
That structure can amplify gains during Bitcoin rallies, but it can also increase pressure on the stock when Bitcoin declines or MSTR trades closer to the value of the company's underlying assets.
The company could deploy that capital to purchase additional Bitcoin , buy back MSTR or preferred shares, or repay outstanding debt.
Saylor acknowledged that current market conditions have made Strategy's position "tougher," cautioning that shareholders may need to tolerate prolonged periods of volatility.
Saylor also stressed that Strategy must retain the ability to sell Bitcoin , despite building its identity around continuous accumulation.

Although Saylor remains firmly bullish on the cryptocurrency's long-term prospects, Strategy needs sufficient flexibility to meet debt obligations, fund dividends and respond to changing market conditions.

His remarks come as Strategy 's Bitcoin acquisition program has remained paused for seven weeks, while the company has instead directed recently raised capital toward preferred-stock repurchases, dividend payments and its dollar reserve.
The decision suggests Strategy is currently emphasizing liquidity and management of its broader capital structure rather than immediately expanding its Bitcoin holdings.

relevantPassages.text: So, could the same phenomenon happen again as soon as Bitcoin goes into bull market mode?
Strategy CEO Phong Le is convinced that it could happen; all that's required is for investors to patiently wait out the current crypto bear market.
Some other company will certainly find a way to outperform Bitcoin.
Most likely, it will be a winner from the new Digital Asset Market Clarity Act.
That's not to say other companies won't outperform Bitcoin during the next Bitcoin bull market.
Just two years ago, Strategy (NASDAQ: MSTR) was the talk of the stock market.

The problem, quite frankly, is that Strategy has already ruffled the feathers of quite a few crypto investors with its new approach of "Sometimes sell your Bitcoin." Remember, this was the company that famously told investors, "Never sell your Bitcoin."
At one point, Strategy Executive Chairman Michael Saylor told investors they might want to think about mortgaging their homes or selling other financial assets to buy more Bitcoin.
Unfortunately, the biggest winner is unlikely to be Strategy or any of the other Bitcoin treasury companies.
Strategy has started to sell some of its Bitcoin, prompting a loud outcry in the crypto community.

sources.title: Michael Saylor’s $200T Strategy: U.S. Bitcoin Strategic Reserve & Immortality - CoinDesk
passages: This is the future imagined by bitcoin evangelist Michael Saylor, the executive chairman of Strategy (MSTR).
Saylor pioneered the bitcoin corporate treasury – turning his flailing software firm into a Nasdaq-listed $85 billion leveraged bitcoin powerhouse.
President Trump’s executive order to establish a U.S.
Bitcoin Strategic Reserve represents a milestone in realizing bitcoin’s manifest destiny.
At one point, the U.S. held about 400,000 bitcoins, but sold half of it for proceeds of $366 million.
Trump’s crypto czar David Sacks lamented that the cost to American taxpayers for selling this bitcoin prematurely is $17 billion at current market value.
Michael Saylor was born in Lincoln, Nebraska.
He grew up on Air Force bases across the Midwest, as well as in Japan and New Zealand.
An Air Force scholarship sent Saylor to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he obtained dual degrees in aeronautics, astronautics, and the history of science.
A literal rocket scientist, Saylor’s systems mindset attracted him to bitcoin’s “thermodynamically sound” design.
President Donald Trump, bitcoin has maintained a 26% gain, peaking at a $2.1 trillion market cap, and touching a January all time high of $109,000.
He’s bet everything on BTC price going up forever, and the sovereignty, sound money, freedom, and property rights idealized by the community.
He has gone from encouraging corporations to adopt bitcoin treasuries to advising nation states on establishing strategic bitcoin reserves.
MicroStrategy, rebranded and doing business as “Strategy,” proved to be an incredibly desirable stock for institutional investors wanting exposure to the volatile ups and downs of bitcoin.
In December, Strategy was admitted to the Nasdaq 100 .
It is now eyeing membership to the S&P 500, which would spark an additional tidal wave of public market access.
Last week, Strategy brought its bitcoin holdings above 500,000 tokens by purchasing an additional 6,911 bitcoins for $584 million , using proceeds from the sale of MSTR common stock.
They further announced their new STRF perpetual offering raised $711 million to buy more bitcoin, when its initial goal was to raise $500 million.
Strategy has also eliminated any collateralized debt and therefore liquidation risk of the company’s bitcoin assets.
Ultimately, the dates to watch are when Strategy’s loans to bondholders become due.

If Strategy fails to incentivize bondholders to convert their bonds to MSTR stock or persuade them to await principal repayment the following year, these bondholders might demand Strategy buy back their $1.8 billion loan in cash.
If the markets are still hungry for bitcoin exposure, it will be easier to raise capital and pay back investors.
If there is a market downturn, and the Wall Street spigot runs dry, Strategy may have to consider selling its bitcoin or default.
CoinDesk recently sat down with Saylor, Bitcoin’s ultimate maximalist, for a two-hour interview to break down his vision for global bitcoin domination.
“[Bitcoin] became an opportunity,” said Saylor.
Satoshi Namamoto, the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin, created “digital gold” that Saylor discovered while under lockdown during the Covid-19 pandemic.

By constantly weighing market conditions, tweaking yield parameters and conversion factors, Strategy has engineered "intelligent leverage” designed to lure demand and ensure each successive series of securities amp each other up in an endless positive feedback loop.
Before he dies, Saylor may burn bitcoin rather than give his assets away.

“ It creates more pressure to drive up the price of bitcoin, which drives up the price of MSTR, which drives up the leverage of MSTR, which drives up the value of the options, which drives up the demand for the equity, which drives up the demand and the value of the [convertible bonds], which drives up the price of and the demand for the preferred [shares].”
The instruments that are constructed don't have Bitcoin pledged as collateral,” said Saylor.
“ If I believe that and I burn those keys, then I have made everybody in the [Bitcoin] network that much richer and more powerful forever,” said Saylor.
The executive order directs the Secretary of the Treasury to never sell the United States’ bitcoin and to develop budget neutral ways to acquire more bitcoin.

coreStoryFacts.text: The post Michael Saylor Warns MSTR Investors to Prepare for 'Difficult Years' — Hold for at Least 4 Years appeared first on ccn.com .
Speaking during a live investor Q&A on Monday, Saylor said investors should approach both Bitcoin and Strategy shares with a time horizon of at least four years.
Holding for seven to 10 years would be preferable, he added.
For MSTR investors, Saylor's message was straightforward: short-term volatility , and potentially several painful years, should be expected rather than treated as an exception.
His preferred four-year horizon broadly corresponds with Bitcoin's halving cycle and allows investors to look beyond temporary bull and bear markets.
Despite weakness in MSTR , Saylor said repurchasing common shares is not currently a priority.
Strategy currently holds approximately $4.8 billion in cash, according to Saylor, providing several possible uses for its reserve.
Strategy is not prioritizing MSTR share buybacks and would likely consider them only if the stock traded at a substantial discount to net asset value.
Strategy's business model gives MSTR shareholders leveraged exposure to Bitcoin through a capital structure that includes common stock, convertible debt and several classes of preferred shares.
That structure can amplify gains during Bitcoin rallies, but it can also increase pressure on the stock when Bitcoin declines or MSTR trades closer to the value of the company's underlying assets.
The company could deploy that capital to purchase additional Bitcoin , buy back MSTR or preferred shares, or repay outstanding debt.
Saylor acknowledged that current market conditions have made Strategy's position "tougher," cautioning that shareholders may need to tolerate prolonged periods of volatility.

His remarks come as Strategy 's Bitcoin acquisition program has remained paused for seven weeks, while the company has instead directed recently raised capital toward preferred-stock repurchases, dividend payments and its dollar reserve.
So, could the same phenomenon happen again as soon as Bitcoin goes into bull market mode?
Strategy CEO Phong Le is convinced that it could happen; all that's required is for investors to patiently wait out the current crypto bear market.
Some other company will certainly find a way to outperform Bitcoin.
Most likely, it will be a winner from the new Digital Asset Market Clarity Act.
That's not to say other companies won't outperform Bitcoin during the next Bitcoin bull market.
Just two years ago, Strategy (NASDAQ: MSTR) was the talk of the stock market.

The problem, quite frankly, is that Strategy has already ruffled the feathers of quite a few crypto investors with its new approach of "Sometimes sell your Bitcoin." Remember, this was the company that famously told investors, "Never sell your Bitcoin."
At one point, Strategy Executive Chairman Michael Saylor told investors they might want to think about mortgaging their homes or selling other financial assets to buy more Bitcoin.
Unfortunately, the biggest winner is unlikely to be Strategy or any of the other Bitcoin treasury companies.
Strategy has started to sell some of its Bitcoin, prompting a loud outcry in the crypto community.
MicroStrategy (NASDAQ:MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction), now operating as Strategy, trades at $159.93 after a brutal 56.72% 12-month drawdown that mirrors bitcoin’s slide to $75,870.71.

Holding for seven to 10 years would be preferable, he added.

"If you're a short-term price predictor, you're a trader," Saylor said. "I don't really have much useful wisdom for you."

His remarks come as Strategy 's Bitcoin acquisition program has remained paused for seven weeks, while the company has instead directed recently raised capital toward preferred-stock repurchases, dividend payments and its dollar reserve.
Saylor acknowledged that current market conditions have made Strategy's position "tougher," cautioning that shareholders may need to tolerate prolonged periods of volatility.
"We might have to actually ride through some number of months or a year or two to get to the point where things start to work to the benefit of the equity," he said.

Strategy has raised $11.68 billion year to date, roughly half via common equity and half via the STRC preferred, which carries an $8.5 billion notional value, $375 million in daily trading volume, and 3% volatility achieved during a bitcoin bear market.

At $116.56, Strategy Inc. looks bearish on a risk-reward basis.

Three converging headwinds drive further downside. The at-the-market equity machine funding bitcoin purchases mechanically dilutes common holders, and Saylor confirmed the company will keep pressing it. The risk-reward at $116 is unattractive. A retreat to $65 would mark MSTR back to where it traded five years ago, before the leverage stack ballooned.

The thesis breaks if Warsh signals a fast cutting cycle, bitcoin reclaims $90,000, and the STRC dilution pace cools. Until those three line up, the risk-reward looks unfavorable. Investors tracking the name should monitor Warsh’s policy signals and watch for a retest near $65.

passages: This is the future imagined by bitcoin evangelist Michael Saylor, the executive chairman of Strategy (MSTR).
Saylor pioneered the bitcoin corporate treasury – turning his flailing software firm into a Nasdaq-listed $85 billion leveraged bitcoin powerhouse.
President Trump’s executive order to establish a U.S.
Bitcoin Strategic Reserve represents a milestone in realizing bitcoin’s manifest destiny.
At one point, the U.S. held about 400,000 bitcoins, but sold half of it for proceeds of $366 million.
Trump’s crypto czar David Sacks lamented that the cost to American taxpayers for selling this bitcoin prematurely is $17 billion at current market value.
Michael Saylor was born in Lincoln, Nebraska.
He grew up on Air Force bases across the Midwest, as well as in Japan and New Zealand.
An Air Force scholarship sent Saylor to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he obtained dual degrees in aeronautics, astronautics, and the history of science.
A literal rocket scientist, Saylor’s systems mindset attracted him to bitcoin’s “thermodynamically sound” design.
President Donald Trump, bitcoin has maintained a 26% gain, peaking at a $2.1 trillion market cap, and touching a January all time high of $109,000.
He’s bet everything on BTC price going up forever, and the sovereignty, sound money, freedom, and property rights idealized by the community.
He has gone from encouraging corporations to adopt bitcoin treasuries to advising nation states on establishing strategic bitcoin reserves.
MicroStrategy, rebranded and doing business as “Strategy,” proved to be an incredibly desirable stock for institutional investors wanting exposure to the volatile ups and downs of bitcoin.
In December, Strategy was admitted to the Nasdaq 100 .
It is now eyeing membership to the S&P 500, which would spark an additional tidal wave of public market access.
Last week, Strategy brought its bitcoin holdings above 500,000 tokens by purchasing an additional 6,911 bitcoins for $584 million , using proceeds from the sale of MSTR common stock.
They further announced their new STRF perpetual offering raised $711 million to buy more bitcoin, when its initial goal was to raise $500 million.
Strategy has also eliminated any collateralized debt and therefore liquidation risk of the company’s bitcoin assets.
Ultimately, the dates to watch are when Strategy’s loans to bondholders become due.

If Strategy fails to incentivize bondholders to convert their bonds to MSTR stock or persuade them to await principal repayment the following year, these bondholders might demand Strategy buy back their $1.8 billion loan in cash.
If the markets are still hungry for bitcoin exposure, it will be easier to raise capital and pay back investors.
If there is a market downturn, and the Wall Street spigot runs dry, Strategy may have to consider selling its bitcoin or default.
CoinDesk recently sat down with Saylor, Bitcoin’s ultimate maximalist, for a two-hour interview to break down his vision for global bitcoin domination.
“[Bitcoin] became an opportunity,” said Saylor.
Satoshi Namamoto, the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin, created “digital gold” that Saylor discovered while under lockdown during the Covid-19 pandemic.

By constantly weighing market conditions, tweaking yield parameters and conversion factors, Strategy has engineered "intelligent leverage” designed to lure demand and ensure each successive series of securities amp each other up in an endless positive feedback loop.
Before he dies, Saylor may burn bitcoin rather than give his assets away.

“ It creates more pressure to drive up the price of bitcoin, which drives up the price of MSTR, which drives up the leverage of MSTR, which drives up the value of the options, which drives up the demand for the equity, which drives up the demand and the value of the [convertible bonds], which drives up the price of and the demand for the preferred [shares].”
The instruments that are constructed don't have Bitcoin pledged as collateral,” said Saylor.
“ If I believe that and I burn those keys, then I have made everybody in the [Bitcoin] network that much richer and more powerful forever,” said Saylor.
The executive order directs the Secretary of the Treasury to never sell the United States’ bitcoin and to develop budget neutral ways to acquire more bitcoin.

Bitcoin has reached “escape velocity,” he said, because once the U.S. government begins to acquire it aggressively, the U.S. will become a beneficiary and force every country to adopt bitcoin as the global capital. President Trump’s executive order to establish a U.S. Bitcoin Strategic Reserve represents a milestone in realizing bitcoin’s manifest destiny. Eventually, they settled with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for about $11 million . At MicroStrategy, Saylor invented over 48 patents and deployed dozens of business ideas. Some succeeded, most of them failed. Saylor said the irony is that his greatest success was somebody else’s idea. Satoshi Namamoto, the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin, created “digital gold” that Saylor discovered while under lockdown during the Covid-19 pandemic. He grabbed onto it out of desperation, preferring MicroStrategy to have a quick death over a slow one if it failed. In July 2020, MicroStrategy began to steadily and continuously purchase bitcoin through cash flows, equity and debt , basically any way it could. It climbed the highs of the 2021 bull run and withstood the impairment charges of the 2022 crypto winter. By 2024, the Bitcoin corporate treasury strategy emerged battle tested. It survived its first crypto market cycle and the Trump bump catapulted MicroStrategy from a $1 billion to a $100 billion market cap company. “[Bitcoin] became an opportunity,” said Saylor. “Then it became a strategy, and then all of a sudden in the past 12 months, we realized it was a really good business.” MicroStrategy, rebranded and doing business as “Strategy,” proved to be an incredibly desirable stock for institutional investors wanting exposure to the volatile ups and downs of bitcoin. In December, Strategy was admitted to the Nasdaq 100 . It is now eyeing membership to the S&P 500, which would spark an additional tidal wave of public market access. To generate positive momentum, Strategy is laser-focused on raising capital to buy more bitcoin through a plethora of fixed income securities, creating a casino of financial products for traders addicted to bitcoin’s volatility. By constantly weighing market conditions, tweaking yield parameters and conversion factors, Strategy has engineered "intelligent leverage” designed to lure demand and ensure each successive series of securities amp each other up in an endless positive feedback loop. “If you were to say, it sounds like financial engineering, it absolutely is financial engineering,” said Saylor. “ It creates more pressure to drive up the price of bitcoin, which drives up the price of MSTR, which drives up the leverage of MSTR, which drives up the value of the options, which drives up the demand for the equity, which drives up the demand and the value of the [convertible bonds], which drives up the price of and the demand for the preferred [shares].” Last week, Strategy brought its bitcoin holdings above 500,000 tokens by purchasing an additional 6,911 bitcoins for $584 million , using proceeds from the sale of MSTR common stock. Strategy has also eliminated any collateralized debt and therefore liquidation risk of the company’s bitcoin assets. ”We've built an indestructible balance sheet. Bitcoin could trade down 99%. There’s no margin call coming. The instruments that are constructed don't have Bitcoin pledged as collateral,” said Saylor. Ultimately, the dates to watch are when Strategy’s loans to bondholders become due. The first “put date” is September 16, 2027. If Strategy fails to incentivize bondholders to convert their bonds to MSTR stock or persuade them to await principal repayment the following year, these bondholders might demand Strategy buy back their $1.8 billion loan in cash. If the markets are still hungry for bitcoin exposure, it will be easier to raise capital and pay back investors. If there is a market downturn, and the Wall Street spigot runs dry, Strategy may have to consider selling its bitcoin or default. But Saylor said Strategy, like the U.S. government, will “never sell” its bitcoin. He’s bet everything on BTC price going up forever, and the sovereignty, sound money, freedom, and property rights idealized by the community. Before he dies, Saylor may burn bitcoin rather than give his assets away. That would be a “more ethically proper, ethically sound form of charity” and would bestow “economic immortality.” “ If I believe that and I burn those keys, then I have made everybody in the [Bitcoin] network that much richer and more powerful forever,” said Saylor. “We're all in it together, from now to eternity. So yeah, that's my legacy.”

Giants like Spotify, Amazon, Apple and YouTube duke it out at the top, while plenty of other players like Qobuz, Tidal, Deezer try their best to stand out from the pack. Somewhat surprisingly, though, a new player emerged in September. Coda Music used the recent backlash around Spotify co-founder Daniel Ek as a way to differentiate itself from the number one streamer, calling out Ek's controversial funding of defense technology firm Helsing earlier in the year. (Spotify's refusal to stop airing ICE recruitment ads certainly hasn't helped the platform, either.) Today, the fledgling service is announcing a new feature that feels designed to answer another of the recent Spotify controversies: AI slop music flooding the platform . In response, Coda Music is launching AI identification tools with the purpose of finding and labeling songs that weren't composed by actual humans. There are a few prongs to Coda's approach. For starters, any artist added to Coda will be reviewed for AI origins, and their profile will be labeled "AI Artist" so that listeners know what they're getting into. Coda is also letting users flag profiles of artists if they suspect the music is AI-generated; the company will then review them and label them if necessary. Finally, there's a toggle in settings that just lets you turn off AI artists entirely. Obviously, how useful this setting is will depend on how good Coda gets at labeling AI-created music as such, but I can definitely see the appeal in just flipping that to "off" and avoiding as much slop as possible. Besides its stance on AI and the assurance that the company does not "invest in war," there are a few other differentiators about Coda Music. The company says that it currently paying the "highest per-stream rate" in the industry — while at the same time, it acknowledges that no one is paying enough to artists. "The real problem isn't how much is paid per stream, it's that streaming alone doesn't pay enough," the company's website says . "And minor improvements to a fundamentally flawed per stream model will not help." To that end, the company also lets users pick an "independent or qualifying artist" who gets $1 of their monthly subscription fee. Sure, it's only a dollar, but it's the kind of thing that sweetens the pot at least a little bit for musicians. And Coda has good reason to want to make itself visible to users and artists alike. The last major differentiator for Coda is the company's ambitions to turn its app into a social, music-sharing feed where you get recommendations from humans rather than algorithms. To that end, users can share anything from the app in their feed, and it also allows you to share external links and photos as well (go ahead and post your blurry images from that NIN concert!). The app's home page prominently features fan-made playlists and recommended users to follow in addition to the usual suggestions based on what you're listening to already. And there's a social tab where you can see posts from people you follow; share songs, artists or albums; and see posts from artists you follow. That last part is key, as Coda wants artists interacting and sharing as well as just end users. It reminds me a little bit of the Fan Groups feature that Amazon Music just announced — and as with that feature, the problem facing Coda is getting people to start contributing to a new network rather than just posting things on whatever app they're already using. Fortunately, music nerds love a community, so it'll be interesting to see if this takes off at all. The company doesn't have a web interface yet, but says it is coming soon. If ducking AI-generated tunes is something that catches your attention, Coda currently costs $11 a month, or $17 per month for a family plan with up to four listeners.

sources.title: YouTube Music launches new labels as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms
passages: The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches.
For instance, Apple Music has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year.
Spotify also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.
Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily.
According to its help page , partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI.
YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions.
Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization.

YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool Dream Track , which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.
Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.
TIDAL also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution.
Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app.
Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.

passages: YouTube is rolling out "Made with AI" labels for music tracks that were altered or fully generated using artificial intelligence, marking a significant step in content transparency as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms.

coreStoryFacts.text: As for the new features for reporting and filtering out AI music, Coda says they're available as of today in its iOS and Android apps.
The company doesn't have a web interface yet, but says it is coming soon.
If ducking AI-generated tunes is something that catches your attention, Coda currently costs $11 a month, or $17 per month for a family plan with up to four listeners.
For starters, any artist added to Coda will be reviewed for AI origins, and their profile will be labeled "AI Artist" so that listeners know what they're getting into.
Coda is also letting users flag profiles of artists if they suspect the music is AI-generated; the company will then review them and label them if necessary.
Today, the fledgling service is announcing a new feature that feels designed to answer another of the recent Spotify controversies: AI slop music flooding the platform .
In response, Coda Music is launching AI identification tools with the purpose of finding and labeling songs that weren't composed by actual humans.
Besides its stance on AI and the assurance that the company does not "invest in war," there are a few other differentiators about Coda Music.
At this point, the streaming music landscape feels pretty well settled.

Obviously, how useful this setting is will depend on how good Coda gets at labeling AI-created music as such, but I can definitely see the appeal in just flipping that to "off" and avoiding as much slop as possible.
The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches.
For instance, Apple Music has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year.
Spotify also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.
Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily.
According to its help page , partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI.
YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions.
Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization.

YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool Dream Track , which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.
Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.
TIDAL also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution.
Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app.
Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.
The divergent strategies reflect an industry still deciding how to handle synthetic content.
Some platforms treat AI music as spam to filter.

sources.title: YouTube Music launches new labels as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms
passages: The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches.
For instance, Apple Music has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year.
Spotify also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.
Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily.
According to its help page , partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI.
YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions.
Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization.

YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool Dream Track , which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.
Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.
TIDAL also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution.
Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app.
Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.

sources.title: YouTube Adds 'Made with AI' Labels to Music Tracks
passages: YouTube is rolling out "Made with AI" labels for music tracks that were altered or fully generated using artificial intelligence, marking a significant step in content transparency as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms.
The labeling system, launching today in YouTube Music, combines creator disclosure requirements with automated detection signals to identify AI-generated compositions and vocals.

How users respond to AI labels - whether they embrace, ignore, or actively avoid labeled content - will signal the market's appetite for synthetic music and influence how other platforms approach similar transparency measures.
YouTube's AI music labeling system represents a pragmatic approach to content transparency in the age of generative AI.
YouTube just changed the game for AI transparency in music streaming.
This move positions YouTube ahead of competitors like Spotify and Apple Music, which haven't implemented systematic AI disclosure for music content.
AI-assisted music production tools are becoming increasingly sophisticated, and the line between "AI-generated" and "AI-assisted" will likely continue blurring as technology advances.
The music streaming landscape is watching closely.

The labeling system, launching today in YouTube Music, combines creator disclosure requirements with automated detection signals to identify AI-generated compositions and vocals. YouTube just changed the game for AI transparency in music streaming. The platform is rolling out "Made with AI" labels starting today, targeting tracks that were "altered or fully generated" using artificial intelligence - a move that could reshape how millions of listeners discover and consume AI-created content. Music partners uploading content must disclose when they've used generative AI tools, particularly for creating compositions and vocals. But YouTube isn't just relying on the honor system - the company says it may use "other signals" to identify AI-generated content when creators fail to disclose. YouTube's approach mirrors its existing video AI labeling system, focusing specifically on generative models that create core musical elements rather than basic AI-assisted mixing or mastering tools that have been industry standard for years. AI-generated music has exploded across streaming platforms, with tools like Suno and Udio enabling anyone to create full songs from text prompts. Google's recent push into AI detection technology through SynthID has given the company sophisticated tools to identify synthetic content across media formats. For the music industry, this represents both transparency and potential disruption. Record labels have been grappling with AI-generated tracks flooding playlists, sometimes mimicking popular artists or gaming recommendation algorithms. YouTube's labeling system provides a middle ground - allowing AI content while ensuring listeners know what they're hearing. Unlike heavy-handed content removal, YouTube is betting on informed choice. Users will see clear "Made with AI" indicators in the app interface, similar to how the platform already handles sponsored content or age-restricted material. This move positions YouTube ahead of competitors like Spotify and Apple Music, which haven't implemented systematic AI disclosure for music content. The labeling system could become an industry standard, especially as regulatory pressure mounts around AI transparency. The company has been balancing AI innovation with responsible deployment across its ecosystem, from enterprise workflow automation to consumer applications. For creators, the system creates new considerations around disclosure and audience expectations. AI-assisted music production tools are becoming increasingly sophisticated, and the line between "AI-generated" and "AI-assisted" will likely continue blurring as technology advances. The music streaming landscape is watching closely. passages: The Chinese social media company is in advanced talks with MediaTek over the supply of bespoke chips that will help run ByteDance data centers, people familiar with the matter said.

The Taiwanese firm will provide an unspecified amount of Application Specific Integrated Circuits, or chips customized to work with a clients' platform, the people said, asking to remain anonymous to talk about a private arrangement.

passages: Trump's repeated claims of brokering an end to the recent war with Pakistan have irked Delhi, while a much-hyped trade deal appears to have stalled, reportedly over US demands for greater access to India's farm markets.
Donald Trump's America has turned from cheerleader to critic, accusing India of bankrolling Moscow's war chest with discounted oil purchases.
Delhi now faces the sting of Trump's public rebuke and higher tariffs.
But the alternative of aligning with anyone is worse.
India's best choice is the bad choice, which is hedging," Jitendra Nath Misra, a former Indian ambassador and currently a professor at OP Jindal Global University, told the BBC.
But Mr Jacob also cautions that without normalcy with India, China can't leverage "Indian unhappiness" with Trump for its "own larger geopolitical purposes".
As Sumit Ganguly of Stanford University's Hoover Institution points out, US-China rivalry remains "structurally irreconcilable", while Russia has been reduced to Beijing's "junior partner".
Against this backdrop, India's room for manoeuvre becomes clearer.

Mr Ganguly says India is also deepening its relationship with Russia largely because of two reasons: it fears a further closing of ranks between Moscow and Beijing, and due to the souring of ties between Delhi and Washington under Trump.
In a new essay in Foreign Affairs, Ashley Tellis, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, argues that India's flirtation with multipolarity undermines its security.
Russia, he adds, "can be relied upon but only to an extent".
As for Washington, "even though Trump is likely to be in office for another three years or so, the US-India relationship will endure.
Both countries have too much at stake to let it fall apart over Trump's idiosyncrasies."
"Frankly, India's choices are limited," says Mr Ganguly.
"There is no prospect of a rapprochement with China - the rivalry will endure."
"India doesn't appear to have a better choice than to take the blows from the US on the chin and let the storm pass," says Mr Misra.
In the end, strategic patience may be India's only real leverage - the wager that storms pass and partners return.
Yet, Delhi's foreign policy is at an uneasy crossroads.
To be sure, India's global ambitions still outpace its capacities.

Jaishankar's recent visit to Moscow signalled that despite Western sanctions and Russia's deepening dependence on China, Delhi still sees value in keeping the relationship warm - both as an energy lifeline and as a reminder of its foreign policy autonomy.
Since the US, even in relative decline, will "tower over both Asian giants", India should cement a "privileged partnership" with Washington to contain China, he says.
Delhi's refusal to choose, he warns, risks leaving it exposed to a "hostile superpower" on its doorstep.

"This is a time for us to engage America, manage China, cultivate Europe, reassure Russia, bring Japan into play, draw neighbours in, extend the neighbourhood and expand traditional constituencies of support," Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar wrote in his 2020 book The India Way: Strategies for an Uncertain World.

India sits in two camps at once: a pillar of Washington's Indo-Pacific Quad with Japan, the US and Australia, and a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), the China and Russia-led bloc that often runs counter to US interests.
Delhi buys discounted Russian oil even as it courts American investment and technology and prepares to sit at the SCO table in Tianjin next week.
"India may not be fully confident of holding its own by aligning with a great power.
As a civilisational state, India seeks to follow the course of other great powers in history who achieved that status on their own."
Its tradition and interests demand flexibility in a world that is not splitting neatly into two camps but fracturing in more complex ways.
Strategic ambiguity, she argues, is not weakness but autonomy.
Analysts say this balancing act is no accident.
India prizes strategic autonomy and argues that engaging with competing camps gives it leverage rather than exposure.

So, when Modi met with President Donald Trump at the G7 Summit in France last week with a handshake and not an embrace (Opens in new window) , it was as clear a signal as any that the India–US relationship has taken a hit. The roots of the downturn with Washington can be found in New Delhi’s response to the four-day conflict between India and Pakistan in May 2025. While Islamabad was happy to give Trump his “win” by claiming that he brokered the ceasefire between both countries – going as far as nominating him for a Nobel Peace Prize – New Delhi stuck to its guns that the conflict ended without third-party involvement. This was in line with India’s long-standing principle of opposing third-party mediation on the Kashmir issue. This became the “original sin” in the bilateral relationship. It was soon followed by the Trump administration’s imposition of higher tariffs on India, and then secondary sanctions for its purchase of Russian crude. Adding insult to injury is the deepening relationship between Islamabad and Washington, which has been fuelled by Pakistan’s mediation role during the Iran conflict. India’s proclivity to make decisions based on high-handed principles over practical considerations predates the recent downturn in India–US relations. New Delhi has made a string of strategic misjudgements since India’s emergence as an independent nation-state in 1947 – and arguably even before that during the country’s independence struggle rooted in Gandhian principles of non-violence ( Ahimsa ) and truth ( Satyagraha ). India needs a more pragmatic and less preachy foreign policy in a world where values no longer carry the same currency. Shortly after gaining independence, India’s first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru took its conflict with Pakistan to the United Nations, which led to the internationalisation of the Kashmir dispute. Throughout the Cold War, New Delhi propagated non-alignment and third-world solidarity, often to its own detriment. Nowhere was this more apparent than in China–India ties: while Nehru advocated for Communist China to get a permanent seat on the UN Security Council, he downplayed the looming China threat on India’s border, which culminated in the disastrous war of 1962. India was a recipient of aid from both the United States and the Soviet Union, but its non-aligned stance was often a thorn in New Delhi’s engagement with the superpowers. It was only when India faced an existential threat during the 1962 war with China, and the 1971 war with Pakistan, that New Delhi lowered its self-imposed barrier to step up defence cooperation with Washington and Moscow, respectively. Many attribute India’s idealistic foreign policy to Nehru’s leadership. However, this continued well beyond Nehru’s death in 1964. New Delhi’s position on the Israeli–Palestinian conflict is an example, with India’s staunch support for the Palestinian cause undermining New Delhi’s efforts to deepen relations with Israel. New Delhi’s similarly vocal condemnation of the military junta in Myanmar after it suppressed pro-democracy protests in 1988 and dismissed the results of the 1990 election undermined India’s relations with the regime and pushed it into the arms of China. New Delhi now maintains an aversion to third-party mediation on the Kashmir issue. Israel has emerged as a key partner for India, as noted by Modi’s second visit to the country shortly before the start of the Iran conflict. India is also happy to engage military leaders in Myanmar, hosting junta chief Min Aung Hlaing in April. These shifts, however, have often come slowly or in response to a major shock. The recent downturn in India–US relations showed that a streak of idealism has continued into the present day. New Delhi could have mirrored Pakistan by thanking Trump for his role in helping to de-escalate tensions between India and Pakistan in May 2025 but instead held firm on principle. New Delhi did eventually make a course correction by acknowledging Trump’s need for flattery. During their G7 meeting, Modi thanked (Opens in new window) Trump for bringing “new hope for peace and stability” to the Middle East, downplaying that instability was fuelled by the US–Israel attacks on Iran that commenced in February. But the damage is done. Modi’s statement (Opens in new window) during the G7 Summit that the world was suffering from a shortage of trust was squarely aimed at the Trump administration’s actions. The Quad has lost momentum. The announcement by the US Department of War to drop (Opens in new window) “Indo” from its Indo-Pacific Command may be more symbolic (Opens in new window) than substantive but reflects a relative downgrade of India’s position in Washington’s Asia strategy. The relationship is facing several thorns, including delays (Opens in new window) in securing a bilateral trade agreement, the deaths (Opens in new window) of Indian seafarers from US strikes on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and the expiry of a US sanctions waiver (Opens in new window) that gave India a temporary reprieve on its purchase of Russian oil. extraction.body: As India celebrates its 72nd Independence Day this Wednesday, there is a new spring in its steps as it straddles the global firmament. India is no longer the coy diffident power of the past, when it was constantly treading on eggshells for fear of offending this or that power. Today’s India is a self-confident nation able to manage its external relations on its own terms without any ideological baggage. It can stand with China to raise its voice against global protectionism and yet it can stand up to China when its vital interests are targeted, like in Doklam last year. It can proclaim a historic relationship with Russia, but can manage to be candid about Russia’s obsession in viewing its every partnership through the prism of its struggle with the West. If there is one power that sits relatively confident in today’s rapidly evolving global dynamic when all other powers are openly competing with each other, it is India. As India’s economic weight has grown in international relations, its voice and partnerships are much sought after. A pluralist democracy growing rapidly at its own pace with all its inherent contradictions is a story which a world deeply in crisis wants to hear. And Indian policy makers increasingly are not averse to narrating their case. For any nation -- and in particular for a self-proclaimed rising power -- it is crucial that it sets out its own narrative about its place in the global pecking order. For the last two decades, China has managed to do it extremely effectively that after two decades of being a rising power, the world suddenly woke up one day to a China which has seemingly arrived. Indian leadership today is signaling that it too has grown up and has recognized that the need of the hour is to link India domestic development story with the global one. The Modi government has given Indian foreign policy a new dynamism: on this there is no debate. Any honest assessment of this will have to wait for a few years but the approach to reach out to most parts of the world in a regular manner is well-intentioned. African nations, despite our historical ties, have often complained that New Delhi has been episodic in its engagement with the continent. In the last four years, there has been a sustained outreach to our traditional friends. And this is an aspect of Indian foreign policy that we see evolving over the last few years as New Delhi’s engagements with Africa, Latin America, West Asia, and Southeast Asia have gained a new traction. As the world changes around India in ways that at times seems incomprehensible, New Delhi doesn’t really have the luxury of banking on age-old slogans. India needs new partners and new partnerships, it needs a more robust footprint in various parts of the world, and it needs a narrative about what it intends to do with the accretion of its material capabilities. Indian policymakers too are coming to terms with this weight of history. India’s evolving debates about its environmental policy or trade policy or even military presence abroad underscore this reality. The challenge from Pakistan remains as contentious as ever and the growing Chinese footprint in the wider South Asian and Indian Ocean region is challenging India on multiple fronts. After refusing to build capabilities to deter China for decades, China’s rise will remain the single most important issue facing the nation for the foreseeable future. Yet, it is a sign of India’s strategic evolution that today Pakistan problem is widely considered a subset of India’s China problem. India’s horizons are widening and China’s rise has compelled our policymakers to take this challenge seriously. A positive legacy of Modi’s foreign policy over the last four years is a growing interest among the nation’s youth about Indian foreign policy priorities beyond Pakistan. As India rises and overcomes the hesitations of history, a more dynamic conversation on the causes and consequences of India’s rise is the need of the hour. And Modi has indeed pushed foreign policy to the center stage of India’s everyday discourse. Governments will come and go but India’s sustenance of its foreign commitments will ultimately depend on how invested the common Indian is in shaping her nation’s foreign policy profile.

Russia, he adds, "can be relied upon but only to an extent". As for Washington, "even though Trump is likely to be in office for another three years or so, the US-India relationship will endure. Both countries have too much at stake to let it fall apart over Trump's idiosyncrasies."
Others agree: India's best option is simply to absorb the pain.

"India doesn't appear to have a better choice than to take the blows from the US on the chin and let the storm pass," says Mr Misra. In the end, strategic patience may be India's only real leverage - the wager that storms pass and partners return.

Delhi now faces the sting of Trump's public rebuke and higher tariffs.

As Sumit Ganguly of Stanford University's Hoover Institution points out, US-China rivalry remains "structurally irreconcilable", while Russia has been reduced to Beijing's "junior partner".
Against this backdrop, India's room for manoeuvre becomes clearer.

Mr Ganguly says India is also deepening its relationship with Russia largely because of two reasons: it fears a further closing of ranks between Moscow and Beijing, and due to the souring of ties between Delhi and Washington under Trump.
In a new essay in Foreign Affairs, Ashley Tellis, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, argues that India's flirtation with multipolarity undermines its security.

To be sure, India's global ambitions still outpace its capacities.

Delhi's refusal to choose, he warns, risks leaving it exposed to a "hostile superpower" on its doorstep.

India sits in two camps at once: a pillar of Washington's Indo-Pacific Quad with Japan, the US and Australia, and a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), the China and Russia-led bloc that often runs counter to US interests.

"India may not be fully confident of holding its own by aligning with a great power.

Its tradition and interests demand flexibility in a world that is not splitting neatly into two camps but fracturing in more complex ways.
Strategic ambiguity, she argues, is not weakness but autonomy.
Analysts say this balancing act is no accident.
