Standard Chartered has launched direct Bitcoin and Ether trading for eligible wealthy clients in the UAE after securing regulatory approval from VARA. Professional Investor clients can buy and sell cryptocurrencies through their existing bank accounts without using separate wallets or external exchanges. The service was developed with Zodia Markets and uses a closed loop model in which Standard Chartered manages custody and settlement. The launch follows the bank's institutional crypto trading and custody services, with plans to introduce the wealth offering in other markets over time. According to the bank's announcement, the service has received approval from Dubai's Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA) and will initially be available to Professional Investor clients in the UAE. The offering allows customers to trade cryptocurrencies without opening accounts on separate exchanges or setting up personal digital wallets. Standard Chartered will handle custody and settlement within its banking ecosystem. The bank described the launch as its first cryptocurrency trading service for affluent wealth clients globally and the first such offering from an international bank in the UAE. Standard Chartered developed the service through cooperation between its Wealth and Retail Banking and Corporate and Investment Banking divisions, working with Zodia Markets, a digital asset business backed by its venture arm, SC Ventures. The bank plans to introduce the service in other markets over time, although it has not provided a timetable or identified the countries under consideration. Standard Chartered brings crypto trading into wealth accounts Under the new arrangement, eligible customers can purchase and sell Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH) using their existing Standard Chartered banking relationships. The service uses a closed-loop operating model, under which the bank manages transactions, custody and settlement without requiring clients to transfer assets through external wallets. Standard Chartered said the structure was designed to reduce exposure to risks associated with third-party wallets while providing institutional-grade custody and operational safeguards. Zodia Markets is participating in the service alongside the bank's wealth and investment banking businesses, bringing digital asset market capabilities into the trading arrangement. The announcement did not specify minimum investment amounts, trading fees, transaction limits or whether customers would eventually gain access to cryptocurrencies beyond BTC and ETH. Samir Subberwal, Standard Chartered's Global Head of Wealth Solutions, Retail Products, Data & Analytics, said demand for digital assets was becoming part of the bank's wealth management business. "With digital assets moving into mainstream wealth conversations, clients are increasingly looking not only for access, but also for the security, trust and confidence that comes from investing through a regulated and trusted institution," Subberwal said. Before introducing direct cryptocurrency trading, Standard Chartered already allowed eligible wealth clients to access cryptocurrency exchange-traded funds through its cash equities platform. Its existing investment products included structured products and over-the-counter derivatives that provide exposure to cryptocurrency markets. The new service introduces direct BTC and ETH transactions into that range of investment options, with custody and settlement handled by the bank. UAE launch follows Standard Chartered's institutional trading rollout Standard Chartered's latest UAE offering follows a series of cryptocurrency services introduced for institutional customers over the past two years. In September 2026, the bank introduced institutional spot trading for Bitcoin and Ether through its Dubai International Financial Centre branch. As crypto.news previously reported, the institutional service allowed eligible clients to execute deliverable BTC and ETH trades through the bank's existing electronic trading channels and foreign exchange interfaces. Those customers could choose their preferred custodian for settlement, including Standard Chartered's own digital asset custody service. The institutional arrangement differs operationally from the newly announced wealth product, which places trading, custody and settlement within the bank's closed-loop environment. Standard Chartered's UAE institutional trading operations followed its July 2025 launch of spot cryptocurrency trading through its UK branch. The earlier service targeted institutional customers, including corporations, asset managers and professional investors, and supported Bitcoin and Ether transactions through established foreign exchange trading systems. The bank had entered the UAE digital asset custody market in September 2024 after securing authorization from the Dubai Financial Services Authority within the DIFC. Brevan Howard Digital was named as the inaugural customer for that custody platform, which initially supported Bitcoin and Ether. For the new wealth service, Standard Chartered has obtained VARA licensing approval, according to its announcement. Rola Abu Manneh, the bank's Chief Executive Officer for the UAE, Middle East and Pakistan, described the country as a natural location for the launch because of its regulatory environment and approach to digital asset innovation. "The UAE was a natural choice for this launch, given the country's forward-looking approach to innovation, strong regulatory environment and growing leadership in digital assets," she said. Abu Manneh identified the UAE as one of Standard Chartered's four global wealth hubs. Standard Chartered develops crypto custody and stablecoin services Beyond Bitcoin and Ether trading, Standard Chartered has been developing custody services for stablecoins and tokenized financial assets. On October 12, the bank launched RLUSD custody services through its DIFC branch, allowing eligible institutional clients to hold Ripple's dollar-backed stablecoin on the XRP Ledger.

extraction.body: If you are trying to do some online grocery shopping with Giant, Stop & Shop or Food Lion, you may notice that their websites and apps are currently unavailable. Dutch supermarket giant Ahold Delhaize said Tuesday it was working to restore systems it had shut down following what it described as a security issue. The company said its stores — including Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium and Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant in the United States — remained open, but the websites for those brands remained offline. There are published reports of a cybersecurity incident at the company that owns the chains. Each chains' website says they are "working to restore service as quickly as possible," adding that customers can still place delivery orders through Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats. Any unfulfilled web and app orders will be refunded. The chains' pharmacies and fueling stations are also still open. Ahold Delhaize said it had no evidence that customer or employee data had been stolen. This comes as cyberattacks disrupted European supermarket chains, affecting refrigeration systems at hundreds of stores in France and forcing a major grocer to shut down websites serving customers in Europe and the United States. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected. He said there was no risk to France's food supplies but acknowledged that the attack "touches the heart of our food security." "It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said. The French government's cybersecurity agency said Tuesday it was "aware of numerous compromises" involving refrigeration system remote control modules made by Danish company Danfoss as well as U.S.-based Copeland. Danfoss said Monday that most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates, and that it was working with affected customers to limit the damage. "Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware, as well as to operate behind a firewall," the company said. In an August report, U.S. cybersecurity firm Claroty identified vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Copeland XWeb Pro platforms, which are used to manage refrigeration infrastructure in supermarkets, warehouses and other facilities. For example, Claroty said "numerous controllers" using the Danfoss system were directly accessible from the public internet, leaving them wide open for cyberattacks. But it noted that Danfoss and Copeland had since fixed the vulnerabilities. Copeland said Tuesday that a vulnerability had been identified in "a discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers," and that it was working with impacted customers. Christopher Whyte, an associate professor of homeland security and emergency preparedness at Virginia Commonwealth University, said it's "not too difficult" to carry out such an attack. "It looks like almost certainly what happened here was these controls were left open to the broader network being used by the supermarket," Whyte said. Similar attacks on water systems, power infrastructure and other kinds of physical operations have been fairly common for years, often coming from Iran and other state actors, Whyte said. Over the summer, Minnesota and Michigan reported cyberattacks on their states' water systems. Whyte said attacks on refrigerator systems are not unprecedented. Last month, Stars and Stripes reported that three military agencies were investigating refrigeration outages at U.S. military commissaries that occurred within days of each other. The Associated Press left a message Tuesday seeking comment on that case with the U.S. Army's Criminal Investigation Division Cyber Field Office. But Whyte said the scale of the French attack, and the fact that there appeared to be no ransom demand or stealing of information, made this situation unusual. It was unclear Tuesday whether the French cyberattack involved artificial intelligence. But advances in AI have contributed to an increase in cybersecurity incidents, said Varun Chandrasekaran, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Illinois' Grainger College of Engineering. Chandrasekaran said there's also a possibility that the attack happened because of an experiment an AI lab was doing — like what happened with OpenAI's breach of an Australian health department website last month. He said people should absolutely expect an increase in such cyberattacks in the future thanks to AI. But Chandrasekaran said AI could also be useful in preventing such hacks. "Right now it seems like a lot of the defensive countermeasures people have are quite passive," Chandrasekaran said. "What we need is a proactive defender, like another AI model sitting on the defender side that's trying to counter whatever the attacker AI is doing."

extraction.body:
Websites and apps for grocery chains Stop & Shop, Hannaford, and Giant Food were offline Monday and Tuesday after their Dutch parent company experienced a cyber incident. Ahold Delhaize said in a statement Tuesday that it was experiencing a cyberattack within its network and took some systems offline “to help protect them.” The company said stores continued to be open while teams worked to assess and mitigate the security issue. While customers cannot purchase groceries online and have them delivered through Peapod, they could place orders through third-party sites like DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Instacart. Other store operations like refrigeration and sale systems are unaffected, a spokesperson confirmed to the Globe. “We recognize that these actions have caused disruption for customers, associates and partners, but protecting our infrastructure in the best interest of our customers, associates and partners is a top priority,” they said in a statement. “Our teams are working with urgency to investigate the incident and restore affected systems safely. “As they make progress in assessing and mitigating the issues, we are in the process of starting a controlled re-launch of certain systems,” the statement added. The company said there has been no indication that client data has been stolen in the incident. The regional stores’ webpages and apps were offline both Monday and Tuesday, and maintenance messages were in place, alerting customers that stores, pharmacies, and fuel stations were operating as normal. The maintenance message said that any unfulfilled orders placed online or through the app would be refunded. “As a result, our website and app are not available at this time — but we are working as quickly as possible to restore them,” a spokesperson said in a statement. Hannaford Supermarkets said in a statement that its website, mobile app, and To Go pickup and delivery services have been affected by the security issue. “Hannaford stores remain open and continue to welcome customers,” a spokesperson said. “We apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate our customers’ patience and understanding. We’ll provide an update once the issue has been resolved.” Ahold Delhaize has five brands in the United States: Stop & Shop, Hannaford, Giant Food, The GIANT Company, and Food Lion. The company is based in the Netherlands and has 17 local brands across nine countries. Separately, cyberattacks have disrupted other European supermarket chains, which have affected refrigeration systems at hundreds of stores in France. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that roughly 700 supermarkets were impacted. He said that while there was no risk to France’s supplies, the attack “touches the heart of our food security.” Alexa Gagosz can be reached at alexa.gagosz@globe.com . The chains in question are Food Lion, Giant, The Giant Company, Hannaford, and Stop & Shop. Any unfulfilled orders placed through GiantFood.com or the Giant Food app will be refunded. “For prescriptions or vaccination appointments, please contact your local Giant Pharmacy. “Giant Food stores, pharmacies, and fuel stations remain open during normal business hours. “We apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate your patience.” All that being said, you’re probably wondering what the issue is. Well, it looks like it boils down to a security problem within the network of the parent company of all five store chains. The parent company in question is Ahold Delhaize USA (which is a branch of the original Ahold Delhaize based in the Netherlands). Between the five grocery brands, Ahold Delhaize USA has over 2,000 stores along the East Coast, from Maine to Georgia. As you can imagine, that means a lot of customers have seen an error message trying to shop online. In a statement to customers, Ahold Delhaize stated: “Ahold Delhaize is experiencing a security issue within its network. Our teams are taking steps to assess and mitigate the issue. This includes taking some systems offline to help protect them. At this time, our stores are open and serving customers. “Protecting our infrastructure in the best interest of our customers, associates and partners is a top priority. We apologize for any inconvenience this issue may have caused customers and partners.” As of publication, a timetable for all the sites and apps to be back up and running has not been released. So for now, it’s a wait-and-see game. In the meantime, you’re more than welcome to physically go to these stores to get the items you need. extraction.body: If you are trying to do some online grocery shopping with Giant, Stop & Shop or Food Lion, you may notice that their websites and apps are currently unavailable. Dutch supermarket giant Ahold Delhaize said Tuesday it was working to restore systems it had shut down following what it described as a security issue. The company said its stores — including Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium and Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant in the United States — remained open, but the websites for those brands remained offline. There are published reports of a cybersecurity incident at the company that owns the chains. Each chains' website says they are "working to restore service as quickly as possible," adding that customers can still place delivery orders through Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats. Any unfulfilled web and app orders will be refunded. The chains' pharmacies and fueling stations are also still open. Ahold Delhaize said it had no evidence that customer or employee data had been stolen. This comes as cyberattacks disrupted European supermarket chains, affecting refrigeration systems at hundreds of stores in France and forcing a major grocer to shut down websites serving customers in Europe and the United States. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected. He said there was no risk to France's food supplies but acknowledged that the attack "touches the heart of our food security." "It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said. The French government's cybersecurity agency said Tuesday it was "aware of numerous compromises" involving refrigeration system remote control modules made by Danish company Danfoss as well as U.S.-based Copeland. Danfoss said Monday that most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates, and that it was working with affected customers to limit the damage. "Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware, as well as to operate behind a firewall," the company said. In an August report, U.S. cybersecurity firm Claroty identified vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Copeland XWeb Pro platforms, which are used to manage refrigeration infrastructure in supermarkets, warehouses and other facilities. For example, Claroty said "numerous controllers" using the Danfoss system were directly accessible from the public internet, leaving them wide open for cyberattacks. But it noted that Danfoss and Copeland had since fixed the vulnerabilities. Copeland said Tuesday that a vulnerability had been identified in "a discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers," and that it was working with impacted customers. Christopher Whyte, an associate professor of homeland security and emergency preparedness at Virginia Commonwealth University, said it's "not too difficult" to carry out such an attack. "It looks like almost certainly what happened here was these controls were left open to the broader network being used by the supermarket," Whyte said. Similar attacks on water systems, power infrastructure and other kinds of physical operations have been fairly common for years, often coming from Iran and other state actors, Whyte said. Over the summer, Minnesota and Michigan reported cyberattacks on their states' water systems. Whyte said attacks on refrigerator systems are not unprecedented. Last month, Stars and Stripes reported that three military agencies were investigating refrigeration outages at U.S. military commissaries that occurred within days of each other. The Associated Press left a message Tuesday seeking comment on that case with the U.S. Army's Criminal Investigation Division Cyber Field Office. But Whyte said the scale of the French attack, and the fact that there appeared to be no ransom demand or stealing of information, made this situation unusual. It was unclear Tuesday whether the French cyberattack involved artificial intelligence. But advances in AI have contributed to an increase in cybersecurity incidents, said Varun Chandrasekaran, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Illinois' Grainger College of Engineering. Chandrasekaran said there's also a possibility that the attack happened because of an experiment an AI lab was doing — like what happened with OpenAI's breach of an Australian health department website last month. He said people should absolutely expect an increase in such cyberattacks in the future thanks to AI. But Chandrasekaran said AI could also be useful in preventing such hacks. "Right now it seems like a lot of the defensive countermeasures people have are quite passive," Chandrasekaran said. "What we need is a proactive defender, like another AI model sitting on the defender side that's trying to counter whatever the attacker AI is doing."

passages: For many people, buying groceries has become easier ever since grocery stores have rolled out convenient websites and apps.
Sadly, since October 12, five major chains have been hit with technology issues, making it impossible for would-be shoppers to purchase their usual items online.
The chains in question are Food Lion, Giant, The Giant Company, Hannaford, and Stop & Shop.
When you go to the sites or apps for these stores, you’re likely to be met with a variation of a message that reads:
Well, it looks like it boils down to a security problem within the network of the parent company of all five store chains.
“Ahold Delhaize is experiencing a security issue within its network.
“Our Giant Food website and app are currently unavailable.
Any unfulfilled orders placed through GiantFood.com or the Giant Food app will be refunded.
“Giant Food stores, pharmacies, and fuel stations remain open during normal business hours.

extraction.body: For many people, buying groceries has become easier ever since grocery stores have rolled out convenient websites and apps. Sadly, since October 12, five major chains have been hit with technology issues, making it impossible for would-be shoppers to purchase their usual items online. The chains in question are Food Lion, Giant, The Giant Company, Hannaford, and Stop & Shop. When you go to the sites or apps for these stores, you’re likely to be met with a variation of a message that reads: “Our Giant Food website and app are currently unavailable. “We are working to restore service as quickly as possible. Customers may place delivery orders through Instacart, DoorDash, and Uber Eats. Any unfulfilled orders placed through GiantFood.com or the Giant Food app will be refunded. “For prescriptions or vaccination appointments, please contact your local Giant Pharmacy. “Giant Food stores, pharmacies, and fuel stations remain open during normal business hours. “We apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate your patience.” All that being said, you’re probably wondering what the issue is. Well, it looks like it boils down to a security problem within the network of the parent company of all five store chains. The parent company in question is Ahold Delhaize USA (which is a branch of the original Ahold Delhaize based in the Netherlands). Between the five grocery brands, Ahold Delhaize USA has over 2,000 stores along the East Coast, from Maine to Georgia. As you can imagine, that means a lot of customers have seen an error message trying to shop online. In a statement to customers, Ahold Delhaize stated: “Ahold Delhaize is experiencing a security issue within its network. Our teams are taking steps to assess and mitigate the issue. This includes taking some systems offline to help protect them. At this time, our stores are open and serving customers. “Protecting our infrastructure in the best interest of our customers, associates and partners is a top priority. We apologize for any inconvenience this issue may have caused customers and partners.” As of publication, a timetable for all the sites and apps to be back up and running has not been released. So for now, it’s a wait-and-see game. In the meantime, you’re more than welcome to physically go to these stores to get the items you need. sources.title: The US-Japan-India-Australia Quadrilateral Security Dialogue: Indo-Pacific alignment or foam in the ocean? - FIIA - Finnish Institute of International Affairs
passages: In November 2017 the US, Japan, India and Australia re-launched the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QSD) after a ten-year hiatus.
The meeting was little more than an informal consultation at the level of senior officials on “measures to ensure a free and open international order based on the rule of law in the Indo-Pacific”.
Issues addressed included freedom of navigation and overflight, but also maritime security, terrorism, proliferation, and enhanced regional connectivity.
The revival of “the Quad”, as it is commonly called, set off a flurry of references to a renewed attempt to create a potential anti-China alliance.
The Chinese media criticised the gathering as a possible first step towards an Asian NATO.
The Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs, Wang Yi, on the other hand, compared the idea of reviving the Quad to sea foam, destined to dissipate soon.
FIIA Briefing Paper (239). Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

The prime driver of Japan’s alignment policy, within as well as beyond the Quad, is the urge to counter what it perceives as China challenging the regional balance of power in East Asia, accompanied by Beijing’s rapid militarization.
The Japanese government has responded by legally enabling a more autonomous role for Japan in its security alliance with the US, and by beefing up its own military deterrence.
This has included naval exercises with, and export of defence equipment to India, and close defence cooperation with Australia, through what has been labelled a quasi-alliance.

In a book that appeared just before the start of his first stint as Japanese Prime Minister in 2006, Shinzō Abe emphasized the need for Japan to take the lead in establishing a high-level strategic dialogue among the “Asia-Pacific Democratic G3 plus America”.

While Trump’s China policy has fluctuated between confrontation and conciliation, he has now come full circle to the conflict-mongering rhetoric adopted during his election campaign and the early days of his presidency, where he questioned the One China policy and threatened to label China a “currency manipulator”.

In fact, the National Security Strategy (NSS) released in December 2017 suggests that Washington perceives China’s market-distorting practices and intellectual property theft as only one example of Beijing’s attempt to undercut American influence in the world.
In this regard, India, as “a leading global power” [12] , is particularly important.
Consistent with this realization, the Trump administration has upgraded the strategic importance of its relations with New Delhi.

For instance, since 2014 India has had a “Special Strategic and Global Partnership” with Japan that primarily focuses on shared geo-economic interests, including infrastructure and connectivity, but which also has a strong security dimension encompassing bilateral and multilateral military exercises, cooperation in anti-piracy operations, on defence equipment and technology, and on the sharing of military intelligence.

Furthermore, establishing stronger links with other countries such as Japan and the US has also been a core component of India’s “Act East” policy launched in 2014, which aims to serve as India’s own pivot to Asia and increase economic and security cooperation in the region. [6]
In Australia’s 2017 Foreign Policy White Paper – the first since 2003 – India is mentioned 64 times (as opposed to only six times in 2003).
Clearly, Washington may well strengthen the relationships needed for containing China through already existing formats – most importantly its two trilaterals with Japan, Australia, and India.

Trump’s initial moves and speeches (on many of which he has back-pedalled since) signalled retrenchment from the region, including his decision not to join the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), his initial threat to withdraw US troops from Japan and South Korea, lest the allies pay more for their presence, and an early all-too-accommodating approach towards China.
More than ten years after first participating and then withdrawing from Exercise Malabar for fear of enraging China, Australia has now voiced interest in re-engaging.
After this wake-up call, Australia has adopted a tougher stance on China.

After all, the format allows Canberra to kill two birds with one stone: It may help bind the US, Australia’s long-standing ally, to the region, while simultaneously hedging against the US retreat by boosting ties with India – a country that not only possesses a powerful navy, but whose growing market may also help Australia reduce its economic dependency on China.
In 2017, China already accounted for almost 30 percent of Australian exports – iron ore and coal for the most part.
Clearly, this decision was motivated by fears of antagonizing China – and Rudd’s personal hopes to reboot the Sino-Australian relationship.

Nevertheless, also for Japan the grouping’s ultimate utility is largely determined by the extent to which it allows Tokyo to reset its ties with Beijing, in terms of both economic links and regional security issues.

extraction.body: Etusivu / Julkaisut / The US-Japan-India-Australia Quadrilateral Security Dialogue: In ... FIIA Briefing Paper (239). Finnish Institute of International Affairs. Yhdysvallat, Japani, Intia ja Australia aloittivat vuoden 2017 lopussa uudestaan neljän valtion välisen turvallisuusdialogin (Quadrilateral Security Dialogue/Quad). Valtiot olivat toimineet yhteistyössä aiemmin vuosina 2007–2008. Ryhmän uudelleenperustaminen keräsi runsaasti huomiota mutta sai osakseen myös voimakasta kritiikkiä siitä, että nelikko olisi Kiinan vastainen liittouma. Valtioiden lähentymisestä huolimatta ryhmän todellista uudelleenvirkoamista estävät muutamat tekijät. Niitä ovat yhteistyön hutera normatiivinen pohja, maiden sisäpolitiikan ailahtelevat vaikutukset, riski Kiinan provosoitumisesta ja symbolinen viesti, jonka ryhmän muodostuminen lähettää Pekingille. In November 2017 the US, Japan, India and Australia re-launched the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QSD) after a ten-year hiatus. The meeting was little more than an informal consultation at the level of senior officials on “measures to ensure a free and open international order based on the rule of law in the Indo-Pacific”. Issues addressed included freedom of navigation and overflight, but also maritime security, terrorism, proliferation, and enhanced regional connectivity. The revival of “the Quad”, as it is commonly called, set off a flurry of references to a renewed attempt to create a potential anti-China alliance. The Chinese media criticised the gathering as a possible first step towards an Asian NATO. The Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs, Wang Yi, on the other hand, compared the idea of reviving the Quad to sea foam, destined to dissipate soon. Which of the two assessments is more plausible? To answer this question, the Briefing Paper first looks into the background of the revamped Quad, examines cooperation among the four members as it has developed since 2008, including at bilateral and trilateral levels, and analyses what each of the players involved aims to achieve through the grouping. The paper then concludes by assessing the future prospects for the forum. The US-Japan security alliance and the US-Australia military alliance have been key elements of the US-created “Hub-and-Spoke” security system in the Asia Pacific since the end of the Second World War, and the US has significantly tightened strategic-military ties with India since the early 2000s. The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, however, is a Japanese idea. In a book that appeared just before the start of his first stint as Japanese Prime Minister in 2006, Shinzō Abe emphasized the need for Japan to take the lead in establishing a high-level strategic dialogue among the “Asia-Pacific Democratic G3 plus America”. According to Abe, there was a need to discuss how the four countries could better cooperate and promote their common values in the rest of Asia. [1] The initial idea for the grouping may have derived from joint disaster relief operations between the four following the deadly tsunami that hit Southeast Asia in 2004. [2] Building on the existing Trilateral Security Dialogue between the US, Japan and Australia, Abe’s proposal to include India in early 2007 resulted in a first meeting in May of that year. The meeting was followed in September 2007 by Exercise Malabar, a joint large-scale naval drill that had originated in 1992 and initially only included the US and India. The dialogue, in combination with the war games off the Japanese island of Okinawa, aroused suspicion in Beijing that the Quad was aiming to become a military alliance directed against China. Soon after, however, the Quad died a quiet death. Japanese Prime Minister Abe resigned, and new Australian Prime Minister Rudd pulled out of the grouping, prioritizing good relations with China. The four countries are now connected via three important trilateral meetings that ensure an ongoing strategic dialogue on issues of common concern: the Australia-Japan-US trilateral strategic dialogue (TSD), as well as the India-Japan-US and the Australia-India-Japan trilateral dialogues. The countries have also moved closer together on joint naval exercises. In 2015, Japan joined the Malabar exercise between the US and India as a third permanent member. More than ten years after first participating and then withdrawing from Exercise Malabar for fear of enraging China, Australia has now voiced interest in re-engaging. However, at least for Malabar 2018, its bid has been declined by India. Bilateral ties among the four have also been upgraded. While Trump’s efforts to seek stronger bonds with India were recently in the limelight, the greatest boost in relationships certainly occurred among Australia, Japan, and India. Their desire to strengthen cooperation among themselves is driven as much by growing suspicions of China as by serious fears of US retrenchment from Asia. As such, increased defence cooperation between Australia and Japan is also a combined effort to keep the US in the region. At the same time, both countries seek to reduce their dependency on America by significantly strengthening their ties with India. In Australia’s 2017 Foreign Policy White Paper – the first since 2003 – India is mentioned 64 times (as opposed to only six times in 2003). The two countries held their first two-plus-two foreign and defence secretaries meeting at the end of 2017 – a format already employed in all other bilateral relationships, except between the US and India. [3] Institutionalized bilateral ties between Japan and India are also deepening: economic cooperation, infrastructure development, and connectivity projects, as well as security-related and military cooperation are increasingly rooted in a shared geostrategic rationale. Both countries seek to manage as well as minimize possible negative ramifications of the strong Chinese presence in the region, even if Japan sees China more as a physical threat whereas India is dependent on China for economic growth. [4] While some observers rightly contend that the increasing amount of cooperation observed need not be equated with a substantive deepening of ties, there is no denying the fact that Australia, the US, Japan, and India are keenly aware of the importance of their mutual bonds and have made serious investments to strengthen them since 2008. In this light, how can the importance of the Quad be assessed, and what motivates each of its members? It was Australia that killed off the Quad in 2008. Reportedly, it did so without much consultation with its Quad partners. Instead, Kevin Rudd, a fluent Mandarin speaker, who had been elected prime minister in November 2007, unilaterally announced that the format had been a one-off and that Australia did not plan to pursue it further. Clearly, this decision was motivated by fears of antagonizing China – and Rudd’s personal hopes to reboot the Sino-Australian relationship. In fact, Rudd’s foreign minister, Stephen Smith, announced the decision to withdraw from the Quad while standing next to China's foreign minister at that time, Yang Jiechi. Rudd’s fears were not unjustified. Ryhmän uudelleenperustaminen keräsi runsaasti huomiota mutta sai osakseen myös voimakasta kritiikkiä siitä, että nelikko olisi Kiinan vastainen liittouma.

Valtioiden lähentymisestä huolimatta ryhmän todellista uudelleenvirkoamista estävät muutamat tekijät. Niitä ovat yhteistyön hutera normatiivinen pohja, maiden sisäpolitiikan ailahtelevat vaikutukset, riski Kiinan provosoitumisesta ja symbolinen viesti, jonka ryhmän muodostuminen lähettää Pekingille.

In November 2017 the US, Japan, India and Australia re-launched the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QSD) after a ten-year hiatus. The meeting was little more than an informal consultation at the level of senior officials on “measures to ensure a free and open international order based on the rule of law in the Indo-Pacific”. The Chinese media criticised the gathering as a possible first step towards an Asian NATO. The Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs, Wang Yi, on the other hand, compared the idea of reviving the Quad to sea foam, destined to dissipate soon.

To answer this question, the Briefing Paper first looks into the background of the revamped Quad, examines cooperation among the four members as it has developed since 2008, including at bilateral and trilateral levels, and analyses what each of the players involved aims to achieve through the grouping. The paper then concludes by assessing the future prospects for the forum.

The US-Japan security alliance and the US-Australia military alliance have been key elements of the US-created “Hub-and-Spoke” security system in the Asia Pacific since the end of the Second World War, and the US has significantly tightened strategic-military ties with India since the early 2000s.

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, however, is a Japanese idea. In a book that appeared just before the start of his first stint as Japanese Prime Minister in 2006, Shinzō Abe emphasized the need for Japan to take the lead in establishing a high-level strategic dialogue among the “Asia-Pacific Democratic G3 plus America”. According to Abe, there was a need to discuss how the four countries could better cooperate and promote their common values in the rest of Asia. [1] The initial idea for the grouping may have derived from joint disaster relief operations between the four following the deadly tsunami that hit Southeast Asia in 2004. [2]

The prime driver of Japan’s alignment policy, within as well as beyond the Quad, is the urge to counter what it perceives as China challenging the regional balance of power in East Asia, accompanied by Beijing’s rapid militarization.
The Japanese government has responded by legally enabling a more autonomous role for Japan in its security alliance with the US, and by beefing up its own military deterrence.
This has included naval exercises with, and export of defence equipment to India, and close defence cooperation with Australia, through what has been labelled a quasi-alliance.

In a book that appeared just before the start of his first stint as Japanese Prime Minister in 2006, Shinzō Abe emphasized the need for Japan to take the lead in establishing a high-level strategic dialogue among the “Asia-Pacific Democratic G3 plus America”.

While Trump’s China policy has fluctuated between confrontation and conciliation, he has now come full circle to the conflict-mongering rhetoric adopted during his election campaign and the early days of his presidency, where he questioned the One China policy and threatened to label China a “currency manipulator”.

In fact, the National Security Strategy (NSS) released in December 2017 suggests that Washington perceives China’s market-distorting practices and intellectual property theft as only one example of Beijing’s attempt to undercut American influence in the world.
In this regard, India, as “a leading global power” [12] , is particularly important.
Consistent with this realization, the Trump administration has upgraded the strategic importance of its relations with New Delhi.

For instance, since 2014 India has had a “Special Strategic and Global Partnership” with Japan that primarily focuses on shared geo-economic interests, including infrastructure and connectivity, but which also has a strong security dimension encompassing bilateral and multilateral military exercises, cooperation in anti-piracy operations, on defence equipment and technology, and on the sharing of military intelligence.

Furthermore, establishing stronger links with other countries such as Japan and the US has also been a core component of India’s “Act East” policy launched in 2014, which aims to serve as India’s own pivot to Asia and increase economic and security cooperation in the region. [6]
In Australia’s 2017 Foreign Policy White Paper – the first since 2003 – India is mentioned 64 times (as opposed to only six times in 2003).
Clearly, Washington may well strengthen the relationships needed for containing China through already existing formats – most importantly its two trilaterals with Japan, Australia, and India.

Trump’s initial moves and speeches (on many of which he has back-pedalled since) signalled retrenchment from the region, including his decision not to join the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), his initial threat to withdraw US troops from Japan and South Korea, lest the allies pay more for their presence, and an early all-too-accommodating approach towards China.
More than ten years after first participating and then withdrawing from Exercise Malabar for fear of enraging China, Australia has now voiced interest in re-engaging.
After this wake-up call, Australia has adopted a tougher stance on China.

After all, the format allows Canberra to kill two birds with one stone: It may help bind the US, Australia’s long-standing ally, to the region, while simultaneously hedging against the US retreat by boosting ties with India – a country that not only possesses a powerful navy, but whose growing market may also help Australia reduce its economic dependency on China.
In 2017, China already accounted for almost 30 percent of Australian exports – iron ore and coal for the most part.
Clearly, this decision was motivated by fears of antagonizing China – and Rudd’s personal hopes to reboot the Sino-Australian relationship.

Nevertheless, also for Japan the grouping’s ultimate utility is largely determined by the extent to which it allows Tokyo to reset its ties with Beijing, in terms of both economic links and regional security issues.

It explains how we can protect Australia’s security, stability and prosperity at this time of growing uncertainty: focusing on our region, where our interests are most at stake; investing not only in traditional but also in more diverse relationships; and upholding international rules that protect us all.
There are more than one million Australians overseas at any time.

Following disasters and conflicts in recent years, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade assisted the departure of over 3,400 Australians and their families from Lebanon, more than 850 from Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territories, over 680 from Vanuatu, more than 450 from New Caledonia and over 200 from Sudan.
In our region, Australia is progressing Pacific partnerships in unprecedented ways, turbocharging our economic ties with Southeast Asia, and upgrading and diversifying key relationships.

Through direct dialogue, as well as advocacy at the World Trade Organization, Australia has secured China's agreement to lift all trade impediments that it had placed on $20 billion of Australian exports.

In 2024, Prime Minister Albanese hosted leaders of ASEAN and Timor-Leste for the ASEAN-Australia Special Summit in Melbourne to celebrate 50 years since Australia became ASEAN's first formal Dialogue Partner.
The Prime Minister launched Invested: Australia's Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040 in Jakarta in September 2023.
As part of that Strategy, initiatives are now being implemented to help more Australian businesses seize the opportunities in one of the world's fastest growing regions.
This includes the establishment of the $2 billion Southeast Asia Investment Financing Facility (SEAIFF).

These reforms include a greater emphasis on students learning languages and undertaking longer-term study experiences in the Indo-Pacific, and augment our reputation for world-class international education.
In December 2024, Australia launched the Southeast Asia Maritime Institute in Malaysia, led by the University of Wollongong's Australian National Centre for Ocean Resources and Security.
The Australian Passport Office and its agents are committed to providing a secure, efficient and responsive passport service for Australia.

We are working closely with regional partners to uphold international law in the South China Sea, including through the cooperative maritime activity between Australia, the Philippines, Japan and the United States held in 2024.
Together, we are modernising our substantial trade, investment, defence and security links.
We have agreed a Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation and a Reciprocal Access Agreement, enabling closer cooperation in peacetime and in conflict.
Australia and Japan are also pooling our resources and capabilities to support joint projects, such as Telstra's acquisition of Digicel Pacific and the East Micronesia Cable.
Australia and China continue to have different systems and values.
We seek to address our concerns through dialogue and by upholding rules, while working with our partners to do the same.
The Australian Government has also brought home Australian citizens Ms Cheng Lei, Professor Sean Turnell, Dr Ken Elliot and many others from their detention overseas.
Australia has taken its strongest action ever on Iran, with sanctions on hundreds of Iranian-linked individuals and entities, including with links to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Australia has an abiding commitment to helping others in crisis, which keeps our region secure and our people safe.

The starting point of my work as Australia's Minister for Foreign Affairs has always been who we are and what we want - because these are the overriding national interests that our foreign policy projects and protects. We are one of the world's great and enduring democracies. Our people have an abiding tradition of respect for the dignity, rights and freedoms of every individual, founded upon the rule of law. Our national power comes from our people, our economic strength, our military and strategic capabilities, our development assistance and our diplomatic engagement with other countries. This 2025 Snapshot focuses on a key element of our national power: our foreign policy. It explains how we can protect our security, stability and prosperity at this time of growing uncertainty: focusing on our region, where our interests are most at stake; investing not only in traditional but also in more diverse relationships; and upholding international rules that protect us all. In my first year as Foreign Minister, I emphasised our commitment by travelling to every Pacific Islands Forum member and all of the countries of ASEAN, other than Myanmar - engagement we continue to build on. By combining all arms of our national power - including economic, strategic, diplomatic, development and military - as well as by working with our partners, we can advance our interests and values, and create a credible deterrent for any potential adversary. In our region, Australia is progressing Pacific partnerships in unprecedented ways, turbocharging our economic ties with Southeast Asia, and upgrading and diversifying key relationships. In the world, we are defending and upholding global rules, protecting Australian citizens, and promoting Australia's interests in peace, security and trade. We live in an interconnected world, but what matters most to Australia's future is our own region, the Indo-Pacific. Over 50,000 Australian students have participated in New Colombo Plan study programs, language training, internships, and research across 40 locations in our region. Recent reforms to the New Colombo Plan will ensure the program supports Australia's strategic objectives to deepen engagement in our region and lift the capability of our people. These reforms include a greater emphasis on students learning languages and undertaking longer-term study experiences in the Indo-Pacific, and augment our reputation for world-class international education. Nowhere better encapsulates Australia's opportunities and challenges than the region to our north: Southeast Asia. We are working to support Timor-Leste's long-term economic growth and advance our shared interest in a peaceful, stable and prosperous region. In 2024, Prime Minister Albanese hosted leaders of ASEAN and Timor-Leste for the ASEAN-Australia Special Summit in Melbourne to celebrate 50 years since Australia became ASEAN's first formal Dialogue Partner. During the Summit, the Australian Government announced over $500 million in new and expanded initiatives to deepen our economic and cultural ties, further our people-to-people engagement and strengthen our educational and environmental cooperation, reinforcing Australia's deep commitment to Southeast Asia and ASEAN. Indonesia stands as a major and growing power in our region and beyond, and is one of Australia's closest friends and partners. Indonesia is the world's largest Muslim-majority country, the world's third largest democracy, and over the next fifteen years, it is projected to become the world's fifth largest economy. Indonesia's success has always been central to Australia's success, which is why Australia was one of the earliest supporters of a sovereign and independent Indonesia. We will continue to deepen our trade and investment, development, security and defence ties, including through our landmark Defence Cooperation Agreement, the Indonesia-Australia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, and Invested: Australia's Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040. We are working closely with regional partners to uphold international law in the South China Sea, including through the cooperative maritime activity between Australia, the Philippines, Japan and the United States held in 2024. In December 2024, Australia launched the Southeast Asia Maritime Institute in Malaysia, led by the University of Wollongong's Australian National Centre for Ocean Resources and Security. The Prime Minister launched Invested: Australia's Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040 in Jakarta in September 2023. As part of that Strategy, initiatives are now being implemented to help more Australian businesses seize the opportunities in one of the world's fastest growing regions. This includes the establishment of the $2 billion Southeast Asia Investment Financing Facility (SEAIFF). The SEAIFF will provide loans, guarantees, equity and insurance for projects that will boost Australian trade and investment in Southeast Asia, particularly in support of the region's clean energy transition and infrastructure development. The Australian Prime Minister visited China in 2023, and the Chinese Premier visited Australia in 2024, with both visits taking place for the first time in seven years. Through direct dialogue, as well as advocacy at the World Trade Organization, Australia has secured China's agreement to lift all trade impediments that it had placed on $20 billion of Australian exports. Australia and China continue to have different systems and values. Australia is clear about our concerns with China's human rights record or when China's actions run counter to the region's interests in peace and stability - including in the South China Sea and the Taiwan Strait. We seek to address our concerns through dialogue and by upholding rules, while working with our partners to do the same. Japan's status as an Indo-Pacific power makes it central to Australia's security and prosperity. As democracies and middle powers, we share perspectives on responding to challenges in our region. Together, we are modernising our substantial trade, investment, defence and security links. We have agreed a Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation and a Reciprocal Access Agreement, enabling closer cooperation in peacetime and in conflict. Australia and Japan are also pooling our resources and capabilities to support joint projects, such as Telstra's acquisition of Digicel Pacific and the East Micronesia Cable. Our history of investment and scientific research collaboration are helping us both decarbonise our economies and achieve net zero. The new Australia-Japan Critical Minerals Partnership will contribute to building secure and trusted supply chains for these important resources. While sanctions are rarely our first choice in sending a strong message, targeted sanctions are one of the key tools for Australia to respond to situations of international concern, including to deter and disrupt breaches of international law, egregious human rights abuses and other threats to our national interest. Where it is in our national interest to do so, Australia coordinates with international partners to apply sanctions, and is investing $26.4 million in monitoring and enforcement. Australia has taken its strongest action ever on Iran, with sanctions on hundreds of Iranian-linked individuals and entities, including with links to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Australia has an abiding commitment to helping others in crisis, which keeps our region secure and our people safe. Australia's new Humanitarian Policy outlines the role Australia will play at a time when need is outstripping the world's capacity to respond, and disregard for international law is increasing. We are building readiness and preparedness, responding to crises and disasters with support that meets needs and protects the most vulnerable, and reinforces the international humanitarian system. Australia's efforts in the world keep Australians more secure at home, but as the world becomes more uncertain and unstable, the Australian Government's support for Australians overseas is increasingly important. sources.title: Eyes on the Prize: Australia, China, and the Antarctic Treaty System - Lowy Institute
passages: Despite China’s increasing assertiveness in Antarctica, the Antarctic Treaty System is not failing and Australia should refrain from geostrategic panic
Reducing our research output relative to others’ would lower our status, since science and Antarctic experience underpin many ATS debates.
It would also weaken our presence in the AAT and undermine our claim under international law should the Treaty one day fail.

The ­20 Year Australian Antarctic Strategic Plan , produced in 2014 by former Australian Antarctic Division (AAD) director AJ Press, found that “Australia’s standing in Antarctic affairs is eroding because of historical under-investment at a time when new players are emerging” — a reference predominantly to China.
In the past two years, Treaty members have rejected Chinese proposals that sought special treatment for the isolated station.
A joint project between China and Australia would justify a joint Code of Conduct for the area.
Copyright © 2026 Lowy Institute, 31 Bligh Street, Sydney NSW 2000, Australia
12 China’s compliance with the ATS needs to be monitored, but Antarctica should not become another arena for great power competition.
We should be guided by a policy of engaging and balancing China, and keep the ATS free, as far as possible, of Australia–China tensions.
There are principles we cannot resile from, such as precautionary fishing regimes and the monitoring of states’ compliance with ATS obligations.
15 We should avoid being at the forefront of every dispute over Chinese actions in Antarctica.
China is also suspected of prospecting with a view to mining the Antarctic sea floor in the future, consistent with its stated interest in the global commons and the marine economy.
Yet, the line is blurry between geological exploration, which is allowed under the Treaty, and prospecting with an eye to future mining, 27 which is not.
28 We should investigate any exploitation of this ambiguity, but not overreact.
But China wants to benefit economically, and potentially militarily, from Antarctica.
It is increasingly assertive in the ATS, primarily over fisheries access, and active on the ice.
We cannot assume that our historical and current activities would be sufficient to legally assert ownership of the Antarctic region directly to our south if the Treaty failed.
The Madrid Protocol to the Treaty prohibits mining, which Australia supports for environmental reasons and to avoid the continent becoming an area of contention.
Fear of missing out on imagined future riches still drives Antarctic funding in many states, but the Protocol sets a high threshold for reversing the ban.
14 We should commission polling in Australia and elsewhere to determine the depth of public support for Antarctica as a place dedicated to science.
Beijing has tried to change the language of ATS meetings to redirect their purpose from ‘protection’ as well as ‘utilisation’ of Antarctica to favour ‘utilisation’.
Chinese officials tried to give the two terms equal weight at the 2017 Treaty meeting in Beijing.

31 At the 2019 CCAMLR meeting, China refused to accept it was non-compliant even on a minor issue, 32 exhorting members to “come back to the right path towards mutual respect and win-win cooperation” — terminology China uses in the United Nations (UN) and elsewhere when it rejects multilateral constraints.
33 China also criticised Australia for non-compliance, a form of offence-as-defence displayed in other forums.
Diplomatic and scientific entrepreneurialism and detailed negotiations do most to protect our interests.
Consensus decisions in ATS forums are mostly respected once reached, and there is a strong tradition of scientific cooperation, international rescue efforts, and environmental protection.
This is not to suggest Australia back away from its claim.
But drawing international attention to the AAT helps China and Russia insinuate that claimants propose MPAs only to extend their sovereignty.
Australia should forestall the emergence of a ‘fishing bloc’.
China’s pursuit of utilisation over preservation of Antarctica could rally support for such a bloc.
37 Russia and other fishing countries already adopt some similar positions to China in the CCAMLR.
38 To counter this trend, we should build influence with these countries through cooperation in logistics support, environmental clean-ups and tourism policy.

We need to stand with states that challenge fisheries abuse, as New Zealand recently did when it detected a Russian craft spoofing its vessel-monitoring device while fishing in a closed area many kilometres away.

The claimant states are a natural grouping, but we could also help aspiring Consultative members, such as Turkey, with their Antarctic science and diplomacy, partly to underline that the ATS is not a rich-world club.
Australia should front load its support for the ATS, increasing both the substance and profile of our Antarctic activities.
We should emphasise ATS ideals rather than our claim to Australian Antarctic Territory (AAT).
The Lowy Institute is an independent Australian think tank producing authoritative research, innovative data tools, and expert commentary on international affairs.

For some countries, our influence in Antarctic matters will depend on our attitude to resource extraction in the Great Australian Bight, our stance on global sustainability such as World Trade Organization measures to reduce fuel subsidies to distant-water fishing fleets, and especially our climate change policies.
Our Antarctic interests should be supported with other means: stepped-up intelligence collection and analysis outside Antarctica, and more international cooperation against illegal fishing.

We should coordinate our fisheries patrols with New Zealand’s proposed ice-hardened naval vessels 54 and return Maritime Border Command’s Ocean Shield to patrolling our sub-Antarctic islands (which it has not done since 2015, leaving Australian Border Force officers to ride on French vessels).

Despite China’s increasing assertiveness in Antarctica, the Antarctic Treaty System is not failing and Australia should refrain from geostrategic panic
Eyes on the Prize: Australia, China, and the Antarctic Treaty System

The Antarctic Treaty System (ATS) provides Australia with a peaceful, non-militarised south; a freeze on challenges to our territorial claim; a ban on mining and an ecosystem-based management of fisheries. But China wants to benefit economically, and potentially militarily, from Antarctica. It is increasingly assertive in the ATS, primarily over fisheries access, and active on the ice.

Australia should front load its support for the ATS, increasing both the substance and profile of our Antarctic activities. We should emphasise ATS ideals rather than our claim to Australian Antarctic Territory (AAT). We should work hard internationally to dispel the myth that Antarctica’s resource wealth will be unlocked in 2048 on review of the Madrid Protocol. Inside the ATS, we should play to our strengths in multilateral diplomacy. Canberra should monitor Chinese activities in Antarctica and the ATS and step up its maritime awareness of the Southern Ocean, but refrain from geostrategic panic.

The Antarctic Treaty requires that Antarctica be used only for peaceful, scientific purposes (Box 1). The Treaty also ‘freezes’ challenges to our claim of the Australian Antarctic Territory (AAT) — the largest of the seven claims, at around 42 per cent of the continent. Without the Treaty and its supporting agreements, Australia could not afford to defend the AAT, ensure a non-militarised southern border, or prohibit mining in the area. We cannot assume that our historical and current activities would be sufficient to legally assert ownership of the Antarctic region directly to our south if the Treaty failed.

The Treaty does, however, give us a voice in the consensus forums of the Antarctic Treaty System (ATS), including a host of scientific and practical committees and the annual Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meeting (ATCM) where we have a vote along with the other 29 signatories that conduct substantial scientific research on the continent. Diplomatic and scientific entrepreneurialism and detailed negotiations do most to protect our interests. Consensus decisions in ATS forums are mostly respected once reached, and there is a strong tradition of scientific cooperation, international rescue efforts, and environmental protection.

The Madrid Protocol to the Treaty prohibits mining, which Australia supports for environmental reasons and to avoid the continent becoming an area of contention. Even if Australian attitudes on this change, mining on the continent is unlikely to be profitable within the foreseeable future, although seabed mining below 60° south (the Antarctic Treaty area) is conceivable. Fear of missing out on imagined future riches still drives Antarctic funding in many states, but the Protocol sets a high threshold for reversing the ban.

To shore up its domestic rule, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) needs to keep China’s economy strong, secure technological leadership, and demonstrate China’s power in global affairs. In Antarctica, that translates into growing exploitation of fisheries, Chinese ownership of tourism opportunities, access to Western technology through joint projects, and international acquiescence to China’s preferences in the ATS. Before 2016, China’s Antarctic stations and science seemed designed to position it for a territorial claim in the AAT if the Antarctic Treaty were overturned at some point in the future. 4

Australia should work to ensure that US Antarctic policy under President Joe Biden is integrated into the new US administration’s commitment to a more rules-based global order, that it is not dominated by competition with China, and that it continues to accord with the ideals and norms of the ATS. 12 China’s compliance with the ATS needs to be monitored, but Antarctica should not become another arena for great power competition.

We should work hard internationally to dispel the myth that Antarctica is a pot of gold that will be opened in 2048 when the Madrid Protocol could technically be reviewed. The idea that the Protocol (or worse, the Antarctic Treaty) ‘expires in 2048’ is fed by commentary portraying the ATS as weak 13 and implying that its collapse is inevitable. 14 We should commission polling in Australia and elsewhere to determine the depth of public support for Antarctica as a place dedicated to science.

We should be guided by a policy of engaging and balancing China, and keep the ATS free, as far as possible, of Australia–China tensions. There are principles we cannot resile from, such as precautionary fishing regimes and the monitoring of states’ compliance with ATS obligations. But many ATS meetings focus on practical, day-to-day issues, where Australian and Chinese collegiality in science and logistics continues — as evident in the recent rescue of an Australian expeditioner. 15 We should avoid being at the forefront of every dispute over Chinese actions in Antarctica.

In promoting the ATS internationally, Australia should not highlight its claim over the AAT. This is not to suggest Australia back away from its claim. But drawing international attention to the AAT helps China and Russia insinuate that claimants propose MPAs only to extend their sovereignty. 16 Our support for MPA proposals beyond the AAT helps.

China is also suspected of prospecting with a view to mining the Antarctic sea floor in the future, consistent with its stated interest in the global commons and the marine economy. Yet, the line is blurry between geological exploration, which is allowed under the Treaty, and prospecting with an eye to future mining, 27 which is not. 28 We should investigate any exploitation of this ambiguity, but not overreact.

China’s approach to the ATS resembles its increasingly assertive conduct in other international organisations. Beijing has tried to change the language of ATS meetings to redirect their purpose from ‘protection’ as well as ‘utilisation’ of Antarctica to favour ‘utilisation’. Chinese officials tried to give the two terms equal weight at the 2017 Treaty meeting in Beijing. 31 At the 2019 CCAMLR meeting, China refused to accept it was non-compliant even on a minor issue, 32 exhorting members to “come back to the right path towards mutual respect and win-win cooperation” — terminology China uses in the United Nations (UN) and elsewhere when it rejects multilateral constraints. 33 China also criticised Australia for non-compliance, a form of offence-as-defence displayed in other forums.

Australia should point out China’s tactics to other states and, as in other rules-based systems, work with more and wider groupings. The claimant states are a natural grouping, but we could also help aspiring Consultative members, such as Turkey, with their Antarctic science and diplomacy, partly to underline that the ATS is not a rich-world club.

Australia should forestall the emergence of a ‘fishing bloc’. China’s pursuit of utilisation over preservation of Antarctica could rally support for such a bloc. 37 Russia and other fishing countries already adopt some similar positions to China in the CCAMLR. 38 To counter this trend, we should build influence with these countries through cooperation in logistics support, environmental clean-ups and tourism policy. We need to stand with states that challenge fisheries abuse, as New Zealand recently did when it detected a Russian craft spoofing its vessel-monitoring device while fishing in a closed area many kilometres away. 39

However, if we are to work effectively with others to engage China’s desire to appear environmentally responsible, our wider environmental policies need to be consistent. For some countries, our influence in Antarctic matters will depend on our attitude to resource extraction in the Great Australian Bight, our stance on global sustainability such as World Trade Organization measures to reduce fuel subsidies to distant-water fishing fleets, and especially our climate change policies.

Reducing our research output relative to others’ would lower our status, since science and Antarctic experience underpin many ATS debates. It would also weaken our presence in the AAT and undermine our claim under international law should the Treaty one day fail. The ­20 Year Australian Antarctic Strategic Plan , produced in 2014 by former Australian Antarctic Division (AAD) director AJ Press, found that “Australia’s standing in Antarctic affairs is eroding because of historical under-investment at a time when new players are emerging” — a reference predominantly to China. 46

Our science should meet ATS ideals — particularly openness and relevance to all. The new Australian Antarctic Science Strategic Plan heads in the right direction, with an emphasis on global concerns of climate change, Antarctica’s impact on global weather, and the sustainability of marine living resources. 50

Australia could also reduce friction over Chinese activities at Dome A 51 in the AAT by offering to participate in research with China there, fully funding our involvement as equal partners. In the past two years, Treaty members have rejected Chinese proposals that sought special treatment for the isolated station. A joint project between China and Australia would justify a joint Code of Conduct for the area. 52

Our Antarctic interests should be supported with other means: stepped-up intelligence collection and analysis outside Antarctica, and more international cooperation against illegal fishing. We should coordinate our fisheries patrols with New Zealand’s proposed ice-hardened naval vessels 54 and return Maritime Border Command’s Ocean Shield to patrolling our sub-Antarctic islands (which it has not done since 2015, leaving Australian Border Force officers to ride on French vessels).

Although ATS commitments are not always complied with fully, powerful states seeking an outsized share of resources beyond their national jurisdiction can be swayed by smart diplomacy and international public opinion. Antarctica is still remarkable enough, in its wilderness, scientific cooperation, and governance, that with concerted effort it has a chance of remaining separate from the worst of international geopolitics and exploitation.

Claire Young is a former senior analyst with the Australian Government, who covered Antarctica as well as emerging issues such as climate change, social cohesion, and water stress. Ms Young has worked on Australian security issues for over 40 years, including strategic policy analysis in the Department of Defence and writing for the Pacific Defence Reporter, a magazine established by her family.

passages: Home Australian Outlook Blog Posts Analysis Australia Should Stop Competing with China in the Pacific
At first blush, Wong’s framing is understandable.
China has built several infrastructure projects in the region.
Chinese migrants are highly visible in the small business sector, and most Pacific capitals have a “Chinatown”.
But Australian officials and consultants are embedded across many Pacific governments, as well as all major regional bodies, including the Pacific Islands Forum.

For example, Australia offers extensive maritime security assistance , including patrol boats (with accompanying maritime security and technical advisors ) and aerial surveillance, with Australians working at the Forum Fisheries Agency.
Australia also engages in wide-ranging defence cooperation, policing assistance, and disaster response.
And Australia offers labour mobility and permanent migration opportunities .
Importantly, Australia cooperates closely with the other major regional partners, including New Zealand, the US, the UK, France, and Japan.
Australia remains – by far – the region’s largest development partner.

Australia disbursed US$1.5 billion in ODF to the Pacific in 2024 , which was 37 percent of all development flows to the region and more than three times as much as the next largest partner, the Asian Development Bank.
China disbursed only 6 percent of regional ODF.
Joanne is a leading academic voice within the Australian strategic and foreign affairs policy community.

She has been a delegate to the Australia-America Leadership Dialogue, has been invited to participate in strategic dialogues in Washington, Wellington, Canberra, Taipei and Port Moresby, and has appeared before the Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade.
Australia’s interests are best served by being a good neighbour and giving Pacific Island countries space to reach their own conclusions.

Australia can assist their decision-making by sharing information candidly and by continuing to support the independent media, parliaments, ombudsmen, and civil society organisations that let Pacific communities scrutinise all partners, including China and Australia.
This is also the most sustainable approach, because a “permanent” contest has no obvious end point – escalation is often the most likely outcome.
In June 2024 Foreign Minister Penny Wong told the ABC that Australia had lost the chance to be the Pacific’s “ only partner of choice ”.
Because China is further away from the region it has been less involved, which may make it seem like a more benign partner.

But China is a single-party state, which Freedom House describes as “ a repressive authoritarian regime ” that “maintains tight control over all aspects of life and governance, including the state bureaucracy, the media, online speech, religious practice, universities, and businesses”.
China is ranked 178 out of 180 countries on the World Press Freedom Index .
China’s citizens therefore cannot hold their government to account.
Nor can Pacific citizens: the 2022 security agreement with Solomon Islands has never been published.
The government’s Pacific policies are debated in Parliament, scrutinised in Senate Estimates, reported by a free press, tested in the courts ( when necessary ), and held to account at the ballot box.
Pacific leaders can therefore be confident that policies that negatively affect their region will be scrutinised and that broken promises will be noticed.
But Australia should step back from this framing.
The contest framing treats Australia and China as interchangeable partners.
China has neither the inclination nor – arguably – the capacity, to replicate what Australia delivers.
