Copyright © 2026 Lowy Institute, 31 Bligh Street, Sydney NSW 2000, Australia Despite China’s increasing assertiveness in Antarctica, the Antarctic Treaty System is not failing and Australia should refrain from geostrategic panic Eyes on the Prize: Australia, China, and the Antarctic Treaty System The Antarctic Treaty System (ATS) provides Australia with a peaceful, non-militarised south; a freeze on challenges to our territorial claim; a ban on mining and an ecosystem-based management of fisheries. But China wants to benefit economically, and potentially militarily, from Antarctica. It is increasingly assertive in the ATS, primarily over fisheries access, and active on the ice. Australia should front load its support for the ATS, increasing both the substance and profile of our Antarctic activities. We should emphasise ATS ideals rather than our claim to Australian Antarctic Territory (AAT). We should work hard internationally to dispel the myth that Antarctica’s resource wealth will be unlocked in 2048 on review of the Madrid Protocol. Inside the ATS, we should play to our strengths in multilateral diplomacy. Canberra should monitor Chinese activities in Antarctica and the ATS and step up its maritime awareness of the Southern Ocean, but refrain from geostrategic panic. The Antarctic Treaty requires that Antarctica be used only for peaceful, scientific purposes (Box 1). The Treaty also ‘freezes’ challenges to our claim of the Australian Antarctic Territory (AAT) — the largest of the seven claims, at around 42 per cent of the continent. Without the Treaty and its supporting agreements, Australia could not afford to defend the AAT, ensure a non-militarised southern border, or prohibit mining in the area. We cannot assume that our historical and current activities would be sufficient to legally assert ownership of the Antarctic region directly to our south if the Treaty failed. The Treaty does, however, give us a voice in the consensus forums of the Antarctic Treaty System (ATS), including a host of scientific and practical committees and the annual Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meeting (ATCM) where we have a vote along with the other 29 signatories that conduct substantial scientific research on the continent. Diplomatic and scientific entrepreneurialism and detailed negotiations do most to protect our interests. Consensus decisions in ATS forums are mostly respected once reached, and there is a strong tradition of scientific cooperation, international rescue efforts, and environmental protection. The Madrid Protocol to the Treaty prohibits mining, which Australia supports for environmental reasons and to avoid the continent becoming an area of contention. Even if Australian attitudes on this change, mining on the continent is unlikely to be profitable within the foreseeable future, although seabed mining below 60° south (the Antarctic Treaty area) is conceivable. Fear of missing out on imagined future riches still drives Antarctic funding in many states, but the Protocol sets a high threshold for reversing the ban. To shore up its domestic rule, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) needs to keep China’s economy strong, secure technological leadership, and demonstrate China’s power in global affairs. In Antarctica, that translates into growing exploitation of fisheries, Chinese ownership of tourism opportunities, access to Western technology through joint projects, and international acquiescence to China’s preferences in the ATS. Before 2016, China’s Antarctic stations and science seemed designed to position it for a territorial claim in the AAT if the Antarctic Treaty were overturned at some point in the future. 4 Australia should work to ensure that US Antarctic policy under President Joe Biden is integrated into the new US administration’s commitment to a more rules-based global order, that it is not dominated by competition with China, and that it continues to accord with the ideals and norms of the ATS. 12 China’s compliance with the ATS needs to be monitored, but Antarctica should not become another arena for great power competition. We should work hard internationally to dispel the myth that Antarctica is a pot of gold that will be opened in 2048 when the Madrid Protocol could technically be reviewed. The idea that the Protocol (or worse, the Antarctic Treaty) ‘expires in 2048’ is fed by commentary portraying the ATS as weak 13 and implying that its collapse is inevitable. 14 We should commission polling in Australia and elsewhere to determine the depth of public support for Antarctica as a place dedicated to science. We should be guided by a policy of engaging and balancing China, and keep the ATS free, as far as possible, of Australia–China tensions. There are principles we cannot resile from, such as precautionary fishing regimes and the monitoring of states’ compliance with ATS obligations. But many ATS meetings focus on practical, day-to-day issues, where Australian and Chinese collegiality in science and logistics continues — as evident in the recent rescue of an Australian expeditioner. 15 We should avoid being at the forefront of every dispute over Chinese actions in Antarctica. In promoting the ATS internationally, Australia should not highlight its claim over the AAT. This is not to suggest Australia back away from its claim. But drawing international attention to the AAT helps China and Russia insinuate that claimants propose MPAs only to extend their sovereignty. 16 Our support for MPA proposals beyond the AAT helps. China is also suspected of prospecting with a view to mining the Antarctic sea floor in the future, consistent with its stated interest in the global commons and the marine economy. Yet, the line is blurry between geological exploration, which is allowed under the Treaty, and prospecting with an eye to future mining, 27 which is not. 28 We should investigate any exploitation of this ambiguity, but not overreact. Despite China’s increasing assertiveness in Antarctica, the Antarctic Treaty System is not failing and Australia should refrain from geostrategic panic
Eyes on the Prize: Australia, China, and the Antarctic Treaty System

The Antarctic Treaty System (ATS) provides Australia with a peaceful, non-militarised south; a freeze on challenges to our territorial claim; a ban on mining and an ecosystem-based management of fisheries. But China wants to benefit economically, and potentially militarily, from Antarctica. It is increasingly assertive in the ATS, primarily over fisheries access, and active on the ice.

Australia should front load its support for the ATS, increasing both the substance and profile of our Antarctic activities. We should emphasise ATS ideals rather than our claim to Australian Antarctic Territory (AAT). We should work hard internationally to dispel the myth that Antarctica’s resource wealth will be unlocked in 2048 on review of the Madrid Protocol. Inside the ATS, we should play to our strengths in multilateral diplomacy. Canberra should monitor Chinese activities in Antarctica and the ATS and step up its maritime awareness of the Southern Ocean, but refrain from geostrategic panic.

The Antarctic Treaty requires that Antarctica be used only for peaceful, scientific purposes (Box 1). The Treaty also ‘freezes’ challenges to our claim of the Australian Antarctic Territory (AAT) — the largest of the seven claims, at around 42 per cent of the continent. Without the Treaty and its supporting agreements, Australia could not afford to defend the AAT, ensure a non-militarised southern border, or prohibit mining in the area. We cannot assume that our historical and current activities would be sufficient to legally assert ownership of the Antarctic region directly to our south if the Treaty failed.

The Treaty does, however, give us a voice in the consensus forums of the Antarctic Treaty System (ATS), including a host of scientific and practical committees and the annual Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meeting (ATCM) where we have a vote along with the other 29 signatories that conduct substantial scientific research on the continent. Diplomatic and scientific entrepreneurialism and detailed negotiations do most to protect our interests. Consensus decisions in ATS forums are mostly respected once reached, and there is a strong tradition of scientific cooperation, international rescue efforts, and environmental protection.

The Madrid Protocol to the Treaty prohibits mining, which Australia supports for environmental reasons and to avoid the continent becoming an area of contention. Even if Australian attitudes on this change, mining on the continent is unlikely to be profitable within the foreseeable future, although seabed mining below 60° south (the Antarctic Treaty area) is conceivable. Fear of missing out on imagined future riches still drives Antarctic funding in many states, but the Protocol sets a high threshold for reversing the ban.

To shore up its domestic rule, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) needs to keep China’s economy strong, secure technological leadership, and demonstrate China’s power in global affairs. In Antarctica, that translates into growing exploitation of fisheries, Chinese ownership of tourism opportunities, access to Western technology through joint projects, and international acquiescence to China’s preferences in the ATS. Before 2016, China’s Antarctic stations and science seemed designed to position it for a territorial claim in the AAT if the Antarctic Treaty were overturned at some point in the future. 4

Australia should work to ensure that US Antarctic policy under President Joe Biden is integrated into the new US administration’s commitment to a more rules-based global order, that it is not dominated by competition with China, and that it continues to accord with the ideals and norms of the ATS. 12 China’s compliance with the ATS needs to be monitored, but Antarctica should not become another arena for great power competition.

We should work hard internationally to dispel the myth that Antarctica is a pot of gold that will be opened in 2048 when the Madrid Protocol could technically be reviewed. The idea that the Protocol (or worse, the Antarctic Treaty) ‘expires in 2048’ is fed by commentary portraying the ATS as weak 13 and implying that its collapse is inevitable. 14 We should commission polling in Australia and elsewhere to determine the depth of public support for Antarctica as a place dedicated to science.

We should be guided by a policy of engaging and balancing China, and keep the ATS free, as far as possible, of Australia–China tensions. There are principles we cannot resile from, such as precautionary fishing regimes and the monitoring of states’ compliance with ATS obligations. But many ATS meetings focus on practical, day-to-day issues, where Australian and Chinese collegiality in science and logistics continues — as evident in the recent rescue of an Australian expeditioner. 15 We should avoid being at the forefront of every dispute over Chinese actions in Antarctica.

In promoting the ATS internationally, Australia should not highlight its claim over the AAT. This is not to suggest Australia back away from its claim. But drawing international attention to the AAT helps China and Russia insinuate that claimants propose MPAs only to extend their sovereignty. 16 Our support for MPA proposals beyond the AAT helps.

China is also suspected of prospecting with a view to mining the Antarctic sea floor in the future, consistent with its stated interest in the global commons and the marine economy. Yet, the line is blurry between geological exploration, which is allowed under the Treaty, and prospecting with an eye to future mining, 27 which is not. 28 We should investigate any exploitation of this ambiguity, but not overreact.

China’s approach to the ATS resembles its increasingly assertive conduct in other international organisations. Beijing has tried to change the language of ATS meetings to redirect their purpose from ‘protection’ as well as ‘utilisation’ of Antarctica to favour ‘utilisation’. Chinese officials tried to give the two terms equal weight at the 2017 Treaty meeting in Beijing. 31 At the 2019 CCAMLR meeting, China refused to accept it was non-compliant even on a minor issue, 32 exhorting members to “come back to the right path towards mutual respect and win-win cooperation” — terminology China uses in the United Nations (UN) and elsewhere when it rejects multilateral constraints. 33 China also criticised Australia for non-compliance, a form of offence-as-defence displayed in other forums.

Australia should point out China’s tactics to other states and, as in other rules-based systems, work with more and wider groupings. The claimant states are a natural grouping, but we could also help aspiring Consultative members, such as Turkey, with their Antarctic science and diplomacy, partly to underline that the ATS is not a rich-world club.

Australia should forestall the emergence of a ‘fishing bloc’. China’s pursuit of utilisation over preservation of Antarctica could rally support for such a bloc. 37 Russia and other fishing countries already adopt some similar positions to China in the CCAMLR. 38 To counter this trend, we should build influence with these countries through cooperation in logistics support, environmental clean-ups and tourism policy. We need to stand with states that challenge fisheries abuse, as New Zealand recently did when it detected a Russian craft spoofing its vessel-monitoring device while fishing in a closed area many kilometres away. 39

However, if we are to work effectively with others to engage China’s desire to appear environmentally responsible, our wider environmental policies need to be consistent. For some countries, our influence in Antarctic matters will depend on our attitude to resource extraction in the Great Australian Bight, our stance on global sustainability such as World Trade Organization measures to reduce fuel subsidies to distant-water fishing fleets, and especially our climate change policies.

Reducing our research output relative to others’ would lower our status, since science and Antarctic experience underpin many ATS debates. It would also weaken our presence in the AAT and undermine our claim under international law should the Treaty one day fail. The ­20 Year Australian Antarctic Strategic Plan , produced in 2014 by former Australian Antarctic Division (AAD) director AJ Press, found that “Australia’s standing in Antarctic affairs is eroding because of historical under-investment at a time when new players are emerging” — a reference predominantly to China. 46

Our science should meet ATS ideals — particularly openness and relevance to all. The new Australian Antarctic Science Strategic Plan heads in the right direction, with an emphasis on global concerns of climate change, Antarctica’s impact on global weather, and the sustainability of marine living resources. 50

Australia could also reduce friction over Chinese activities at Dome A 51 in the AAT by offering to participate in research with China there, fully funding our involvement as equal partners. In the past two years, Treaty members have rejected Chinese proposals that sought special treatment for the isolated station. A joint project between China and Australia would justify a joint Code of Conduct for the area. 52

Our Antarctic interests should be supported with other means: stepped-up intelligence collection and analysis outside Antarctica, and more international cooperation against illegal fishing. We should coordinate our fisheries patrols with New Zealand’s proposed ice-hardened naval vessels 54 and return Maritime Border Command’s Ocean Shield to patrolling our sub-Antarctic islands (which it has not done since 2015, leaving Australian Border Force officers to ride on French vessels).

Although ATS commitments are not always complied with fully, powerful states seeking an outsized share of resources beyond their national jurisdiction can be swayed by smart diplomacy and international public opinion. Antarctica is still remarkable enough, in its wilderness, scientific cooperation, and governance, that with concerted effort it has a chance of remaining separate from the worst of international geopolitics and exploitation.

passages: Home Australian Outlook Blog Posts Analysis Australia Should Stop Competing with China in the Pacific
At first blush, Wong’s framing is understandable.
China has built several infrastructure projects in the region.
Chinese migrants are highly visible in the small business sector, and most Pacific capitals have a “Chinatown”.
But Australian officials and consultants are embedded across many Pacific governments, as well as all major regional bodies, including the Pacific Islands Forum.

For example, Australia offers extensive maritime security assistance , including patrol boats (with accompanying maritime security and technical advisors ) and aerial surveillance, with Australians working at the Forum Fisheries Agency.
Australia also engages in wide-ranging defence cooperation, policing assistance, and disaster response.
And Australia offers labour mobility and permanent migration opportunities .
Importantly, Australia cooperates closely with the other major regional partners, including New Zealand, the US, the UK, France, and Japan.
Australia remains – by far – the region’s largest development partner.

Australia disbursed US$1.5 billion in ODF to the Pacific in 2024 , which was 37 percent of all development flows to the region and more than three times as much as the next largest partner, the Asian Development Bank.
China disbursed only 6 percent of regional ODF.
Joanne is a leading academic voice within the Australian strategic and foreign affairs policy community.

She has been a delegate to the Australia-America Leadership Dialogue, has been invited to participate in strategic dialogues in Washington, Wellington, Canberra, Taipei and Port Moresby, and has appeared before the Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade.
Australia’s interests are best served by being a good neighbour and giving Pacific Island countries space to reach their own conclusions.

Australia can assist their decision-making by sharing information candidly and by continuing to support the independent media, parliaments, ombudsmen, and civil society organisations that let Pacific communities scrutinise all partners, including China and Australia.
This is also the most sustainable approach, because a “permanent” contest has no obvious end point – escalation is often the most likely outcome.
In June 2024 Foreign Minister Penny Wong told the ABC that Australia had lost the chance to be the Pacific’s “ only partner of choice ”.
Because China is further away from the region it has been less involved, which may make it seem like a more benign partner.

But China is a single-party state, which Freedom House describes as “ a repressive authoritarian regime ” that “maintains tight control over all aspects of life and governance, including the state bureaucracy, the media, online speech, religious practice, universities, and businesses”.
China is ranked 178 out of 180 countries on the World Press Freedom Index .
China’s citizens therefore cannot hold their government to account.
Nor can Pacific citizens: the 2022 security agreement with Solomon Islands has never been published.
The government’s Pacific policies are debated in Parliament, scrutinised in Senate Estimates, reported by a free press, tested in the courts ( when necessary ), and held to account at the ballot box.
Pacific leaders can therefore be confident that policies that negatively affect their region will be scrutinised and that broken promises will be noticed.
But Australia should step back from this framing.
The contest framing treats Australia and China as interchangeable partners.
China has neither the inclination nor – arguably – the capacity, to replicate what Australia delivers.

But they are different kinds of states. Australia’s long history in the Pacific is far from blameless , but we know a lot about it because Australia is a democracy. The government’s Pacific policies are debated in Parliament, scrutinised in Senate Estimates, reported by a free press, tested in the courts ( when necessary ), and held to account at the ballot box. The contest framing also implies moral equivalence between Australia and China. But they are different kinds of states.

The government’s Pacific policies are debated in Parliament, scrutinised in Senate Estimates, reported by a free press, tested in the courts ( when necessary ), and held to account at the ballot box. Pacific leaders can therefore be confident that policies that negatively affect their region will be scrutinised and that broken promises will be noticed.

Because China is further away from the region it has been less involved, which may make it seem like a more benign partner. But China is a single-party state, which Freedom House describes as “ a repressive authoritarian regime ” that “maintains tight control over all aspects of life and governance, including the state bureaucracy, the media, online speech, religious practice, universities, and businesses”. China is ranked 178 out of 180 countries on the World Press Freedom Index . China’s citizens therefore cannot hold their government to account. Nor can Pacific citizens: the 2022 security agreement with Solomon Islands has never been published.

No country is a perfect partner, but Australia is a more accountable one. If China begins to coerce Pacific Island countries as it has done the Philippines , there will be little they or Chinese citizens can do to hold it to account.
Contests are intended to be won. But Pacific Island countries are not “prizes”.

Pacific Island countries make their own foreign and strategic policy decisions for their own reasons. The contest framing implies that engagements between Pacific Island countries and China are “losses” for Australia, which underestimates the ability of Pacific Island countries to distinguish between partners and their offerings. This framing also risks provoking the outcome that it fears: Pacific Island countries may calculate that the best way to resist perceived Australia pressure to “ choose ” a “side” and to demonstrate their sovereignty is to seek greater engagement with China.

Australia’s interests are best served by being a good neighbour and giving Pacific Island countries space to reach their own conclusions. Australia should be confident that Pacific Island countries can evaluate the risks of normalising China’s presence in their region. Australia can assist their decision-making by sharing information candidly and by continuing to support the independent media, parliaments, ombudsmen, and civil society organisations that let Pacific communities scrutinise all partners, including China and Australia.

None of this means that Australia does not have legitimate strategic concerns about China’s interest in the Pacific, particularly about the risk of a Chinese military presence. But Australia’s best protection against that outcome is to be the partner that Pacific Island countries engage with because of what its policies offer for their people, rather than because Australia is involved in a cycle of reacting to Chinese initiatives . This is also the most sustainable approach, because a “permanent” contest has no obvious end point – escalation is often the most likely outcome.

Joanne Wallis is Professor of International Security in the Department of Politics and International Relations at the University of Adelaide. Joanne is a leading academic voice within the Australian strategic and foreign affairs policy community. She has been a delegate to the Australia-America Leadership Dialogue, has been invited to participate in strategic dialogues in Washington, Wellington, Canberra, Taipei and Port Moresby, and has appeared before the Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade. Joanne is the author or editor of seven books, including Constitution making during State building (CUP 2014) and Pacific Power? Australia’s Strategy in the Pacific Islands (MUP 2017).

extraction.body: Flock’s founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn’t think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards. “If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress,” Langley said, speaking on stage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday. During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces — which has since led to cancelled contracts and even layoffs . Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people’s concerns. In doing so, Langley positioned Flock as an advance in technology that was somewhat inevitable. He stressed that if people wanted to live in a better society — that is, one with reduced crime — they would have to offer up their privacy in return. A similar argument about the trade-offs and rewards could be made for AI, which is marketed to the public as vastly improving our lives, automating tedious tasks, and making things more convenient. The flip side is the cost of sharing everything about ourselves with the makers of the AI agents themselves — and the possibility of the destruction of humanity , according to some. It’s no surprise that the AI backlash shares some overlap with Flock. Much like AI, Flock is a technology that some feel has been forced upon the public without their consent. For Langley, this is just the nature of progress, he explained. “Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It’s not doing things perfect,” he said. “Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there’s one accident, I don’t think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, ‘Hey, let’s talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future’.” But driverless car makers don’t shrug their shoulders at crashes; the companies pause their fleets and apply fixes. Flock, meanwhile, seems to wrestle as a company with understanding when it’s the company’s responsibility to intervene. From Langley’s answers, it’s clear that the ethics around how Flock should be used is a decision he would much rather leave up to others. “We don’t want to tell city leaders how to do their job,” he noted. “We will provide recommendations, we’ll provide defaults, but we’re going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies,” he said. Among the many rebuttals to his critics that Langley raised during the interview was the idea that misinformation about Flock had led to some of its customers’ cancellations. For instance, he referenced a time when a customer ended their contract because they believed the devices performed facial recognition. While Flock cameras do not have facial recognition, they do have the ability to detect and track people . Langley also spent a fair amount of time admonishing those who think his technology, or any technology, should be perfect, attributing the quote to some unnamed community leader. “He was describing that, too often as a society we judge technology not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect. And Flock is far from perfect; I’m far from perfect — I’ve made plenty of mistakes,” Langley said. Another area of pushback was in positioning Flock as a more effective form of policing, and one that allowed police departments to do more with reduced staff. “If you look at where policing has gone over the last decade, but particularly post-COVID, law enforcement employment is declining rapidly. I think about a place like San Francisco, and there’s hundreds of open positions. They will probably never be filled,” he said, positioning Flock as the tech that would fill in those gaps. But pressed about abuse and the invasiveness of his company’s surveillance technology, Langley had no substantive answers. “I think if the idea is to curb abuse, I think there’s a way to do that that doesn’t disrupt the legal system, that doesn’t disrupt the efficacy and flow of a police department,” Langley said, without spelling out what those ideas were. For Langley, those seem to be matters of secondary importance, because his belief in Flock as a public good is so strong. “I think one of the unfortunate consequences of building a consequential company is this is the price you pay, and I think it’s worth it because there’s millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock,” he said. “And clearly we’ve made our fair share of mistakes, and there’s some folks who disagree with what we do, but it’s worth it because one day they might be a victim,” Langley added. Critics argue that both Flock and AI technologies are being used without adequate consent from the public, leading to a growing backlash.

He compared Flock's surveillance solutions to the development of driverless cars, asserting that while they have their problems, the focus should be on making them safer rather than shutting them down entirely.

Langley stated, "If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress." He emphasized the importance of technology in creating a safer society while downplaying the criticisms that have recently led to contract cancellations and layoffs at Flock.

extraction.body: At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco, Garrett Langley, founder and CEO of Flock, defended the implementation of surveillance technology, arguing that the potential benefits in crime reduction outweigh privacy concerns. Langley's comments came during a panel discussion where he faced a barrage of questions about the controversy surrounding Flock's products, particularly its license plate cameras and other monitoring devices. Langley stated, "If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress." He emphasized the importance of technology in creating a safer society while downplaying the criticisms that have recently led to contract cancellations and layoffs at Flock. Throughout the interview, Langley frequently referenced discussions with law enforcement officials and city leaders, citing instances where Flock's technology had reportedly helped solve crimes. However, he often sidestepped specific concerns raised by critics. Instead, he framed the deployment of surveillance technology as an inevitable advancement, suggesting that privacy must be sacrificed for enhanced public safety. This rationale echoes broader debates surrounding artificial intelligence, which also faces scrutiny for its intrusive nature despite claims of improving efficiency and convenience in daily life. Critics argue that both Flock and AI technologies are being used without adequate consent from the public, leading to a growing backlash. Langley defended his viewpoint by noting that all technology has flaws. He compared Flock's surveillance solutions to the development of driverless cars, asserting that while they have their problems, the focus should be on making them safer rather than shutting them down entirely. However, driverless car manufacturers typically implement fixes after accidents, a proactive approach Langley’s company seems reluctant to adopt, as he minimized the company's responsibility for ethical considerations. "We don’t want to tell city leaders how to do their job," he stated. Instead, he claimed that Flock would provide recommendations but not impose regulations, effectively distancing the company from accountability in how its technology is applied. Langley argued that misconceptions about Flock's capabilities, such as the false belief that it uses facial recognition technology, have contributed to negative perceptions and some cancelled contracts. He clarified that while Flock cameras track individuals, they do not perform facial recognition. During the discussion, Langley pushed back against the expectation that technology must be flawless. He quoted an unnamed community leader who observed that society often compares technology to an ideal rather than its historical counterparts. "Flock is far from perfect; I’m far from perfect — I’ve made plenty of mistakes," he said. He also highlighted the declining workforce in law enforcement, especially in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, suggesting that Flock’s technology could help fill the gaps left by staffing shortages. However, he struggled to provide substantial answers regarding concerns about potential misuse of surveillance technology. When addressing calls for measures to prevent abuse, Langley offered vague sentiments, stating, "I think there's a way to do that that doesn’t disrupt the legal system...," yet did not elaborate on what those measures would entail. Despite the criticism, Langley's conviction that Flock represents a "public good" remains strong. He concluded, "There’s millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock." He acknowledged the company's missteps but maintained that the overarching goal justifies the means, cautioning that even critics might one day find themselves in need of Flock’s safety benefits.

Garrett Langley defended the technology by citing "the rescue of an 11-year-old girl in Tennessee" as an example where a camera recorded the vehicle’s license plate used by her kidnapper.
South Windsor voted to remove Flock cameras over privacy concerns and AI monitoring.

South Windsor, Connecticut ordered the removal of Flock Safety surveillance cameras after the South Windsor Town Council approved a resolution requiring the local police to immediately suspend the use of the cameras and proceed with their removal within a maximum period of 60 days.
The cameras use Automatic License Plate Recognition (ALPR) technology to photograph vehicles, identify plates, and record information in a private database that can be accessed by authorities.

extraction.body: Flock’s founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn’t think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards. “If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress,” Langley said, speaking on stage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday. During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces — which has since led to cancelled contracts and even layoffs . Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people’s concerns. In doing so, Langley positioned Flock as an advance in technology that was somewhat inevitable. He stressed that if people wanted to live in a better society — that is, one with reduced crime — they would have to offer up their privacy in return. A similar argument about the trade-offs and rewards could be made for AI, which is marketed to the public as vastly improving our lives, automating tedious tasks, and making things more convenient. The flip side is the cost of sharing everything about ourselves with the makers of the AI agents themselves — and the possibility of the destruction of humanity , according to some. It’s no surprise that the AI backlash shares some overlap with Flock. Much like AI, Flock is a technology that some feel has been forced upon the public without their consent. For Langley, this is just the nature of progress, he explained. “Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It’s not doing things perfect,” he said. “Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there’s one accident, I don’t think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, ‘Hey, let’s talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future’.” But driverless car makers don’t shrug their shoulders at crashes; the companies pause their fleets and apply fixes. Flock, meanwhile, seems to wrestle as a company with understanding when it’s the company’s responsibility to intervene. From Langley’s answers, it’s clear that the ethics around how Flock should be used is a decision he would much rather leave up to others. “We don’t want to tell city leaders how to do their job,” he noted. “We will provide recommendations, we’ll provide defaults, but we’re going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies,” he said. Among the many rebuttals to his critics that Langley raised during the interview was the idea that misinformation about Flock had led to some of its customers’ cancellations. For instance, he referenced a time when a customer ended their contract because they believed the devices performed facial recognition. While Flock cameras do not have facial recognition, they do have the ability to detect and track people . Langley also spent a fair amount of time admonishing those who think his technology, or any technology, should be perfect, attributing the quote to some unnamed community leader. “He was describing that, too often as a society we judge technology not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect. And Flock is far from perfect; I’m far from perfect — I’ve made plenty of mistakes,” Langley said. Another area of pushback was in positioning Flock as a more effective form of policing, and one that allowed police departments to do more with reduced staff. “If you look at where policing has gone over the last decade, but particularly post-COVID, law enforcement employment is declining rapidly. I think about a place like San Francisco, and there’s hundreds of open positions. They will probably never be filled,” he said, positioning Flock as the tech that would fill in those gaps. But pressed about abuse and the invasiveness of his company’s surveillance technology, Langley had no substantive answers. “I think if the idea is to curb abuse, I think there’s a way to do that that doesn’t disrupt the legal system, that doesn’t disrupt the efficacy and flow of a police department,” Langley said, without spelling out what those ideas were. For Langley, those seem to be matters of secondary importance, because his belief in Flock as a public good is so strong. “I think one of the unfortunate consequences of building a consequential company is this is the price you pay, and I think it’s worth it because there’s millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock,” he said. “And clearly we’ve made our fair share of mistakes, and there’s some folks who disagree with what we do, but it’s worth it because one day they might be a victim,” Langley added. extraction.body: At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco, Garrett Langley, founder and CEO of Flock, defended the implementation of surveillance technology, arguing that the potential benefits in crime reduction outweigh privacy concerns. Langley's comments came during a panel discussion where he faced a barrage of questions about the controversy surrounding Flock's products, particularly its license plate cameras and other monitoring devices. Langley stated, "If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress." He emphasized the importance of technology in creating a safer society while downplaying the criticisms that have recently led to contract cancellations and layoffs at Flock. Throughout the interview, Langley frequently referenced discussions with law enforcement officials and city leaders, citing instances where Flock's technology had reportedly helped solve crimes. However, he often sidestepped specific concerns raised by critics. Instead, he framed the deployment of surveillance technology as an inevitable advancement, suggesting that privacy must be sacrificed for enhanced public safety. This rationale echoes broader debates surrounding artificial intelligence, which also faces scrutiny for its intrusive nature despite claims of improving efficiency and convenience in daily life. Critics argue that both Flock and AI technologies are being used without adequate consent from the public, leading to a growing backlash. Langley defended his viewpoint by noting that all technology has flaws. He compared Flock's surveillance solutions to the development of driverless cars, asserting that while they have their problems, the focus should be on making them safer rather than shutting them down entirely. However, driverless car manufacturers typically implement fixes after accidents, a proactive approach Langley’s company seems reluctant to adopt, as he minimized the company's responsibility for ethical considerations. "We don’t want to tell city leaders how to do their job," he stated. Instead, he claimed that Flock would provide recommendations but not impose regulations, effectively distancing the company from accountability in how its technology is applied. Langley argued that misconceptions about Flock's capabilities, such as the false belief that it uses facial recognition technology, have contributed to negative perceptions and some cancelled contracts. He clarified that while Flock cameras track individuals, they do not perform facial recognition. During the discussion, Langley pushed back against the expectation that technology must be flawless. He quoted an unnamed community leader who observed that society often compares technology to an ideal rather than its historical counterparts. "Flock is far from perfect; I’m far from perfect — I’ve made plenty of mistakes," he said. He also highlighted the declining workforce in law enforcement, especially in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, suggesting that Flock’s technology could help fill the gaps left by staffing shortages. However, he struggled to provide substantial answers regarding concerns about potential misuse of surveillance technology. When addressing calls for measures to prevent abuse, Langley offered vague sentiments, stating, "I think there's a way to do that that doesn’t disrupt the legal system...," yet did not elaborate on what those measures would entail. Despite the criticism, Langley's conviction that Flock represents a "public good" remains strong. He concluded, "There’s millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock." He acknowledged the company's missteps but maintained that the overarching goal justifies the means, cautioning that even critics might one day find themselves in need of Flock’s safety benefits.

extraction.body: Bitcoin rose to just under $75,000 in Asian morning hours on Friday, up almost 8% on the day and nearly 18% over the week, after touching just above $75,500 overnight. Two days ago it traded near $64,100. Short sellers took another beating, as roughly $1 billion of short positions were liquidated over 24 hours out of $1.23 billion in total, across 140,416 traders, per CoinGlass. That follows the $3 billion of shorts wiped out on Thursday, the largest single-day figure in records going back to 2021, bringing the two-day total to more than $4 billion. The largest individual position closed in the latest session was a $25.13 million bitcoin trade on Hyperliquid. A liquidation happens when a trader borrows to make a bigger bet than their money would cover, the market moves against them, and the exchange closes the position automatically before the losses exceed what they put down. These were traders betting the price would fall, and each forced closure pushed prices up and created a cascade of liquidations. The size of the number matters because it separates a rally built on demand from one built on mechanics. Traders forced to buy are not deciding bitcoin is worth more; they are covering a losing bet. Meanwhile, Hyperliquid's HYPE rose over 4% to nearly $73 and leads the majors on the week at almost 27%. Ether added almost 5% to $2,350 and is up 24.5% over seven days. Dogecoin gained almost 9% to just over 8 cents and solana over 5% to just under $90, both up 17% on the week. BNB rose 6% to $660 and is up 8% over seven days. Tron lagged, up 1.5% to just under 34 cents and barely moved on the week. The rally traces back to Wednesday, when the Treasury doubled the size of its long-end bond buybacks from $2 billion to $4 billion per operation, easing conditions across the roughly $30 trillion Treasury market and lifting appetite for risk. Bitcoin then cleared resistance near $66,600, which put $76,000 on traders' radar as the next level. Washington added to it. President Donald Trump urged Congress to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act at a White House event on Wednesday, flanked by executives from Coinbase, Gemini, Ripple and Chainlink Labs.

extraction.body: Nearly $483 million in bitcoin and ether futures positions were closed over the past 24 hours as cryptocurrency prices fell Thursday, with ether traders taking the largest hit. Crypto losses worsened on Thursday morning as uncertainty over the Federal Reserve’s next interest-rate decision weighed on markets. Bitcoin traded around $81,000, down roughly 3% over 24 hours, while ether lost more than 6% to about $2,350. XRP and Solana’s SOL fell around 5%, and dogecoin dropped roughly 6%. Ether contracts accounted for about $286 million of liquidations, compared with $197 million for bitcoin, according to CoinGlass data checked during Asian morning hours. Ether fell about 6.4% to $2,356, while bitcoin lost roughly 3.2% to trade around $81,000. Liquidations happen when traders use borrowed money and a price move leaves them without enough collateral to keep their bets open. The exchange closes the position automatically. extraction.body: Bitcoin rose to just under $75,000 in Asian morning hours on Friday, up almost 8% on the day and nearly 18% over the week, after touching just above $75,500 overnight. Two days ago it traded near $64,100. Short sellers took another beating, as roughly $1 billion of short positions were liquidated over 24 hours out of $1.23 billion in total, across 140,416 traders, per CoinGlass. That follows the $3 billion of shorts wiped out on Thursday, the largest single-day figure in records going back to 2021, bringing the two-day total to more than $4 billion. The largest individual position closed in the latest session was a $25.13 million bitcoin trade on Hyperliquid. A liquidation happens when a trader borrows to make a bigger bet than their money would cover, the market moves against them, and the exchange closes the position automatically before the losses exceed what they put down. These were traders betting the price would fall, and each forced closure pushed prices up and created a cascade of liquidations. The size of the number matters because it separates a rally built on demand from one built on mechanics. Traders forced to buy are not deciding bitcoin is worth more; they are covering a losing bet. Meanwhile, Hyperliquid's HYPE rose over 4% to nearly $73 and leads the majors on the week at almost 27%. Ether added almost 5% to $2,350 and is up 24.5% over seven days. Dogecoin gained almost 9% to just over 8 cents and solana over 5% to just under $90, both up 17% on the week. BNB rose 6% to $660 and is up 8% over seven days. Tron lagged, up 1.5% to just under 34 cents and barely moved on the week. The rally traces back to Wednesday, when the Treasury doubled the size of its long-end bond buybacks from $2 billion to $4 billion per operation, easing conditions across the roughly $30 trillion Treasury market and lifting appetite for risk. Bitcoin then cleared resistance near $66,600, which put $76,000 on traders' radar as the next level. Washington added to it. President Donald Trump urged Congress to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act at a White House event on Wednesday, flanked by executives from Coinbase, Gemini, Ripple and Chainlink Labs.

sources.title: Ricursive Intelligence is betting on AI-designed chips to help solve the compute crisis
passages: Ricursive Intelligence founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini believe more efficient AI chip design could help solve the compute crisis.

The founders took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Wednesday to detail how their startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from each iteration, and improve subsequent designs, all with the goal of automating and accelerating the chip design process.

We think that we need to help by making chips that are more efficient, that use the bandwidth in those data centers more efficiently, that use the wafers and fabs more efficiently, because even if we make [data centers] in space or something, I don’t know, you won’t see the sun anymore.”
The founders also argued that AI-designed chips will make it possible to create all sorts of chips that might not have been possible before.

While some may be scared by the thought of AI designing its own chips, Goldie argues that letting AI handle chip design will allow humans can focus on developing applications and exploring new possibilities that can expand what they can accomplish with computing.

extraction.body: A new startup is taking aim at the semiconductor industry's biggest bottleneck with an audacious proposition: let AI design the chips themselves. Ricursive Intelligence emerged from stealth today with a platform that promises to automate the notoriously complex chip design process, using machine learning to iterate and improve with each design cycle. The timing couldn't be more critical as the industry grapples with a compute crisis that's throttling everything from data centers to consumer devices. The semiconductor shortage that's been choking tech supply chains for years just got a potential lifeline from an unexpected source: artificial intelligence. Ricursive Intelligence, a startup that's been quietly developing in stealth mode, just unveiled an AI platform designed to revolutionize how chips are created by letting machines handle the entire design process. The company's approach tackles one of the industry's most persistent problems - the months or even years it takes to design and validate new semiconductors. Traditional chip design requires teams of engineers working through countless iterations, debugging complex architectures, and optimizing for performance metrics. Ricursive's AI platform promises to compress these timelines by learning from each design iteration and automatically improving subsequent attempts. The global chip shortage has exposed just how brittle our semiconductor supply chains really are, with everything from cars to gaming consoles sitting idle in factories waiting for processors. While most solutions focus on manufacturing capacity, Ricursive is betting that the real bottleneck is in the design phase itself. The startup's founders detailed how their platform works during the launch, explaining that their AI doesn't just automate existing design processes - it fundamentally reimagines them. The system analyzes successful chip architectures, identifies patterns in performance optimization, and then applies those learnings to generate entirely new designs. Each iteration feeds back into the system, creating what they describe as a "recursive intelligence" loop that gets smarter with every chip it creates. Just as Google Cloud's Gemini Agent has been automating enterprise workflows and Meta's Muse platform has been streamlining small business operations, Ricursive is applying similar principles to semiconductor design. Chip design involves balancing countless variables - power consumption, heat generation, processing speed, manufacturing constraints, and cost optimization. That's why the industry has been so conservative about embracing automation, preferring human expertise over algorithmic decision-making. But Ricursive's bet is that AI has finally reached the sophistication needed to handle this complexity. Their platform reportedly uses advanced machine learning models trained on decades of chip design data, combined with real-time feedback loops that let the system learn from both successes and failures. The goal isn't to replace human designers entirely, but to accelerate the iteration cycles that currently bottleneck the entire process. The startup joins a growing wave of companies applying AI to traditionally manual processes. We've seen similar approaches in supply chain automation, where former Tesla engineers recently raised $12.5 million to automate logistics operations. The pattern suggests we're entering a phase where AI is moving beyond consumer applications into the foundational infrastructure that powers our digital economy. Major players like Nvidia, AMD, and Intel are all racing to develop more powerful chips for AI workloads, while the broader market struggles with supply constraints that have persisted since the pandemic. If Ricursive's approach proves viable, it could help address both challenges simultaneously - accelerating the development of next-generation processors while reducing the time-to-market that's been hampering supply chain recovery. The company hasn't disclosed funding details or customer partnerships yet, but the launch signals growing confidence in AI's ability to tackle increasingly complex engineering challenges. Whether their approach can deliver on its ambitious promises remains to be seen, but the semiconductor industry's desperate need for faster design cycles suggests there's significant appetite for any solution that can compress development timelines. Ricursive Intelligence's AI-powered chip design platform represents a bold bet on automation solving one of tech's most persistent bottlenecks. While the semiconductor industry has traditionally been conservative about embracing algorithmic design, the ongoing compute crisis and supply chain constraints create unprecedented pressure for innovation. If successful, this approach could fundamentally reshape how chips are developed, potentially accelerating the next generation of processors that power everything from smartphones to data centers. The real test will be whether AI can match the precision and creativity that human engineers have brought to chip design for decades.

The founders took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Wednesday to detail how their startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from each iteration, and improve subsequent designs, all with the goal of automating and accelerating the chip design process.

“There is this understanding that in the next five years we are going to have at least 10,000x more demand for compute, and that’s somewhat potentially conservative,” Goldie said on stage. “So we don’t want to build 10,000 times more data centers. We think that we need to help by making chips that are more efficient, that use the bandwidth in those data centers more efficiently, that use the wafers and fabs more efficiently, because even if we make [data centers] in space or something, I don’t know, you won’t see the sun anymore.”

While some may be scared by the thought of AI designing its own chips, Goldie argues that letting AI handle chip design will allow humans can focus on developing applications and exploring new possibilities that can expand what they can accomplish with computing.

“I think the way everything is shifting is that humans come bring their great ideas and creative thoughts, and execution is handled by AI,” Goldie said. “And this is happening in chip design, software development, and other places. And that’s something that recursive does for chip design.”

The founders say AI is challenging traditional chip design methods by discovering unconventional layouts that can outperform traditional ones. For example, AlphaChip, the AI system the founders previously developed, produced a circular, “donut-shaped” arrangement of chip components that initially surprised engineers but ultimately proved to be successful.

They explained that they are optimizing entire chips rather than following the traditional approach of partitioning them into dozens of smaller blocks. This approach allows AI to create intricate patterns, including wave-like designs, which the pair said they plan to share more about in the future.
The founders also argued that AI-designed chips will make it possible to create all sorts of chips that might not have been possible before.

“If it takes six months or a year or two years to design a new chip, then you really have to be extremely selective about the chips that you design,” Goldie said. “But if you can design a chip in like a week, and then say for manufacturing, you can design custom chips for all sorts of different types of applications in like space and AR, VR, and you biological computing, and it makes sense financially to do that, and we can be more energy efficient.”

sources.title: Ricursive Intelligence Bets AI Can Solve Chip Design Crisis
passages: Ricursive Intelligence emerged from stealth today with a platform that promises to automate the notoriously complex chip design process, using machine learning to iterate and improve with each design cycle.
The real test will be whether AI can match the precision and creativity that human engineers have brought to chip design for decades.
Traditional chip design requires teams of engineers working through countless iterations, debugging complex architectures, and optimizing for performance metrics.
Chip design involves balancing countless variables - power consumption, heat generation, processing speed, manufacturing constraints, and cost optimization.

Just as Google Cloud's Gemini Agent has been automating enterprise workflows and Meta's Muse platform has been streamlining small business operations, Ricursive is applying similar principles to semiconductor design.
While most solutions focus on manufacturing capacity, Ricursive is betting that the real bottleneck is in the design phase itself.
The system analyzes successful chip architectures, identifies patterns in performance optimization, and then applies those learnings to generate entirely new designs.

While the semiconductor industry has traditionally been conservative about embracing algorithmic design, the ongoing compute crisis and supply chain constraints create unprecedented pressure for innovation.
The timing couldn't be more critical as the industry grapples with a compute crisis that's throttling everything from data centers to consumer devices.

If Ricursive's approach proves viable, it could help address both challenges simultaneously - accelerating the development of next-generation processors while reducing the time-to-market that's been hampering supply chain recovery.

extraction.body: A new startup is taking aim at the semiconductor industry's biggest bottleneck with an audacious proposition: let AI design the chips themselves. Ricursive Intelligence emerged from stealth today with a platform that promises to automate the notoriously complex chip design process, using machine learning to iterate and improve with each design cycle. The timing couldn't be more critical as the industry grapples with a compute crisis that's throttling everything from data centers to consumer devices. The semiconductor shortage that's been choking tech supply chains for years just got a potential lifeline from an unexpected source: artificial intelligence. Ricursive Intelligence, a startup that's been quietly developing in stealth mode, just unveiled an AI platform designed to revolutionize how chips are created by letting machines handle the entire design process. The company's approach tackles one of the industry's most persistent problems - the months or even years it takes to design and validate new semiconductors. Traditional chip design requires teams of engineers working through countless iterations, debugging complex architectures, and optimizing for performance metrics. Ricursive's AI platform promises to compress these timelines by learning from each design iteration and automatically improving subsequent attempts. The global chip shortage has exposed just how brittle our semiconductor supply chains really are, with everything from cars to gaming consoles sitting idle in factories waiting for processors. While most solutions focus on manufacturing capacity, Ricursive is betting that the real bottleneck is in the design phase itself. The startup's founders detailed how their platform works during the launch, explaining that their AI doesn't just automate existing design processes - it fundamentally reimagines them. The system analyzes successful chip architectures, identifies patterns in performance optimization, and then applies those learnings to generate entirely new designs. Each iteration feeds back into the system, creating what they describe as a "recursive intelligence" loop that gets smarter with every chip it creates. Just as Google Cloud's Gemini Agent has been automating enterprise workflows and Meta's Muse platform has been streamlining small business operations, Ricursive is applying similar principles to semiconductor design. Chip design involves balancing countless variables - power consumption, heat generation, processing speed, manufacturing constraints, and cost optimization. That's why the industry has been so conservative about embracing automation, preferring human expertise over algorithmic decision-making. But Ricursive's bet is that AI has finally reached the sophistication needed to handle this complexity. Their platform reportedly uses advanced machine learning models trained on decades of chip design data, combined with real-time feedback loops that let the system learn from both successes and failures. The goal isn't to replace human designers entirely, but to accelerate the iteration cycles that currently bottleneck the entire process. The startup joins a growing wave of companies applying AI to traditionally manual processes. We've seen similar approaches in supply chain automation, where former Tesla engineers recently raised $12.5 million to automate logistics operations. The pattern suggests we're entering a phase where AI is moving beyond consumer applications into the foundational infrastructure that powers our digital economy. Major players like Nvidia, AMD, and Intel are all racing to develop more powerful chips for AI workloads, while the broader market struggles with supply constraints that have persisted since the pandemic. If Ricursive's approach proves viable, it could help address both challenges simultaneously - accelerating the development of next-generation processors while reducing the time-to-market that's been hampering supply chain recovery. The company hasn't disclosed funding details or customer partnerships yet, but the launch signals growing confidence in AI's ability to tackle increasingly complex engineering challenges. Whether their approach can deliver on its ambitious promises remains to be seen, but the semiconductor industry's desperate need for faster design cycles suggests there's significant appetite for any solution that can compress development timelines. While the semiconductor industry has traditionally been conservative about embracing algorithmic design, the ongoing compute crisis and supply chain constraints create unprecedented pressure for innovation. If successful, this approach could fundamentally reshape how chips are developed, potentially accelerating the next generation of processors that power everything from smartphones to data centers. The real test will be whether AI can match the precision and creativity that human engineers have brought to chip design for decades.

extraction.body: The FY27 budget request sets aside $994 million in total for small c-UAS, with all of that sum coming from discretionary funding. WASHINGTON — Under the Defense Department’s nearly $1.5 trillion fiscal 2027 budget request, the Army would have almost $1 billion in procurement funding to spend on small counter unmanned aerial system technology (cUAS) capabilities — nearly double the amount the service was granted in its enacted budget for FY26. Should Congress approve it, the FY27 budget would set asi de $994 million in total for small cUAS, with all of that sum coming from discretionary funding. The FY26 enacted budget included $596 million for the same line item with $336 deriving from discretionary spending and $260 coming from mandatory, or reconciliation, funding. The Army is taking the approach of having a “systems of systems” architecture for its small counter-drone capabilities, per budget justification books. Such an architecture will include expeditionary and mobile platforms, sensors, effectors, electronic warfare components and more to make up an interoperable fire control system. There are eight areas where the Army plans to spend the almost $1 billion. The largest chunk is for “operational” small cUAS capabilities at $414 million. This includes broad funding for c-UAS batteries and “expeditionary” mobile platforms and sensors. Next, the Army plans to spend $165 million on “fixed” capabilities, which, according to the justification books, are any “additional” joint force and Army counter-drone capabilities needed for homeland defense and specified fixed sites defense, also known as base or installation defense. This line also includes funding for logistics support efforts for small cUAS. The topic of using counter-drone measures to protect bases and installations has been a hot one in recent months as the Defense Department has struggled to find common ground with other federal agencies, such as the Federal Aviation Administration, on what capabilities can be used to shoot down drones that appear to act as a security threat to such locations. The service plans to spend $132 million on what it calls “effectors,” and though there are sparse details in the justification books on what such capabilities really are, the Army states it is planning to procure 800 kinetic capabilities, 29 non-kinetic capabilities and 24 of the Next Generation cUAS Missile (NGCM). The NGCM, also known as the Freedom Eagle-1 , is a kinetic platform made by Aerovironment . Next, the Army plans to spend $108 million on squad- and individual soldier-level small cUAS capabilities. These include “dismounted, handheld, and wearable systems” for protection against Group 1 and Group 2 UAS threats, per the books. The service also plans to spend $80 million on small cUAS for brigade and below elements, which similar to the squad- and individual soldier-level line, includes capabilities for fighting off Group 1 and 2 drones. Directed energy, a growing cUAS capability within the service, is set to receive $66 milli on, to include two Enduring High Energy Laser ( E-HEL ) systems. This line item is a “rapid prototyping effort” and will be interoperable with the Army’s Integrated Battle Command System -Maneuver, the books read. The service is also looking to spend $24 million on expeditionary launcher systems and mobile launcher systems. Though details for the effort were scant in the justification documents, they noted t he service is looking to acquire 12 expeditionary launcher systems and 10 mobile launcher systems for one service cUAS battery. Lastly, the Army is looking to spend almost $5 million for the small cUAS “ground readiness” lines, which provide funding for logistics support for the Army’s Family of Counter Unmanned Aircraft Systems (FoCUS) program that was procured in prior years. The program oversees the Army’s development of an agnostic, medium-range small cUAS system. The uptick in small counter-drone funding comes as the world continues to see inexpensive, small first-person-view drones taking out muti-million-dollar tanks on the modern battlefield, such as in the Ukraine-Russia war . The Iran conflict has also shown the importance of emerging, cheap cUAS capabilities. For example, interceptors, like the Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement, can cost between $3 million and $4 million, but are reportedly being used to shoot down Iranian-made Shahed drones that cost just $4,000 in Operation Epic Fury .

extraction.body: Counter-drone systems can combine radar, cameras, radio-frequency sensors and other equipment to detect, track and identify potential threats. Honeywell Aerospace’s SAMURAI system is designed to bring information from those disparate sources into a single interface. The system uses UNITAS , Honeywell Aerospace’s battle-management software, to integrate sensors and effectors from different manufacturers. “There is no one solution that solves every threat out there,” said retired Air Force Col. Tom Konicki, director of business at Honeywell Aerospace. The threat ranges from recreational drones flown into restricted airspace to unmanned aircraft that could be used to attack military installations or other critical infrastructure. Konicki said counter-drone systems need to detect, track, identify, classify and ultimately defeat drones, regardless of the operator’s intent. “The threat is real, and the threat is now,” he added. While SAMURAI stands for Stationary and Mobile UAS Reveal and Intercept, UNITAS is not an acronym. Konicki said the name was inspired by football player Johnny Unitas. Counter-drone systems can combine several types of equipment. Radar detects objects at a distance, while radio-frequency sensors can detect signals associated with drones or their controllers. Remote identification equipment can receive identifying information broadcast by compliant drones. Electro-optical and infrared cameras allow operators to examine objects more closely, while acoustic sensors can help detect drones by their sound. Depending on the threat and equipment available, counter-drone systems can also use electronic warfare, directed-energy systems, conventional weapons or interceptor drones to defeat an aircraft. Some systems use nets to capture drones, an approach that can be designed to reduce the risk of debris falling onto people or property. Konicki said operators of some counter-drone systems must monitor six, seven or eight separate screens for radar, cameras, radio-frequency sensors, jamming equipment and other capabilities. That can require one operator to track multiple information streams simultaneously. UNITAS is designed to consolidate the feeds so operators can view information from multiple sensors together in one interface. “We call it a single pane of glass,” Konicki said. “There could be seven different sensors that have identified it and are feeding that into our software.” Konicki said the interface is designed to be straightforward for operators, including younger service members who may be assigned counter-drone duties without extensive experience operating the different systems. He said Honeywell Aerospace has demonstrated the software to U.S. government and military representatives, as well as local law enforcement and state and city representatives. The software also uses an open-architecture approach, allowing customers to integrate equipment they already own instead of replacing it with products from a single manufacturer. “We’re not asking them to go buy new stuff,” Konicki said. “We can integrate with what they already have.” Customers can choose equipment suited to their needs and update components as detection technologies and countermeasures evolve. Konicki said Honeywell Aerospace works with other companies to incorporate their technologies rather than lock customers into a single vendor’s products. He said the company seeks equipment mature enough for operational use rather than untested technology. At the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting, Honeywell Aerospace displayed a mockup of the mobile configuration mounted on the back of a Ford F-150. Konicki called it the “Green Beast.” Honeywell Aerospace is also developing an airborne application of SAMURAI with Odys Aviation. Announced in March 2026, the collaboration aims to adapt the system for Odys’ long-range Laila uncrewed aircraft. The companies said the effort builds on more than a year of joint development and systems-integration work. Laila is intended to be the first airborne application of SAMURAI, extending the system beyond ground-based and mobile configurations. Konicki said SAMURAI can also be configured for fixed-site protection and maritime operations. Depending on the mission, customers might position equipment around a building or installation, use a mobile configuration for temporary protection at an event, or place sensors at distributed locations to cover a larger area. Separately, Honeywell Aerospace announced Oct. 12 that its wholly owned subsidiary, EMS Defense Technologies, was selected for a Department of Homeland Security counter-drone contract vehicle . The five-year, multiple-award vehicle has a $1.5 billion ceiling, was awarded July 31 and took effect Aug. 1. Konicki said Honeywell Aerospace works with international partners, including Lithuania, Slovakia and Colombia, and can integrate locally sourced equipment when customers want to use particular sensors or effectors. For customers protecting an air base or another site, Konicki said the company can assess where radar, cameras and other sensors should be positioned to maximize coverage. Its planning process can map areas with adequate coverage, identify gaps and recommend adjustments to equipment placement. The company can then conduct what Konicki described as a red-team assessment, examining where an adversary might launch a drone and how that approach could affect the site’s defenses. The analysis will help customers tailor sensor placement and other system components to the site and its potential threats. Drawing on her experience as a talent executive and mentor, she writes about the policies, people and programs shaping the military community.

extraction.body: The FY27 budget request sets aside $994 million in total for small c-UAS, with all of that sum coming from discretionary funding. WASHINGTON — Under the Defense Department’s nearly $1.5 trillion fiscal 2027 budget request, the Army would have almost $1 billion in procurement funding to spend on small counter unmanned aerial system technology (cUAS) capabilities — nearly double the amount the service was granted in its enacted budget for FY26. Should Congress approve it, the FY27 budget would set asi de $994 million in total for small cUAS, with all of that sum coming from discretionary funding. The FY26 enacted budget included $596 million for the same line item with $336 deriving from discretionary spending and $260 coming from mandatory, or reconciliation, funding. The Army is taking the approach of having a “systems of systems” architecture for its small counter-drone capabilities, per budget justification books. Such an architecture will include expeditionary and mobile platforms, sensors, effectors, electronic warfare components and more to make up an interoperable fire control system. There are eight areas where the Army plans to spend the almost $1 billion. The largest chunk is for “operational” small cUAS capabilities at $414 million. This includes broad funding for c-UAS batteries and “expeditionary” mobile platforms and sensors. Next, the Army plans to spend $165 million on “fixed” capabilities, which, according to the justification books, are any “additional” joint force and Army counter-drone capabilities needed for homeland defense and specified fixed sites defense, also known as base or installation defense. This line also includes funding for logistics support efforts for small cUAS. The topic of using counter-drone measures to protect bases and installations has been a hot one in recent months as the Defense Department has struggled to find common ground with other federal agencies, such as the Federal Aviation Administration, on what capabilities can be used to shoot down drones that appear to act as a security threat to such locations. The service plans to spend $132 million on what it calls “effectors,” and though there are sparse details in the justification books on what such capabilities really are, the Army states it is planning to procure 800 kinetic capabilities, 29 non-kinetic capabilities and 24 of the Next Generation cUAS Missile (NGCM). The NGCM, also known as the Freedom Eagle-1 , is a kinetic platform made by Aerovironment . Next, the Army plans to spend $108 million on squad- and individual soldier-level small cUAS capabilities. These include “dismounted, handheld, and wearable systems” for protection against Group 1 and Group 2 UAS threats, per the books. The service also plans to spend $80 million on small cUAS for brigade and below elements, which similar to the squad- and individual soldier-level line, includes capabilities for fighting off Group 1 and 2 drones. Directed energy, a growing cUAS capability within the service, is set to receive $66 milli on, to include two Enduring High Energy Laser ( E-HEL ) systems. This line item is a “rapid prototyping effort” and will be interoperable with the Army’s Integrated Battle Command System -Maneuver, the books read. The service is also looking to spend $24 million on expeditionary launcher systems and mobile launcher systems. Though details for the effort were scant in the justification documents, they noted t he service is looking to acquire 12 expeditionary launcher systems and 10 mobile launcher systems for one service cUAS battery. Lastly, the Army is looking to spend almost $5 million for the small cUAS “ground readiness” lines, which provide funding for logistics support for the Army’s Family of Counter Unmanned Aircraft Systems (FoCUS) program that was procured in prior years. The program oversees the Army’s development of an agnostic, medium-range small cUAS system. The uptick in small counter-drone funding comes as the world continues to see inexpensive, small first-person-view drones taking out muti-million-dollar tanks on the modern battlefield, such as in the Ukraine-Russia war . The Iran conflict has also shown the importance of emerging, cheap cUAS capabilities. For example, interceptors, like the Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement, can cost between $3 million and $4 million, but are reportedly being used to shoot down Iranian-made Shahed drones that cost just $4,000 in Operation Epic Fury .
