extraction.body: Adipose tissue has a central role in systemic energy balance and the pathogenesis of obesity and its sequelae 1 , 2 . In contrast to white adipose tissue, brown adipose tissue (BAT) uses energy to produce heat 3 . Detectable BAT in humans is associated with decreased prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases 4 . However, the complete spectrum of health conditions associated with BAT remains unknown, and high-throughput methods to quantify BAT activity in humans are lacking 5 , 6 . Here we leveraged big data and artificial intelligence to systematically define the clinical impact of BAT in a cohort of 101,243 patients from a large cancer centre. Our unbiased analyses revealed that, across all diagnoses, cardiovascular and psychiatric diseases were less prevalent in people with BAT. Using a machine learning approach, we semi-automatically quantified BAT activity in approximately 8,700 patients and demonstrated that higher BAT activity, especially in the axillary depot, is associated with lower odds of cardiometabolic diseases and healthier white fat distribution. People with BAT also exhibited more favourable glycaemic parameters, lipid profiles, inflammatory markers and echocardiographic indices. Analysis of medication usage demonstrated that angiotensin receptor blocker use was positively associated with BAT presence. As proof of concept, we showed that the angiotensin receptor blocker losartan increased brown adipocyte activity and whole-body energy expenditure. Altogether, our studies harnessing artificial intelligence and big data identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT and serve as a platform for drug repurposing to activate this tissue in humans. Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes (T2D), hypertension and cardiovascular disease 2 , 7 . Adipose tissue dysfunction is a hallmark of obesity and contributes to the pathophysiology of cardiometabolic diseases 1 . White adipose tissue (WAT) stores energy as triglyceride 1 in subcutaneous and visceral depots, and visceral adiposity is a key feature of metabolically unhealthy obesity 8 . By contrast, brown adipose tissue (BAT) dissipates energy as heat (thermogenesis) and its activation in animal models protects against obesity and metabolic diseases 3 . However, the relevance of BAT to adult human physiology and whether it can be targeted therapeutically remain unclear 5 , 6 . Since the landmark reports that adult humans have inducible BAT 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , several clinical studies have aimed to recruit BAT through cold exposure or β-adrenergic agonists 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 . Although these interventions activate BAT and improve glucose homeostasis, their side effects and the small number of participants studied have limited their clinical impact 5 . More recently, our group described the largest reported cohort of people with BAT and demonstrated that the presence of BAT in 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)–computed tomography (CT) (18F-FDG-PET–CT) scans obtained for clinical purposes and without previous stimulation was associated with reduced prevalence of cardiometabolic disease 4 . A caveat from this work is that patients were characterized based on BAT presence or absence, rather than by quantitative BAT metabolic activity. Like WAT, human BAT is localized in distinct anatomic depots 18 , but whether these depots uniquely affect health remains unknown. Moreover, most human BAT studies have focused on cardiometabolic outcomes, but how this tissue influences other organ systems and disease types remains largely unexplored. These limitations have hindered the identification of pharmacologic agents that promote BAT activity, and there are no approved, widely used medications to leverage the cardiometabolic benefits linked to this tissue. In this study we expanded our cohort to more than 100,000 patients and performed an unbiased, comprehensive analysis across all diagnostic codes to identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT presence. Furthermore, we harnessed artificial intelligence (AI) to semi-automatically quantify total and depot-specific BAT metabolic activity from 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans. This allowed us to investigate associations between specific BAT depots, WAT distribution and cardiometabolic outcomes. Finally, we combined these approaches with medication use analyses to identify pharmacologic regulators of BAT and performed proof-of-concept experiments to validate losartan as an activator of brown adipocytes through a unique, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPARγ)-dependent mechanism. To discover associations between BAT and diseases beyond the cardiometabolic system, we expanded our previously described cohort (Established BAT Cohort) 4 by reviewing additional FDG-PET–CT scans taken from 2018 to 2024 at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. Of these, 4.4% reported BAT presence and 4,778 patients (7.9%) had at least one scan positive for BAT (hereafter termed BAT positive (BAT + ); Extended Data Fig. 1a ). The remaining patients were designated BAT negative (BAT − ). These newly identified participants were grouped in an Extension BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1a ) that validated findings from our Established BAT Cohort 4 demonstrating lower prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases in people who are BAT + (Extended Data Fig. 1b ). To increase statistical power, we merged the Established and Extension BAT Cohorts to create an Expanded BAT Cohort, consisting of 101,243 patients, of whom 8,897 were BAT + and 92,346 were BAT − . Each patient was assigned an index scan as a reference point for clinical data collection (Extended Data Fig. 1a ). Similar to previous findings 4 , BAT was more prevalent in women in the Expanded BAT Cohort, and its prevalence decreased with age, higher ambient temperature at the time of the scan and increasing body mass index (BMI) (Extended Data Fig. 1c–f ). Given the influence of these variables on BAT prevalence, we used propensity score matching (PSM) to create a cohort of patients in the BAT + ( n = 8,897) and BAT − ( n = 17,405) groups balanced across age, sex, BMI and ambient temperature (Extended Data Fig. 1g,h ). As patients in our cohort come from a cancer centre, we extracted extensive cancer-associated data (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 ) for each patient in our PSM cohort, including site, stage and treatment. We confirmed that certain cancer sites were more frequent (for example, breast and oral cavity), less frequent (for example, digestive) or had no association (for example, skin, urinary) with BAT presence (Table 1 ). As in our previous report, some cancer treatments were used more frequently in the BAT + group 4 (Table 1 ). Consequently, all cancer-associated variables were controlled for unless otherwise stated for the remainder of this study. We then performed multi-variable logistic regression in this new, expanded PSM cohort and confirmed the association between BAT presence and decreased prevalence of select cardiometabolic diseases 4 (Extended Data Fig. 1i ). Given the sexual dimorphism in BAT presence and cardiometabolic traits, we performed separate analyses in women and men and found that BAT was associated with decreased odds of cardiometabolic diseases in both sexes in our PSM and Extension BAT Cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b ). To further investigate clinical correlates of BAT we extracted an expanded battery of available laboratory tests and imaging studies from patients in our PSM cohort (Extended Data Fig. 5a ) and performed analyses to identify differences between patients in the BAT + and BAT − groups (Supplementary Table 5 ). Patients with BAT had lower glucose ( P < 0.001), haemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) ( P < 0.001), triglycerides ( P < 0.001) and triglyceride-glucose index, as well as higher high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol (HDL-C) levels ( P < 0.001), even after adjusting for confounders (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 5b ). Paradoxically, patients with BAT also had higher total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). However, remnant cholesterol (total cholesterol − LDL − HDL)—an independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease 23 —was significantly lower in patients with BAT (Extended Data Fig. 5b ). Finally, patients with BAT exhibited lower circulating brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) (Extended Data Fig. 5b ). a , Comparisons of metabolic laboratory values in patients in the BAT − versus BAT + groups: glucose (BAT − , n = 17,338; BAT + , n = 8,877), HbA1c (BAT − , n = 2,036; BAT + , n = 841), HDL-C (BAT − , n = 1,587; BAT + , n = 828) and triglycerides (BAT − , n = 1,996; BAT + , n = 995). b , Association between total BAT metabolic activity and glucose ( n = 8,709), HbA1c ( n = 822) and systolic blood pressure ( n = 6,482) values. c , Comparisons of echocardiographic measurements in patients in the BAT − versus BAT + groups: left ventricular mass index (BAT − , n = 3,289; BAT + , n = 1,733), LVPWD (BAT − , n = 3,305; BAT + , n = 1,743) and relative wall thickness (RWT) (BAT − , n = 3,305; BAT + , n = 1,743). d , Association between total BAT metabolic activity and PASP ( n = 764), LVPWD ( n = 1,711) and RWT ( n = 1,711). e , Comparisons of hepatic and inflammatory laboratory values in patients in the BAT − versus BAT + groups: aspartate aminotransferase (BAT − , n = 15,506; BAT + , n = 8,078), alanine aminotransferase (BAT − , n = 15,509; BAT + , n = 8,082), neutrophil counts (BAT − , n = 14,874; BAT + , n = 7,827) and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) (BAT − , n = 14,575; BAT + , n = 7,670). f , Comparisons of DEXA scan measurements in patients in the BAT − versus BAT + groups: vertebral T -score (BAT − , n = 911; BAT + , n = 468) and femoral neck T -scores (BAT − , n = 914; BAT + , n = 470). In a , c , e and f , bar graphs depict mean values and error bars depict s.e.m. P values were obtained using a general linear model (GLM) followed by post hoc Tukey’s honest significance difference (HSD) test to compare least square means, adjusted for age, sex, BMI, race, ethnicity, ambient temperature, cancer site and stage, cancer treatment and outpatient medications. In b and d , associations between BAT metabolic activity (expressed as the product of SUV and BAT volume in millilitres) and clinical continuous variables were calculated using linear regression after logarithmic transformation. Regression coefficients ( β ) and corresponding P values are reported. ALT, alanine aminotransferase; AST, aspartate aminotransferase; LV, left ventricular; SBP, systolic blood pressure; TG, triglycerides. To expand on these observations, we used semi-quantitative BAT data from our AI tool to establish associations between continuous clinical parameters and BAT activity. We found an inverse association between total BAT metabolic activity and glucose levels ( P < 0.001), HbA1c ( P = 0.006), systolic blood pressure ( P < 0.001) (Fig. 3b ), mean arterial blood pressure ( P < 0.001) and BNP ( P = 0.01) and a trend with diastolic blood pressure ( P = 0.12) (Extended Data Fig. 5c ). We did not observe statistically significant associations between total BAT activity and lipids (Extended Data Fig. 5c ). Given the absence of large-scale studies linking BAT status with cardiac imaging in humans, and the association of BAT with higher carotid elasticity in a small prospective study 24 , we extracted available echocardiogram data from patients in our PSM cohort and performed association analyses. In alignment with previous findings 25 , patients with BAT had significantly lower left ventricular mass index ( P < 0.001), left ventricular posterior wall thickness in diastole (LVPWD) ( P < 0.001), relative wall thickness ( P < 0.001) (Fig. 3c ), pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) and mitral valve E/e’ ratio, with no changes in ejection fraction, left atrial volume index and mitral valve E/A ratio (Extended Data Fig. 5d ). Similarly, increasing BAT metabolic activity was associated inversely with PASP ( P < 0.001), LVPWD ( P = 0.01), relative wall thickness ( P < 0.001) (Fig. 3d ), mitral valve E/e’ ratio ( P = 0.002) and positively with mitral valve E/A ratio ( P < 0.001) (Extended Data Fig. 5e ). Other echocardiographic parameters did not exhibit associations with semi-quantitative BAT activity (Extended Data Fig. 5e ). These data demonstrate that BAT presence and activity associate with decreased markers of left ventricular remodelling. To unravel pharmacologic determinants of BAT presence, we extracted home medication data 1 month before the index scan in patients from our PSM cohort (Extended Data Fig. 6a ). In total, 125 individual medications were assessed for associations with BAT status after exclusions (Extended Data Fig. 6a ). Multi-variable logistic regression analyses identified that 39 of 125 medications exhibited a significant association with BAT status (Supplementary Table 6 ). Given that antibiotics are generally used in short courses, we excluded them from our list of chronic medications (Extended Data Fig. 6b ). However, as modulation of the microbiome by antimicrobials could affect thermogenic fat 27 , we performed a focused analysis on antibiotics and found that trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and several cephalosporins had positive associations with BAT status (Extended Data Fig. 6b ). Among our 39 candidate medications, we identified agents with known inhibitory effects on human BAT, such as β-blockers 9 , 28 . Specifically, atenolol (OR 0.42; 95% CI 0.27–0.64; P < 0.001) and propranolol (OR 0.38; 95% CI 0.20–0.74; P = 0.02) (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 6c ) exhibited negative associations with BAT presence. Other known negative regulators of BAT, namely, selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs) 29 such as fluoxetine (OR 0.33; 95% CI 0.21–0.51; P < 0.001), escitalopram (OR 0.60; 95% CI 0.48–0.75; P < 0.001) and sertraline (OR 0.57; 95% CI 0.44–0.75; P < 0.001) (Fig. 4a ), were also associated negatively with BAT. Given that people with BAT had a lower prevalence of psychiatric disease, we performed analyses on psychiatric medications controlling for relevant psychiatric diagnoses (Supplementary Table 7 ), and demonstrated that SSRIs retain their negative association with BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6d ). Among medications shown previously to activate BAT, we found that dexamethasone 30 was associated positively with BAT presence (OR 1.22; 95% CI 1.10–1.36; P = 0.001; Fig. 4a ). Mirabegron—a β3-adrenergic agonist that promotes BAT activity in humans 13 , 31 , 32 —also showed a trend towards being associated with BAT positivity (Extended Data Fig. 6e ). β2-adrenergic agonists (for example, inhaled salbutamol), which could promote BAT activity in humans 33 , 34 , did not show a significant association (Supplementary Table 6 ). These findings demonstrate that our platform can identify most known modulators of human BAT and could uncover new pharmacological regulators of this tissue. a , b , Forest plots showing ORs (circles) and 95% CIs (error bars) for associations of medications ( a ) and ARBs ( b ) with BAT status in the PSM cohort; P values, multi-variable logistic regression ( Methods ). c , Ucp1 RNA levels in brown adipocytes pre-treated with losartan or vehicle ± NE. d , UCP1 immunoblot in brown adipocytes pre-treated with losartan or vehicle ± NE. e , Oxygen consumption rate in brown adipocytes pre-treated with losartan or vehicle ( n = 12 technical replicates per group; squares, mean; error bars, s.e.m.). NE peak respiration and mean oxygen consumption rate during oligomycin were compared. f , PPARγ transcriptional activity in HEK293T cells treated with the compounds indicated ( n = 3 biological replicates per treatment per dose; squares, mean; error bars, s.e.m. Experiment repeated twice); P values, one-way analysis of variance. g , Ucp1 RNA levels in brown adipocytes pre-treated with GW9662 or vehicle and stimulated with losartan ± NE. h , Representative thermal camera images following CL-316243 injection in losartan-treated and control mice. i , BAT thermogenesis ( n = 10 mice per group; white, baseline temperature; red, temperature after CL-316243 injection). Baseline versus after CL-316243 injection values, paired t -tests; after CL-316243 injection between groups, unpaired t -test. j – l , Energy expenditure in losartan-treated mice ( n = 7) and controls ( n = 5) at 4 °C: representative 24-h energy expenditure (circles, mean; error bars, s.e.m.) ( j ), mean 24-h, dark- and light-phase energy expenditure ( k ) and analysis of covariance of energy expenditure versus body weight ( l ); P value, simple linear regression and comparing slopes. m , BAT Ucp1 RNA at room temperature ( n = 4 mice per group) or after 5 days at 4 °C (losartan, n = 8; control, n = 7). n , Representative BAT haematoxylin and eosin images at room temperature or 4 °C. In c and g , dots represent biological replicates from one representative experiment. Experiments in c – e and g were repeated three times with similar results. P values in c , e , g , k and m , unpaired, two-tailed t -test. CL, CL-316243; EE, energy expenditure; OCR, oxygen consumption rate; RT, room temperature. Scale bars, 10 μm. To further assess the effects of losartan on whole-body energy expenditure, indirect calorimetry was performed in wild-type mice pre-treated with losartan in their drinking water for 10 days at room temperature (Extended Data Fig. 9a ). Losartan-treated mice exhibited increased energy expenditure, O 2 consumption and CO 2 production, with no changes to their respiratory exchange ratio (RER), physical activity, food intake, body weight, fat mass or lean mass (Extended Data Fig. 9a–l ). To examine the effects of losartan on cold stress, we pre-treated a separate cohort of wild-type mice at room temperature as above and performed indirect calorimetry at 4 °C (Extended Data Fig. 10a ). Upon cold-induced BAT activation, losartan-treated mice again exhibited increased energy expenditure, O 2 consumption and CO 2 production, with no changes in RER (Fig. 4j,k and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e ). This was independent of body weight, as assayed by analysis of covariance (Fig. 4l ). There were no differences in locomotor activity and a trend towards increased food intake in losartan-treated mice (Extended Data Fig. 10f–h ), which probably explains why body weight did not change (Extended Data Fig. 10i ). Moreover, exposing mice treated with losartan to cold resulted in significantly increased BAT Ucp1 (Fig. 4m ), as well as smaller lipid droplets in brown adipocytes (Fig. 4n ). We observed similar histologic findings in inguinal fat; however, there was no statistically significant increase in Ucp1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 10j,k ). Taken together, these data indicate that losartan treatment results in enhanced BAT activation and increased whole-body energy expenditure. Despite substantial advances, the therapeutic potential for targeting BAT to manage metabolic disease remains preliminary 5 , 6 . This retrospective study explored associations between BAT and human health in the largest cohort reported so far. We validated the strong link between BAT and cardiovascular diseases, while uncovering a previously undescribed association with psychiatric diseases. Our new machine learning approach allowed us to quantify depot-specific BAT metabolic activity rapidly and establish that the degree of BAT activity is linked to cardiometabolic health and healthier fat distribution. Finally, medication usage analysis uncovered a positive association between ARB use and BAT presence. Proof-of-concept in vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that losartan activates brown adipocytes and promotes whole-body energy expenditure, demonstrating that our systems approach can identify pharmacologic agents that could be repurposed to activate BAT. Numerous studies in mice have shown that BAT activation protects against obesity and hyperglycaemia through increased energy expenditure, clearance of circulating substrates and secretion of beneficial hormones and metabolites 40 , 41 , 42 . In humans, cold exposure and β-adrenergic agonists increase BAT metabolic activity, which correlates with improved glucose homeostasis 13 , 14 . Our study confirms that, among all diagnoses, BAT is associated primarily with decreased prevalence of cardiovascular diseases, improved glycaemic, lipid and inflammatory profiles, and evidence of decreased pathological cardiac remodelling. Our large-scale, depot-specific analysis allowed us to identify axillary BAT as being linked most strongly with beneficial metabolic outcomes and healthier WAT distribution. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of thermogenic adipose tissues in humans and the importance of dissecting their cellular and molecular characteristics 20 , 21 , 22 . AI tools such as ours will allow other groups to analyse BAT semi-quantitatively in their cohorts and expand these findings to other populations worldwide. This approach continues to rely on BAT glucose uptake on 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans, which may or may not correlate with BAT temperature and thermogenic capacity 43 , 44 , and could be influenced significantly by insulin resistance 45 . To this point, we found that insulin-sensitizing medications such as metformin 46 were associated negatively with BAT presence (adjusting for diabetes status), and medications like olanzapine 47 , which promote insulin resistance, were linked positively to BAT. This indicates that the clinical findings in our study cannot be explained simply by altered insulin sensitivity. Beyond metabolic diseases, BAT presence was associated with a lower prevalence of anxiety and depression. This could be explained by studies linking healthier metabolic profiles and decreased visceral adiposity to lower rates of psychiatric disease 48 , 49 , 50 . Small studies have linked cold exposure—a known activator of BAT—to improved mental health 51 , 52 . Furthermore, BAT prevalence decreased with SSRI use, confirming findings from a recent, prospective human study 29 . Future studies focused on how BAT affects mood and behaviour, and the role of anti-depressants in this crosstalk are warranted. BAT presence was associated with lower prevalence of liver disease and improved hepatic function, consistent with previous studies 53 , 54 . Conversely, patients in the BAT + group showed a trend towards higher prevalence of osteoporosis and decreased lumbar bone mineral density, contrasting with previous reports linking cold-activated BAT with higher bone mineral density 55 . Although mouse studies suggest an endocrine connection between brown fat and bone 56 , we cannot rule out that the observed association is specific to our cancer-centre-based cohort. Future trials on human BAT therapeutics should include assessment of bone health. Our study uses a reverse translational approach, starting with a large human dataset that informs proof-of-concept experiments, to bridge the gap between predominantly mouse-based discoveries and human brown fat biology. Through this platform, we identified several ARBs that are associated positively with BAT and demonstrate that the medication used most widely in this family, losartan, directly activates brown adipocytes through PPARγ, independently of AT1R signalling. In vivo treatment with losartan at baseline and during a cold challenge resulted in increased whole-body energy expenditure. By contrast, a previous report described a role for losartan in beiging of white fat through AT1R-dependent apelin secretion 57 . Compared with losartan, its inactive metabolite EXP3179 exhibits higher PPARγ agonism in vitro, and it probably mediates most of the effects of losartan on BAT in vivo. In humans, chronic treatment with losartan resulted in increased serum levels of EXP3179 with a peak 2 h after treatment, and increased expression of PPARγ gene targets in circulating monocytes 37 . Treatment with ARBs has been associated with reductions in newly diagnosed diabetes 58 , which could be linked to its effects on brown fat. Our study has several limitations. First, its retrospective design highlights the need for large prospective studies; however, we controlled for several clinical confounders and validated the association of losartan with BAT experimentally. Second, 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans were obtained without previous cold exposure, potentially underestimating BAT prevalence. Third, our convenience cohort was derived from a cancer centre and, despite controlling extensively for cancer-related variables, we cannot exclude effects from tumour types or cancer therapies. For instance, BAT is linked to higher breast cancer prevalence, lower odds of gastrointestinal malignancies and higher usage of cancer treatments such as mitotic inhibitors. Studies in mice have suggested activation of BAT reduces cancer progression by decreasing available circulating glucose for tumour metabolism 59 . To our knowledge, there is no literature demonstrating direct effects of mitotic inhibitors or other cancer therapies on brown adipocytes, and future studies of these associations are warranted. Until a reliable biomarker or non-invasive test for BAT is established, a large, prospective study involving 18F-FDG-PET–CT in the non-oncologic setting is highly implausible. At present, a large PSM cohort is the most feasible approach to assess BAT and clinical phenotypes comprehensively in humans. In conclusion, we describe new associations between BAT and clinical outcomes through big data and AI-based analyses. Our systems-approach provides a resource for the field and can be extended to study other regulators of BAT such as genetics. Finally, our proof-of-concept studies demonstrate that losartan activates brown adipocytes through a PPARγ dependent mechanism, raising the possibility that this agent could be repurposed to activate BAT in humans. This retrospective case–control study followed institutional guidelines and was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK), protocol number 17-581. The requirement for informed consent was waived because the study involved secondary analysis of previously acquired PET–CT imaging and clinical data, posed no more than minimal risk to participants and could not be conducted practically with individual informed consent. All patient data were deidentified before use. We previously established a cohort of patients with BAT by analysing 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans performed at MSK from June 2009 through March 2018 4 . Patients who were positive for BAT in at least one scan were termed BAT + , whereas the remaining patients were grouped as BAT − . To expand this cohort, we established a new Extension BAT Cohort by following a similar strategy. We reviewed all 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans performed at MSK from patients aged 18 years and above from April 2018 through July 2024. People who were positive for BAT on at least one scan were termed BAT + , whereas the remaining patients were grouped as BAT − (Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 2 ). For each patient in both groups, an index scan was designated: in patients with BAT reported on at least one 18F-FDG-PET–CT scan, the first scan that reported BAT was defined as the index scan. In patients without BAT on any scan, the first 18F-FDG-PET–CT scan served as the index scan. We collected demographic, BMI, outside temperature data and pertinent ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes corresponding to cardiometabolic diseases 4 (1 year after the index scan) (Supplementary Table 8 ) from the institutional EHR. Average outdoor temperatures in New York City were obtained from the US National Weather Service. An initial logistic regression analysis was performed on patients in the BAT + versus BAT − groups who belonged exclusively to the Extension BAT Cohort to establish associations between BAT presence and cardiometabolic diseases. As the association of BAT presence with reduced prevalence of cardiometabolic disease was confirmed in the Extension BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1b ), we proceeded to merge the Established BAT Cohort with the Extension BAT Cohort to create an Expanded BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1a ). If a patient was present in both cohorts, data from the Established BAT Cohort were used. We collected pertinent clinical data for each patient as described previously 4 . In brief, for cancer site, we included the specific cancer diagnostic code (ICD-0) listed closest to the index scan date (Supplementary Table 1 ). Data referring to cancer treatment were collected if administered within 90 days before the index scan and classified as previously 4 (Supplementary Table 2 ). Pertinent ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes corresponding to cardiometabolic diseases 4 (Supplementary Table 8 ) and all other codes were extracted up to 1 year after the index scan in patients from our PSM cohort. Codes were selected to represent non-paediatric, non-obstetric, adult disorders as explained below. For laboratory values, clinical indices and imaging studies, we extracted available data up to 1 year after the index scan in our PSM cohort. Analyses were performed in BAT + and BAT − patients with available values. To identify individual pharmacological agents associated with BAT presence, we extracted medications in the home medication list and/or medications with an active pharmacy prescription in the EHR from each patient belonging to our PSM cohort. We included only medications listed up to 1 month before the index scan for each patient. We excluded pharmacological agents with unlikely systemic effects, such as those with topical, ophthalmic, nasal and otic administration. Antimicrobials were excluded as they are generally prescribed in short courses. Medications classified as ‘as needed’ and herbal supplements were excluded. Medications with low frequency counts (present in fewer than 40 patients) were excluded. A final list of medications included in the analyses can be found in Supplementary Table 9 . These medications were also grouped by general categories as described in Supplementary Table 9 . To explore unbiased associations between BAT and other diseases, we extracted from the EHR diagnostic codes (ICD-9 and ICD-10) listed up to 1 year after the index scan from patients belonging to our PSM cohort. To select the codes for extraction, we grouped ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes based on their first three letters and/or digits. ICD-10 codes belonging to general groupings: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N and R were included as they group the medical pathologies most likely to be found in a non-paediatric, non-obstetric, adult cancer population. A similar rationale was used for the selection of ICD-9 codes. A total of 1,157 ICD-10 codes and 626 ICD-9 codes were queried for extraction from the EHR. The association between BAT and age, BMI and temperature was assessed by a Pearson’s correlation coefficient. Prevalence of BAT in men and women was compared using a chi-squared test. To assess whether BAT status was a predictor of cardiometabolic diseases in the PSM cohort, we used multi-variable logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, BMI, ambient temperature, self-reported race and ethnicity, smoking history, family history of cardiovascular disease, cancer site, cancer stage, cancer treatment and general groups of outpatient medications. BAT metabolic activity (total and depot-specific) was calculated as the product of SUV mean and BAT volume (in millilitres) and stratified into tertiles. The association of BAT activity with cardiometabolic diseases was assessed using a multi-variable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, BMI and outdoor temperature with patients in the BAT − group or those in tertile 1 (lowest BAT metabolic activity) as reference. The correlation of BAT activity with age and outside temperature was calculated with Pearson correlation coefficient after logarithmic transformation. The association of BAT activity with SAT area, VAT area, SAT to VAT ratio and other continuous clinical variables was calculated with linear regression after logarithmic transformation. The association of BAT status and an expanded set of 511 ICD codes was assessed by univariable logistic regression to identify crude associations. ICD codes associated significantly with BAT were then analysed individually through multi-variable logistic regression analysis adjusting for age, sex, BMI, ambient temperature, self-reported race and ethnicity, smoking history, family history of cardiovascular disease, cancer site, cancer stage, cancer treatment and general groups of outpatient medications. For over-representation analysis, the 511 codes were grouped by organ system. Enrichment for each organ system category was calculated based on the proportion of BAT-associated ICD codes divided by the corresponding proportion among all diagnostic codes in the category set. Statistical significance of over-representation was assessed using Fisher’s exact test and Benjamini–Hochberg FDR was used for multiple test adjustments. Unpaired t -tests were used to compare laboratory values, imaging studies and clinical indices in patients in the BAT + versus BAT − groups. Variance equality was assessed with an F -test. When variances were equal, standard t -tests assuming equal variances were used; otherwise, t -tests with unequal variance adjustments were applied. For adjusted analyses, GLMs were used to estimate least square means, adjusting for age, sex, BMI, self-reported race and ethnicity, ambient temperature, cancer site, cancer stage and cancer treatment. Post hoc pairwise comparisons were performed using Tukey’s HSD method. Categorical variables were compared using Fisher’s exact test. Associations between BAT and individual medications were assessed through multi-variable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, BMI, temperature, ethnicity, race, smoking history, family history of cardiovascular disease, cancer sites, cancer stage, cancer treatment and cardiovascular diagnoses. For in vitro and in vivo proof-of-concept experiments, group comparisons were conducted using unpaired t -tests. To account for multiple comparisons, P values were corrected using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR method, and adjusted P values are reported as such where applicable. Metabolic cage data were analysed, and statistical significance was calculated either using two-way analysis of variance for hourly data or unpaired t -test for 24-h cumulative, light and dark cycle. All analyses were performed using SAS (v.9.4), R software (v.4.5.1) and GraphPad Prism (v.10.5.0). All reported P values are two-sided and statistical significance was defined as α < 0.05. passages: Adipose tissue has a central role in systemic energy balance and the pathogenesis of obesity and its sequelae 1 , 2 . In contrast to white adipose tissue, brown adipose tissue (BAT) uses energy to produce heat 3 . Detectable BAT in humans is associated with decreased prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases 4 . However, the complete spectrum of health conditions associated with BAT remains unknown, and high-throughput methods to quantify BAT activity in humans are lacking 5 , 6 . Here we leveraged big data and artificial intelligence to systematically define the clinical impact of BAT in a cohort of 101,243 patients from a large cancer centre. Our unbiased analyses revealed that, across all diagnoses, cardiovascular and psychiatric diseases were less prevalent in people with BAT. Using a machine learning approach, we semi-automatically quantified BAT activity in approximately 8,700 patients and demonstrated that higher BAT activity, especially in the axillary depot, is associated with lower odds of cardiometabolic diseases and healthier white fat distribution. People with BAT also exhibited more favourable glycaemic parameters, lipid profiles, inflammatory markers and echocardiographic indices. Analysis of medication usage demonstrated that angiotensin receptor blocker use was positively associated with BAT presence. As proof of concept, we showed that the angiotensin receptor blocker losartan increased brown adipocyte activity and whole-body energy expenditure. Altogether, our studies harnessing artificial intelligence and big data identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT and serve as a platform for drug repurposing to activate this tissue in humans.

Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes (T2D), hypertension and cardiovascular disease 2 , 7 . Adipose tissue dysfunction is a hallmark of obesity and contributes to the pathophysiology of cardiometabolic diseases 1 . White adipose tissue (WAT) stores energy as triglyceride 1 in subcutaneous and visceral depots, and visceral adiposity is a key feature of metabolically unhealthy obesity 8 . By contrast, brown adipose tissue (BAT) dissipates energy as heat (thermogenesis) and its activation in animal models protects against obesity and metabolic diseases 3 . However, the relevance of BAT to adult human physiology and whether it can be targeted therapeutically remain unclear 5 , 6 .

Since the landmark reports that adult humans have inducible BAT 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , several clinical studies have aimed to recruit BAT through cold exposure or β-adrenergic agonists 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 . Although these interventions activate BAT and improve glucose homeostasis, their side effects and the small number of participants studied have limited their clinical impact 5 . More recently, our group described the largest reported cohort of people with BAT and demonstrated that the presence of BAT in 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)–computed tomography (CT) (18F-FDG-PET–CT) scans obtained for clinical purposes and without previous stimulation was associated with reduced prevalence of cardiometabolic disease 4 . A caveat from this work is that patients were characterized based on BAT presence or absence, rather than by quantitative BAT metabolic activity. Like WAT, human BAT is localized in distinct anatomic depots 18 , but whether these depots uniquely affect health remains unknown. Moreover, most human BAT studies have focused on cardiometabolic outcomes, but how this tissue influences other organ systems and disease types remains largely unexplored. These limitations have hindered the identification of pharmacologic agents that promote BAT activity, and there are no approved, widely used medications to leverage the cardiometabolic benefits linked to this tissue.

In this study we expanded our cohort to more than 100,000 patients and performed an unbiased, comprehensive analysis across all diagnostic codes to identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT presence. Furthermore, we harnessed artificial intelligence (AI) to semi-automatically quantify total and depot-specific BAT metabolic activity from 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans. This allowed us to investigate associations between specific BAT depots, WAT distribution and cardiometabolic outcomes. Finally, we combined these approaches with medication use analyses to identify pharmacologic regulators of BAT and performed proof-of-concept experiments to validate losartan as an activator of brown adipocytes through a unique, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPARγ)-dependent mechanism.

To discover associations between BAT and diseases beyond the cardiometabolic system, we expanded our previously described cohort (Established BAT Cohort) 4 by reviewing additional FDG-PET–CT scans taken from 2018 to 2024 at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. Of these, 4.4% reported BAT presence and 4,778 patients (7.9%) had at least one scan positive for BAT (hereafter termed BAT positive (BAT + ); Extended Data Fig. 1a ). The remaining patients were designated BAT negative (BAT − ). These newly identified participants were grouped in an Extension BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1a ) that validated findings from our Established BAT Cohort 4 demonstrating lower prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases in people who are BAT + (Extended Data Fig. 1b ). To increase statistical power, we merged the Established and Extension BAT Cohorts to create an Expanded BAT Cohort, consisting of 101,243 patients, of whom 8,897 were BAT + and 92,346 were BAT − . Each patient was assigned an index scan as a reference point for clinical data collection (Extended Data Fig. 1a ). Similar to previous findings 4 , BAT was more prevalent in women in the Expanded BAT Cohort, and its prevalence decreased with age, higher ambient temperature at the time of the scan and increasing body mass index (BMI) (Extended Data Fig. 1c–f ).

Given the influence of these variables on BAT prevalence, we used propensity score matching (PSM) to create a cohort of patients in the BAT + ( n = 8,897) and BAT − ( n = 17,405) groups balanced across age, sex, BMI and ambient temperature (Extended Data Fig. 1g,h ). As patients in our cohort come from a cancer centre, we extracted extensive cancer-associated data (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 ) for each patient in our PSM cohort, including site, stage and treatment. We confirmed that certain cancer sites were more frequent (for example, breast and oral cavity), less frequent (for example, digestive) or had no association (for example, skin, urinary) with BAT presence (Table 1 ). As in our previous report, some cancer treatments were used more frequently in the BAT + group 4 (Table 1 ). Consequently, all cancer-associated variables were controlled for unless otherwise stated for the remainder of this study. We then performed multi-variable logistic regression in this new, expanded PSM cohort and confirmed the association between BAT presence and decreased prevalence of select cardiometabolic diseases 4 (Extended Data Fig. 1i ). Given the sexual dimorphism in BAT presence and cardiometabolic traits, we performed separate analyses in women and men and found that BAT was associated with decreased odds of cardiometabolic diseases in both sexes in our PSM and Extension BAT Cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b ).

To further investigate clinical correlates of BAT we extracted an expanded battery of available laboratory tests and imaging studies from patients in our PSM cohort (Extended Data Fig. 5a ) and performed analyses to identify differences between patients in the BAT + and BAT − groups (Supplementary Table 5 ). Patients with BAT had lower glucose ( P < 0.001), haemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) ( P < 0.001), triglycerides ( P < 0.001) and triglyceride-glucose index, as well as higher high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol (HDL-C) levels ( P < 0.001), even after adjusting for confounders (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 5b ). Paradoxically, patients with BAT also had higher total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). However, remnant cholesterol (total cholesterol − LDL − HDL)—an independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease 23 —was significantly lower in patients with BAT (Extended Data Fig. 5b ). Finally, patients with BAT exhibited lower circulating brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) (Extended Data Fig. 5b ).

To expand on these observations, we used semi-quantitative BAT data from our AI tool to establish associations between continuous clinical parameters and BAT activity. We found an inverse association between total BAT metabolic activity and glucose levels ( P < 0.001), HbA1c ( P = 0.006), systolic blood pressure ( P < 0.001) (Fig. 3b ), mean arterial blood pressure ( P < 0.001) and BNP ( P = 0.01) and a trend with diastolic blood pressure ( P = 0.12) (Extended Data Fig. 5c ). We did not observe statistically significant associations between total BAT activity and lipids (Extended Data Fig. 5c ).

Given the absence of large-scale studies linking BAT status with cardiac imaging in humans, and the association of BAT with higher carotid elasticity in a small prospective study 24 , we extracted available echocardiogram data from patients in our PSM cohort and performed association analyses. In alignment with previous findings 25 , patients with BAT had significantly lower left ventricular mass index ( P < 0.001), left ventricular posterior wall thickness in diastole (LVPWD) ( P < 0.001), relative wall thickness ( P < 0.001) (Fig. 3c ), pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) and mitral valve E/e’ ratio, with no changes in ejection fraction, left atrial volume index and mitral valve E/A ratio (Extended Data Fig. 5d ). Similarly, increasing BAT metabolic activity was associated inversely with PASP ( P < 0.001), LVPWD ( P = 0.01), relative wall thickness ( P < 0.001) (Fig. 3d ), mitral valve E/e’ ratio ( P = 0.002) and positively with mitral valve E/A ratio ( P < 0.001) (Extended Data Fig. 5e ). Other echocardiographic parameters did not exhibit associations with semi-quantitative BAT activity (Extended Data Fig. 5e ). These data demonstrate that BAT presence and activity associate with decreased markers of left ventricular remodelling.

To unravel pharmacologic determinants of BAT presence, we extracted home medication data 1 month before the index scan in patients from our PSM cohort (Extended Data Fig. 6a ). In total, 125 individual medications were assessed for associations with BAT status after exclusions (Extended Data Fig. 6a ). Multi-variable logistic regression analyses identified that 39 of 125 medications exhibited a significant association with BAT status (Supplementary Table 6 ). Given that antibiotics are generally used in short courses, we excluded them from our list of chronic medications (Extended Data Fig. 6b ). However, as modulation of the microbiome by antimicrobials could affect thermogenic fat 27 , we performed a focused analysis on antibiotics and found that trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and several cephalosporins had positive associations with BAT status (Extended Data Fig. 6b ).

Among our 39 candidate medications, we identified agents with known inhibitory effects on human BAT, such as β-blockers 9 , 28 . Specifically, atenolol (OR 0.42; 95% CI 0.27–0.64; P < 0.001) and propranolol (OR 0.38; 95% CI 0.20–0.74; P = 0.02) (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 6c ) exhibited negative associations with BAT presence. Other known negative regulators of BAT, namely, selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs) 29 such as fluoxetine (OR 0.33; 95% CI 0.21–0.51; P < 0.001), escitalopram (OR 0.60; 95% CI 0.48–0.75; P < 0.001) and sertraline (OR 0.57; 95% CI 0.44–0.75; P < 0.001) (Fig. 4a ), were also associated negatively with BAT. Given that people with BAT had a lower prevalence of psychiatric disease, we performed analyses on psychiatric medications controlling for relevant psychiatric diagnoses (Supplementary Table 7 ), and demonstrated that SSRIs retain their negative association with BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6d ). Among medications shown previously to activate BAT, we found that dexamethasone 30 was associated positively with BAT presence (OR 1.22; 95% CI 1.10–1.36; P = 0.001; Fig. 4a ). Mirabegron—a β3-adrenergic agonist that promotes BAT activity in humans 13 , 31 , 32 —also showed a trend towards being associated with BAT positivity (Extended Data Fig. 6e ). β2-adrenergic agonists (for example, inhaled salbutamol), which could promote BAT activity in humans 33 , 34 , did not show a significant association (Supplementary Table 6 ). These findings demonstrate that our platform can identify most known modulators of human BAT and could uncover new pharmacological regulators of this tissue.

To further assess the effects of losartan on whole-body energy expenditure, indirect calorimetry was performed in wild-type mice pre-treated with losartan in their drinking water for 10 days at room temperature (Extended Data Fig. 9a ). Losartan-treated mice exhibited increased energy expenditure, O 2 consumption and CO 2 production, with no changes to their respiratory exchange ratio (RER), physical activity, food intake, body weight, fat mass or lean mass (Extended Data Fig. 9a–l ). To examine the effects of losartan on cold stress, we pre-treated a separate cohort of wild-type mice at room temperature as above and performed indirect calorimetry at 4 °C (Extended Data Fig. 10a ). Upon cold-induced BAT activation, losartan-treated mice again exhibited increased energy expenditure, O 2 consumption and CO 2 production, with no changes in RER (Fig. 4j,k and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e ). This was independent of body weight, as assayed by analysis of covariance (Fig. 4l ). There were no differences in locomotor activity and a trend towards increased food intake in losartan-treated mice (Extended Data Fig. 10f–h ), which probably explains why body weight did not change (Extended Data Fig. 10i ). Moreover, exposing mice treated with losartan to cold resulted in significantly increased BAT Ucp1 (Fig. 4m ), as well as smaller lipid droplets in brown adipocytes (Fig. 4n ). We observed similar histologic findings in inguinal fat; however, there was no statistically significant increase in Ucp1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 10j,k ). Taken together, these data indicate that losartan treatment results in enhanced BAT activation and increased whole-body energy expenditure.

Despite substantial advances, the therapeutic potential for targeting BAT to manage metabolic disease remains preliminary 5 , 6 . This retrospective study explored associations between BAT and human health in the largest cohort reported so far. We validated the strong link between BAT and cardiovascular diseases, while uncovering a previously undescribed association with psychiatric diseases. Our new machine learning approach allowed us to quantify depot-specific BAT metabolic activity rapidly and establish that the degree of BAT activity is linked to cardiometabolic health and healthier fat distribution. Finally, medication usage analysis uncovered a positive association between ARB use and BAT presence. Proof-of-concept in vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that losartan activates brown adipocytes and promotes whole-body energy expenditure, demonstrating that our systems approach can identify pharmacologic agents that could be repurposed to activate BAT.

Numerous studies in mice have shown that BAT activation protects against obesity and hyperglycaemia through increased energy expenditure, clearance of circulating substrates and secretion of beneficial hormones and metabolites 40 , 41 , 42 . In humans, cold exposure and β-adrenergic agonists increase BAT metabolic activity, which correlates with improved glucose homeostasis 13 , 14 . Our study confirms that, among all diagnoses, BAT is associated primarily with decreased prevalence of cardiovascular diseases, improved glycaemic, lipid and inflammatory profiles, and evidence of decreased pathological cardiac remodelling. Our large-scale, depot-specific analysis allowed us to identify axillary BAT as being linked most strongly with beneficial metabolic outcomes and healthier WAT distribution. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of thermogenic adipose tissues in humans and the importance of dissecting their cellular and molecular characteristics 20 , 21 , 22 .

AI tools such as ours will allow other groups to analyse BAT semi-quantitatively in their cohorts and expand these findings to other populations worldwide. This approach continues to rely on BAT glucose uptake on 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans, which may or may not correlate with BAT temperature and thermogenic capacity 43 , 44 , and could be influenced significantly by insulin resistance 45 . To this point, we found that insulin-sensitizing medications such as metformin 46 were associated negatively with BAT presence (adjusting for diabetes status), and medications like olanzapine 47 , which promote insulin resistance, were linked positively to BAT. This indicates that the clinical findings in our study cannot be explained simply by altered insulin sensitivity.

Beyond metabolic diseases, BAT presence was associated with a lower prevalence of anxiety and depression. This could be explained by studies linking healthier metabolic profiles and decreased visceral adiposity to lower rates of psychiatric disease 48 , 49 , 50 . Small studies have linked cold exposure—a known activator of BAT—to improved mental health 51 , 52 . Furthermore, BAT prevalence decreased with SSRI use, confirming findings from a recent, prospective human study 29 . Future studies focused on how BAT affects mood and behaviour, and the role of anti-depressants in this crosstalk are warranted. BAT presence was associated with lower prevalence of liver disease and improved hepatic function, consistent with previous studies 53 , 54 . Conversely, patients in the BAT + group showed a trend towards higher prevalence of osteoporosis and decreased lumbar bone mineral density, contrasting with previous reports linking cold-activated BAT with higher bone mineral density 55 . Although mouse studies suggest an endocrine connection between brown fat and bone 56 , we cannot rule out that the observed association is specific to our cancer-centre-based cohort. Future trials on human BAT therapeutics should include assessment of bone health.

Our study uses a reverse translational approach, starting with a large human dataset that informs proof-of-concept experiments, to bridge the gap between predominantly mouse-based discoveries and human brown fat biology. Through this platform, we identified several ARBs that are associated positively with BAT and demonstrate that the medication used most widely in this family, losartan, directly activates brown adipocytes through PPARγ, independently of AT1R signalling. In vivo treatment with losartan at baseline and during a cold challenge resulted in increased whole-body energy expenditure. By contrast, a previous report described a role for losartan in beiging of white fat through AT1R-dependent apelin secretion 57 . Compared with losartan, its inactive metabolite EXP3179 exhibits higher PPARγ agonism in vitro, and it probably mediates most of the effects of losartan on BAT in vivo. In humans, chronic treatment with losartan resulted in increased serum levels of EXP3179 with a peak 2 h after treatment, and increased expression of PPARγ gene targets in circulating monocytes 37 . Treatment with ARBs has been associated with reductions in newly diagnosed diabetes 58 , which could be linked to its effects on brown fat.

Our study has several limitations. First, its retrospective design highlights the need for large prospective studies; however, we controlled for several clinical confounders and validated the association of losartan with BAT experimentally. Second, 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans were obtained without previous cold exposure, potentially underestimating BAT prevalence. Third, our convenience cohort was derived from a cancer centre and, despite controlling extensively for cancer-related variables, we cannot exclude effects from tumour types or cancer therapies. For instance, BAT is linked to higher breast cancer prevalence, lower odds of gastrointestinal malignancies and higher usage of cancer treatments such as mitotic inhibitors. Studies in mice have suggested activation of BAT reduces cancer progression by decreasing available circulating glucose for tumour metabolism 59 . To our knowledge, there is no literature demonstrating direct effects of mitotic inhibitors or other cancer therapies on brown adipocytes, and future studies of these associations are warranted. Until a reliable biomarker or non-invasive test for BAT is established, a large, prospective study involving 18F-FDG-PET–CT in the non-oncologic setting is highly implausible. At present, a large PSM cohort is the most feasible approach to assess BAT and clinical phenotypes comprehensively in humans.

In conclusion, we describe new associations between BAT and clinical outcomes through big data and AI-based analyses. Our systems-approach provides a resource for the field and can be extended to study other regulators of BAT such as genetics. Finally, our proof-of-concept studies demonstrate that losartan activates brown adipocytes through a PPARγ dependent mechanism, raising the possibility that this agent could be repurposed to activate BAT in humans.

This retrospective case–control study followed institutional guidelines and was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK), protocol number 17-581. The requirement for informed consent was waived because the study involved secondary analysis of previously acquired PET–CT imaging and clinical data, posed no more than minimal risk to participants and could not be conducted practically with individual informed consent. All patient data were deidentified before use.

We previously established a cohort of patients with BAT by analysing 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans performed at MSK from June 2009 through March 2018 4 . Patients who were positive for BAT in at least one scan were termed BAT + , whereas the remaining patients were grouped as BAT − . To expand this cohort, we established a new Extension BAT Cohort by following a similar strategy. We reviewed all 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans performed at MSK from patients aged 18 years and above from April 2018 through July 2024. People who were positive for BAT on at least one scan were termed BAT + , whereas the remaining patients were grouped as BAT − (Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 2 ). For each patient in both groups, an index scan was designated: in patients with BAT reported on at least one 18F-FDG-PET–CT scan, the first scan that reported BAT was defined as the index scan. In patients without BAT on any scan, the first 18F-FDG-PET–CT scan served as the index scan. We collected demographic, BMI, outside temperature data and pertinent ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes corresponding to cardiometabolic diseases 4 (1 year after the index scan) (Supplementary Table 8 ) from the institutional EHR. Average outdoor temperatures in New York City were obtained from the US National Weather Service. An initial logistic regression analysis was performed on patients in the BAT + versus BAT − groups who belonged exclusively to the Extension BAT Cohort to establish associations between BAT presence and cardiometabolic diseases. As the association of BAT presence with reduced prevalence of cardiometabolic disease was confirmed in the Extension BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1b ), we proceeded to merge the Established BAT Cohort with the Extension BAT Cohort to create an Expanded BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1a ). If a patient was present in both cohorts, data from the Established BAT Cohort were used.

We collected pertinent clinical data for each patient as described previously 4 . In brief, for cancer site, we included the specific cancer diagnostic code (ICD-0) listed closest to the index scan date (Supplementary Table 1 ). Data referring to cancer treatment were collected if administered within 90 days before the index scan and classified as previously 4 (Supplementary Table 2 ). Pertinent ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes corresponding to cardiometabolic diseases 4 (Supplementary Table 8 ) and all other codes were extracted up to 1 year after the index scan in patients from our PSM cohort. Codes were selected to represent non-paediatric, non-obstetric, adult disorders as explained below.

For laboratory values, clinical indices and imaging studies, we extracted available data up to 1 year after the index scan in our PSM cohort. Analyses were performed in BAT + and BAT − patients with available values. To identify individual pharmacological agents associated with BAT presence, we extracted medications in the home medication list and/or medications with an active pharmacy prescription in the EHR from each patient belonging to our PSM cohort. We included only medications listed up to 1 month before the index scan for each patient. We excluded pharmacological agents with unlikely systemic effects, such as those with topical, ophthalmic, nasal and otic administration. Antimicrobials were excluded as they are generally prescribed in short courses. Medications classified as ‘as needed’ and herbal supplements were excluded. Medications with low frequency counts (present in fewer than 40 patients) were excluded. A final list of medications included in the analyses can be found in Supplementary Table 9 . These medications were also grouped by general categories as described in Supplementary Table 9 .

To explore unbiased associations between BAT and other diseases, we extracted from the EHR diagnostic codes (ICD-9 and ICD-10) listed up to 1 year after the index scan from patients belonging to our PSM cohort. To select the codes for extraction, we grouped ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes based on their first three letters and/or digits. ICD-10 codes belonging to general groupings: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N and R were included as they group the medical pathologies most likely to be found in a non-paediatric, non-obstetric, adult cancer population. A similar rationale was used for the selection of ICD-9 codes. A total of 1,157 ICD-10 codes and 626 ICD-9 codes were queried for extraction from the EHR.
The association between BAT and age, BMI and temperature was assessed by a Pearson’s correlation coefficient. Prevalence of BAT in men and women was compared using a chi-squared test.

To assess whether BAT status was a predictor of cardiometabolic diseases in the PSM cohort, we used multi-variable logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, BMI, ambient temperature, self-reported race and ethnicity, smoking history, family history of cardiovascular disease, cancer site, cancer stage, cancer treatment and general groups of outpatient medications. BAT metabolic activity (total and depot-specific) was calculated as the product of SUV mean and BAT volume (in millilitres) and stratified into tertiles. The association of BAT activity with cardiometabolic diseases was assessed using a multi-variable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, BMI and outdoor temperature with patients in the BAT − group or those in tertile 1 (lowest BAT metabolic activity) as reference. The correlation of BAT activity with age and outside temperature was calculated with Pearson correlation coefficient after logarithmic transformation. The association of BAT activity with SAT area, VAT area, SAT to VAT ratio and other continuous clinical variables was calculated with linear regression after logarithmic transformation.

The association of BAT status and an expanded set of 511 ICD codes was assessed by univariable logistic regression to identify crude associations. ICD codes associated significantly with BAT were then analysed individually through multi-variable logistic regression analysis adjusting for age, sex, BMI, ambient temperature, self-reported race and ethnicity, smoking history, family history of cardiovascular disease, cancer site, cancer stage, cancer treatment and general groups of outpatient medications. For over-representation analysis, the 511 codes were grouped by organ system. Enrichment for each organ system category was calculated based on the proportion of BAT-associated ICD codes divided by the corresponding proportion among all diagnostic codes in the category set. Statistical significance of over-representation was assessed using Fisher’s exact test and Benjamini–Hochberg FDR was used for multiple test adjustments.

Unpaired t -tests were used to compare laboratory values, imaging studies and clinical indices in patients in the BAT + versus BAT − groups. Variance equality was assessed with an F -test. When variances were equal, standard t -tests assuming equal variances were used; otherwise, t -tests with unequal variance adjustments were applied. For adjusted analyses, GLMs were used to estimate least square means, adjusting for age, sex, BMI, self-reported race and ethnicity, ambient temperature, cancer site, cancer stage and cancer treatment. Post hoc pairwise comparisons were performed using Tukey’s HSD method. Categorical variables were compared using Fisher’s exact test.

Associations between BAT and individual medications were assessed through multi-variable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, BMI, temperature, ethnicity, race, smoking history, family history of cardiovascular disease, cancer sites, cancer stage, cancer treatment and cardiovascular diagnoses. For in vitro and in vivo proof-of-concept experiments, group comparisons were conducted using unpaired t -tests. To account for multiple comparisons, P values were corrected using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR method, and adjusted P values are reported as such where applicable. Metabolic cage data were analysed, and statistical significance was calculated either using two-way analysis of variance for hourly data or unpaired t -test for 24-h cumulative, light and dark cycle. All analyses were performed using SAS (v.9.4), R software (v.4.5.1) and GraphPad Prism (v.10.5.0). All reported P values are two-sided and statistical significance was defined as α < 0.05.

relevantPassages.text: Here we leveraged big data and artificial intelligence to systematically define the clinical impact of BAT in a cohort of 101,243 patients from a large cancer centre.

Our study uses a reverse translational approach, starting with a large human dataset that informs proof-of-concept experiments, to bridge the gap between predominantly mouse-based discoveries and human brown fat biology.
At present, a large PSM cohort is the most feasible approach to assess BAT and clinical phenotypes comprehensively in humans.

Since the landmark reports that adult humans have inducible BAT 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , several clinical studies have aimed to recruit BAT through cold exposure or β-adrenergic agonists 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 .
